Name: belief_source_tags
Title: Where Did You Hear That? Probing and Steering the Provenance of LLM Beliefs
Short Hypothesis: LLMs internally track not only whether they hold a belief about an item's state, but also the epistemic *source* of that belief (pretraining prior vs. in-context assertion vs. tool/retrieval evidence), and this provenance signal is linearly decodable and causally steerable — separately from the truth-value direction. This distinguishes belief-provenance from belief-truth, which prior work conflates.
Related Work: Prior work shows LLMs linearly represent belief/truth directions (Azaria & Mitchell 2023; Truth-value judgment 2024), belief-state geometry (Transformers represent belief state geometry 2024), agents' beliefs in ToM (Language Models Represent Beliefs of Self and Others 2024; Lookbacks 2025), and world states (Propositional Probes 2024). Critically, the paper 'Language models cannot reliably distinguish belief from knowledge and fact' shows models conflate epistemic categories in their *outputs*. Existing probing work asks 'does the model believe X is true?' but not 'why/from where does it believe X?'. We introduce the orthogonal axis of belief PROVENANCE (prior vs. in-context vs. external evidence) as an internal, decodable, steerable variable. This is not a trivial extension: it reframes the belief-knowledge-fact confusion as a possibly-recoverable internal signal, and offers a mechanistic handle on sycophancy, context-vs-prior conflicts, and RAG faithfulness.
Abstract: Large language models represent beliefs about the states of items, and prior interpretability work has isolated linear 'truth-value' directions. But a belief has not only a truth-value, it also has a provenance: the model may hold it because of its pretraining prior, because it was asserted in context, or because it came from retrieved/tool evidence. We hypothesize that LLMs internally tag beliefs with their epistemic source, and that this provenance signal is (i) linearly decodable from residual-stream activations, (ii) largely orthogonal to the truth-value direction, and (iii) causally steerable. We construct a controlled dataset of item-state claims where we independently vary claim truth and claim source (prior-consistent, prior-contradicting-in-context, and retrieval-attributed), including matched cases where the same proposition arrives from different sources. We train linear probes to decode source and truth on frozen open-weight models (Llama-3, Qwen2.5, Gemma-2, Pythia), measure their geometric relationship (subspace angles, joint vs. separate decodability), and localize the responsible attention heads via activation patching. We then test causal control: does steering along the provenance direction change downstream behavior such as sycophancy (adopting user-asserted false claims), citation of sources, and answers under prior-vs-context conflict? We evaluate with probe accuracy, subspace overlap, patching effect sizes, and behavioral metrics (sycophancy rate, context-adherence, source-attribution accuracy). If confirmed, provenance-aware probing offers a practical monitor and controller for RAG faithfulness and sycophancy, and shows that the belief/knowledge/fact confusion in outputs may coexist with a recoverable internal provenance signal.
Experiments: 1) Dataset construction: Generate ~5k item-state propositions (e.g., 'The capital of Country X is Y', synthetic entity-attribute facts to control priors). For each, create matched contexts under three provenance conditions: (a) prior-only (no context, relying on pretraining), (b) in-context assertion (a sentence states the claim), (c) retrieval-attributed (claim embedded in a quoted 'document'/tool output). Cross with true/false labels, plus a prior-vs-context conflict subset where context contradicts the pretraining prior. 2) Probing: Extract residual-stream and per-head activations at the item/state token across layers for open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Pythia-2.8B). Train logistic-regression probes for (i) truth-value and (ii) 3-way source. Report accuracy per layer with control tasks (shuffled labels) to rule out spurious structure. 3) Geometry: Compute cosine/subspace angle between truth and source probe directions; test whether source is decodable after projecting out the truth direction (and vice versa) to establish orthogonality. 4) Localization: Use activation patching / causal mediation to find heads carrying the source signal; compare with heads known to carry belief/truth (from prior work). 5) Causal steering: Add/subtract the source direction (contrastive activation addition) at inference and measure behavioral changes: sycophancy rate on user-asserted false claims, context-adherence under prior-vs-context conflict, and source-attribution accuracy when asked 'where did you learn this?'. 6) Generalization: Test transfer of probes/steering vectors to held-out item domains and to naturalistic RAG-style prompts. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, subspace angle, patching effect size (logit difference), sycophancy rate, context-adherence rate, attribution accuracy.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Provenance may be entangled with surface cues (e.g., quotation marks) rather than an abstract epistemic representation; we mitigate with matched-proposition controls and paraphrase/format perturbations. The three-way source distinction may not be cleanly linearly separable, or may be layer/model-specific. Steering could induce off-manifold degradation of fluency (as noted in belief-manifold work); we monitor perplexity and use small steering magnitudes. Truth and source directions may be less orthogonal than hypothesized, in which case the finding becomes a characterization of their entanglement (still informative). Synthetic facts may not fully reflect real pretraining priors; we complement with well-known real facts. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: belief_entrenchment_probing
Title: Frozen Minds: Probing and Unfreezing Internal Belief Entrenchment During LLM Reasoning
Short Hypothesis: As an LLM generates a multi-step reasoning trace, its internal belief about the answer to an item becomes progressively 'entrenched': the linearly-decodable belief representation stops updating in response to new evidence introduced later in the trace, even when that evidence should rationally shift it. This internal entrenchment is measurable per-step, precedes and predicts behavioral confirmation bias, and can be causally reduced by steering the residual stream to restore belief plasticity, improving truth-seeking on evidence-integration tasks.
Related Work: Prior work establishes that transformers linearly represent belief states (Transformers Represent Belief State Geometry, 2024; Constrained Belief Updates, 2025) and that a 'solvability belief' axis is decodable but causally inert for execution (Confidence is Not Competence, 2025). Behaviorally, the Martingale Score (2025) shows LLM reasoning violates Bayesian martingale updating (belief entrenchment) at the output level, and Confirmation Bias in CoT (2025) shows prior beliefs skew reasoning. The Hypocrisy Gap (2026) contrasts a static internal belief with the CoT text. NONE of these track the trajectory of the internal belief representation itself across reasoning steps, characterize *when/where* it freezes relative to evidence arrival, or test a causal intervention to restore plasticity. We reframe entrenchment as an internal, per-step representational dynamics phenomenon and ask whether it is a causally editable failure mode, distinguishing our proposal from behavioral (Martingale) and static-belief (Hypocrisy Gap) approaches.
Abstract: When a language model reasons step-by-step, its final answer often confirms a hypothesis formed early, even when later steps surface contradicting evidence, a behavior known as confirmation bias or belief entrenchment. Prior studies measure this behaviorally or contrast a single static internal belief against the reasoning text. We instead track the internal belief representation itself as it evolves across reasoning steps. We hypothesize that entrenchment is a representational dynamics phenomenon: an LLM's linearly-decodable belief about an item's answer initially updates with incoming evidence but then 'freezes,' becoming insensitive to later, decision-relevant evidence. We construct controlled evidence-integration tasks in which pieces of evidence pointing toward different answers are revealed in a specified order within the prompt or generated trace, so that the rationally-updated belief has a known ground-truth trajectory. We train linear belief probes on frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and a reasoning-tuned R1-distilled model) and measure, at each step, (i) the probe belief, (ii) its agreement with the rational Bayesian trajectory, and (iii) a per-step plasticity score (belief change per unit of new evidence). We test whether plasticity decays over the trace, whether an early-freezing signature predicts final-answer errors, and whether it correlates with behavioral entrenchment metrics like the Martingale Score. Finally, we identify the layers/heads mediating freezing via activation patching and test a causal 'unfreezing' intervention: injecting a plasticity direction (contrastive activation addition derived from high- vs. low-plasticity steps) to restore late-evidence sensitivity. We evaluate with probe/rational-agreement curves, plasticity decay slopes, entrenchment-error AUROC, patching effect sizes, and post-intervention accuracy and fluency.
Experiments: 1) Task/dataset construction: Build ~4k evidence-integration items where the answer depends on integrating an ordered sequence of evidence pieces (e.g., multi-clue whodunit/deduction puzzles, sequential-evidence forecasting, updating-a-diagnosis medical vignettes, and synthetic entity-attribute tasks with revealed clues). Crucially, insert a controlled 'late reversal' condition where early evidence favors answer A but decisive later evidence favors B, so the rational belief trajectory (computable via an oracle/explicit Bayesian model on the synthetic sets) is known. Include a matched 'consistent' condition (no reversal) as control. 2) Belief probing over reasoning steps: For open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B), generate CoT traces and, at each reasoning-step boundary (and at each evidence-token position for prompt-injected evidence), extract residual-stream activations. Train logistic-regression belief probes (predicting P(answer=A)) on held-out data with control tasks (shuffled labels) to rule out spurious structure. Record the probe belief trajectory. 3) Entrenchment metrics: Define per-step plasticity = |Delta probe-belief| per unit of rational-belief change expected at that step; measure the decay slope of plasticity across the trace; measure 'rational-agreement' = correlation between probe trajectory and oracle Bayesian trajectory, especially post-reversal. Compare reversal vs. consistent conditions. 4) Predictiveness: Test whether an early-freezing signature (low late-step plasticity) predicts final-answer error using AUROC; compare against a log-prob confidence baseline and against the behavioral Martingale Score computed on the same runs. 5) Localization: Use activation patching / causal mediation to find layers and heads whose late-step states carry stale (pre-reversal) belief; contrast heads that do vs. don't update after the reversal. 6) Causal unfreezing intervention: Build a 'plasticity' steering direction via contrastive activation addition from high-plasticity vs. low-plasticity step activations; inject it at inference during late steps and measure (a) restored late-evidence sensitivity (probe follows oracle after reversal), (b) final-answer accuracy on reversal items, (c) collateral effects on consistent items and on general benchmarks (GSM8K, MMLU subset), and (d) fluency/perplexity to check for off-manifold degradation. 7) Generalization: Test probe and steering-vector transfer across task domains and to naturalistic RAG-style prompts. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, plasticity decay slope, rational-agreement correlation, entrenchment-error AUROC, patching logit-difference effect sizes, post-intervention accuracy delta, perplexity delta.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Belief 'freezing' may reflect that the model simply cannot parse late evidence rather than an entrenchment failure; the matched consistent/reversal design and evidence-comprehension checks help disentangle these. The internal belief may not be cleanly linearly decodable at every step, or may be distributed across layers, complicating per-step trajectories; we use multi-layer probes and report layerwise results. The plasticity steering direction could degrade fluency or overshoot (making the model unstable/gullible to any late text); we monitor perplexity, use small magnitudes, and evaluate on consistent-condition and general benchmarks. Oracle Bayesian trajectories are only exact on synthetic sets; naturalistic items rely on approximate rational baselines. Reasoning-tuned models may show qualitatively different dynamics than base models, which is itself an interesting comparison but limits universal claims. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: belief_binding_conflict
Title: One Fact, Many Faces: Do LLMs Bind Beliefs to Meaning or to Surface Form?
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM is told a fact and then queried about it, the internal belief it updates is bound to a surface-form-specific representation rather than a canonical meaning-level slot; consequently, two surface variants of the same proposition carve out *distinct* internal belief tokens that can be independently, and even contradictorily, updated. We hypothesize this 'belief binding' is localizable and that a single mechanism explains both cross-paraphrase inconsistency and the ability to hold contradictory beliefs about the same fact under different phrasings.
Related Work: Prior work shows truthfulness/belief directions are brittle to paraphrase and OOD surface form (Brittle Minds 2024; Representational Stability of Truth 2025; LLM Knowledge is Brittle 2025), that factual knowledge is cross-lingually inconsistent with a middle/final-layer bottleneck (Cross-Lingual Consistency 2025; Lost in Multilinguality 2025), and that PLMs lack factual coherency (Queen of England 2024). Belief directions are context-sensitive causal mediators (Truth-value judgment 2024). All of these *characterize* brittleness as a defect. Our proposal is different: we treat surface-form dependence as evidence of a specific mechanism—that beliefs are *bound* to form-specific internal handles rather than a shared meaning slot—and we directly test this by injecting a fact in form A and reading/steering the belief in form B, measuring belief transfer as a function of representational binding. We introduce a controllable 'belief-binding' probe and a causal test of whether a single fact occupies one slot or many, which prior descriptive work does not do.
Abstract: Large language models can be told a fact and later answer questions about it, but they are notoriously inconsistent: rephrase the query and the answer, and the model's confidence, can flip. Prior work documents this brittleness as a failure of robust knowledge. We reframe it mechanistically: we hypothesize that when an LLM ingests a novel fact stated in a particular surface form, it updates an internal belief that is *bound to that form* rather than to a canonical meaning-level representation. Under this view, two paraphrases of the same proposition instantiate two distinct internal belief handles that can be updated—and even contradicted—independently. We test this with a controlled in-context belief-injection paradigm. We construct synthetic facts (novel entity-attribute pairs, unlikely to be in pretraining) rendered in matched surface variants (paraphrases, syntactic reorderings, and translations). We inject a fact in form A and then probe the internal belief when the model reads the same proposition in form B, quantifying cross-form belief transfer with linear belief probes on frozen open-weight models (Llama-3, Qwen2.5, Gemma-2). We predict transfer is high within form and degrades systematically with surface distance, tracing a layerwise 'binding site' where form-specific and meaning-level representations converge. We then perform the critical causal test: inject *contradictory* facts under two forms and measure whether the model maintains two coexisting internal beliefs (form-bound) or resolves them (meaning-bound), and whether steering along a 'form-invariance' direction (derived contrastively from high- vs. low-transfer pairs) increases cross-form belief consistency without harming fluency. Metrics: cross-form transfer curves, layerwise binding-site localization via activation patching, contradiction-coexistence rate, post-steering consistency gains, and perplexity.
Experiments: 1) Dataset: Generate ~4k novel synthetic facts (invented entities with attributes, e.g., 'Zorblax-9 orbits the star Kelvath') to control for pretraining priors. For each fact, produce matched surface variants: (a) near-paraphrase, (b) syntactic reordering (active/passive, subject/object swap of a symmetric-looking relation), (c) lexical substitution, (d) translation into 2 languages. Include true/false polarity and a control set of well-known real facts. 2) Belief probes: On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B), extract residual-stream activations at the attribute/answer token and train linear belief probes (P(fact holds)) with shuffled-label control tasks. 3) Cross-form belief injection: Present a fact in form A in context, then read the internal belief for the same proposition presented in form B (query). Measure cross-form transfer = probe belief in B given A-injection, minus baseline. Build a transfer matrix across all form pairs and correlate transfer with surface-distance metrics (edit distance, embedding cosine). 4) Binding-site localization: Use activation patching to find the layer(s) where a fact injected in form A begins to influence the form-B representation (patch A-context activations into a B-only run; find minimal set restoring belief). Compare early (form-specific) vs. later (meaning-level) convergence, mapping the 'binding site'. 5) Contradiction test (critical): Inject contradictory facts under two forms (A asserts, B negates) and measure whether internal beliefs coexist (both probes read their injected value → form-bound) or collapse to one (→ meaning-bound); report a contradiction-coexistence rate per layer and behaviorally via direct queries. 6) Form-invariance steering: Derive a steering direction via contrastive activation addition from high-transfer vs. low-transfer form pairs; apply during B-query and measure (a) increased cross-form belief consistency, (b) contradiction resolution, (c) collateral effects on unrelated facts and general benchmarks (MMLU subset), (d) perplexity. 7) Generalization: Test transfer of probes and steering vectors across fact domains and to real-fact and cross-lingual subsets. Metrics: cross-form transfer curves and matrices, surface-distance correlations, patching effect sizes / binding-site layer, contradiction-coexistence rate, post-steering consistency delta, perplexity delta.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Cross-form transfer failures could reflect comprehension failures rather than form-bound belief storage; we include comprehension checks and use matched real-fact controls. Synthetic entities may be represented differently from real knowledge; we complement with real-fact subsets. Linear belief probes may not cleanly capture the belief at every layer; we report layerwise results and use control tasks. The 'binding site' may be distributed rather than a discrete layer, weakening the clean localization story (still informative as a gradient). Form-invariance steering may degrade fluency or overwrite legitimate distinctions (e.g., subject/object asymmetric relations); we monitor perplexity, use small magnitudes, and separately analyze symmetric vs. asymmetric relations. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: suppositional_belief_gating
Title: Suppose It Were True: Do LLMs Internally Flag Entertained Beliefs Apart from Endorsed Ones?
Short Hypothesis: LLMs maintain an internal 'endorsement' (factivity) flag that distinguishes belief content the model merely *entertains* under a supposition ('suppose X were true...') from content it *endorses* as actually true, and this flag is linearly decodable, largely orthogonal to the truth-value direction, and causally gates whether supposed-but-false content leaks into the model's factual assertions. This targets the actual-vs-hypothetical distinction that output-level studies show LLMs conflate.
Related Work: Prior work isolates linear truth-value/belief directions (Azaria & Mitchell 2023; Truth-value judgment: belief directions are context sensitive 2024), belief-state geometry (Transformers represent belief state geometry 2024; Shape of Beliefs 2026), ToM belief tracking of self/others via lookbacks and attention heads (Language Models Represent Beliefs of Self and Others 2024; Lookbacks 2025; Brittle Minds 2024), and in-context counterfactual reasoning where a latent concept is linearly encoded with 'noise-abduction' heads (Counterfactual reasoning: in-context emergence 2025). The paper 'Language models cannot reliably distinguish belief from knowledge and fact' shows LLMs conflate epistemic categories at the OUTPUT level. None of these ask whether an LLM internally tags belief content by its *endorsement status* (entertained-under-supposition vs. endorsed-as-actual), nor whether such a flag causally gates leakage of hypothetical content into factual answers. We introduce this factivity/endorsement axis as an internal, decodable, and steerable variable orthogonal to truth-value, and connect it to a concrete failure mode: suppositional content contaminating factual assertions.
Abstract: When we say 'suppose the moon were made of cheese, then...', we entertain a claim without believing it; humans robustly separate such supposed content from what they endorse as actually true. Large language models routinely reason under suppositions (counterfactuals, role-play, adversarial premises), yet output-level studies show they conflate belief, knowledge, and fact. We ask a sharper, mechanistic question: does an LLM internally tag belief content by its endorsement status, distinguishing content it merely entertains under a supposition from content it endorses as factual? We hypothesize such an 'endorsement' (factivity) flag is (i) linearly decodable from residual-stream activations, (ii) largely orthogonal to the well-studied truth-value direction, and (iii) causally gates whether supposed-but-false content leaks into subsequent factual assertions. We build a controlled dataset of item-state claims embedded in matched frames that vary endorsement (asserted-as-fact vs. entertained-under-supposition such as 'suppose', 'imagine', 'in a story where', 'pretend') while holding proposition content and truth constant, plus a critical leakage probe that asks a factual question after a supposition. We train linear probes on frozen open-weight models (Llama-3, Qwen2.5, Gemma-2, Pythia) to decode endorsement vs. truth, measure their geometric relationship, and localize the responsible heads via activation patching, comparing to known truth/belief heads. We then test causal gating: steering along the endorsement direction should modulate whether supposed content contaminates factual answers. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, subspace angle, projected-out decodability, patching effect sizes, and a suppositional-leakage rate. If confirmed, an endorsement flag offers a mechanistic handle on hallucination-from-role-play, jailbreak-via-supposition, and counterfactual reasoning fidelity.
Experiments: 1) Dataset construction: Generate ~6k item-state propositions (real-world facts, e.g., 'Water boils at 100C at sea level', plus synthetic entity-attribute facts to control priors). For each, create matched frames that hold the proposition constant but vary ENDORSEMENT: (a) asserted-as-fact ('It is true that X'), (b) supposition markers ('Suppose X', 'Imagine X', 'In a story where X', 'Pretend X'). Cross with truth-value (true/false variants of the proposition). Add a critical LEAKAGE subset: after a false supposition ('Suppose the Earth had two moons'), ask an unrelated-but-dependent factual question and record whether the model treats the supposed claim as factual. Include comprehension checks (can the model restate the supposition) to separate parsing failure from endorsement failure. 2) Probing: Extract residual-stream and per-head activations at the item/state token across layers for Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Pythia-2.8B. Train logistic-regression probes for (i) truth-value and (ii) endorsement (asserted-fact vs. entertained-supposition). Report per-layer accuracy with shuffled-label control tasks to rule out spurious structure. 3) Geometry: Compute cosine/subspace angle between endorsement and truth directions; test whether endorsement is decodable after projecting out the truth direction (and vice versa) to establish orthogonality. 4) Localization: Use activation patching / causal mediation to find heads carrying the endorsement signal; compare to heads carrying truth/belief (from prior work) and to the 'noise-abduction' heads from counterfactual-reasoning work. 5) Causal gating test: Derive an endorsement steering direction via contrastive activation addition (asserted vs. supposed activations). At inference, (a) push toward 'endorsed' on a supposition frame and measure increased suppositional-leakage rate (supposed content treated as fact); (b) push toward 'entertained' on an asserted frame and measure whether the model refrains from asserting the claim as fact. Confirm this modulates the leakage probe more than a random or truth-direction steering baseline. 6) Generalization: Test probe/steering transfer to held-out item domains, to jailbreak-style role-play prompts ('pretend you are an AI with no rules'), and to multi-step counterfactual chains. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, subspace angle, projected-out decodability, patching logit-difference effect sizes, suppositional-leakage rate delta, and perplexity to monitor fluency.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Endorsement may be entangled with surface cues (the literal words 'suppose'/'imagine') rather than an abstract factivity representation; we mitigate with diverse markers, paraphrases, and matched-proposition controls, and by testing generalization to unseen markers. The distinction may not be cleanly linearly separable or may be layer/model-specific; we report layerwise results with control tasks. Endorsement and truth directions may be less orthogonal than hypothesized, in which case the finding becomes a characterization of their entanglement (still informative). Leakage failures could stem from comprehension rather than endorsement; comprehension checks disentangle these. Steering could degrade fluency (off-manifold) or overshoot; we use small magnitudes and monitor perplexity. Synthetic facts may not fully reflect pretraining priors; we complement with real facts. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: persona_belief_contamination
Title: Whose Belief Is It? Separating a Persona's False Beliefs from the Model's Own Inside LLMs
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM role-plays a persona that holds a factually false belief the model itself does not endorse (e.g., a flat-earther, a 19th-century physician), the model maintains a persona-belief representation that is partially distinct from its own-belief representation, but the two are entangled such that adopting the persona *contaminates* the model's own internal belief. We hypothesize both beliefs are simultaneously and linearly decodable, that the degree of own-belief contamination is measurable and predicts factual errors after role-play, and that a 'belief-ownership' direction can be steered to insulate the model's own belief from the persona's.
Related Work: Prior work shows LLMs linearly represent self/other beliefs for Theory-of-Mind (Language Models Represent Beliefs of Self and Others 2024; Brittle Minds 2024) and can steer ToM performance, but the 'self' and 'other' beliefs there are ordinary beliefs either agent could hold about a story world, not cases where the persona holds a belief the model *knows to be factually false about the real world*. Persona work (Assistant Axis 2026; Persona Selection Model 2026) shows a persona/Assistant direction governs behavior and 'persona drift', and self-recognition work isolates a 'self' vector, but neither tracks whether adopting a false-believing persona corrupts the model's own factual belief representation. Neuroscience (Thornton & Mitchell 2019; agent-specific learning signals 2018) finds humans represent their own states more distinctly than others'. We combine these: we introduce a controlled 'persona-vs-self false-belief' paradigm and treat contamination of the model's own belief by a persona as a measurable, localizable, and steerable phenomenon distinct from ToM belief decoding. Unlike prior descriptive persona-drift work, we operationalize contamination at the level of the model's *own factual belief representation* and provide a causal insulation intervention.
Abstract: Large language models routinely role-play personas, and users increasingly ask them to speak 'as' a flat-earther, a medieval doctor, or a user who believes a false premise. This raises a mechanistic question with direct safety relevance: when the model adopts a persona that holds a belief the model itself does not endorse, does it keep a clean separation between the persona's belief and its own, or does the persona's false belief contaminate the model's own internal representation? Prior Theory-of-Mind interpretability work decodes self/other beliefs, but only for beliefs either agent could hold in a story; prior persona work characterizes 'persona drift' behaviorally. We study the intersection: personas whose factual beliefs conflict with the model's own knowledge. We build a controlled dataset of real-world item-state facts paired with personas that (dis)believe them, and elicit the model to answer as the persona and then, in a matched clean context, answer in its own voice. We train linear probes on frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B) to simultaneously decode (i) the persona's belief and (ii) the model's own belief, measure their geometric relationship, and quantify a 'contamination' score: the degree to which the model's own-belief representation shifts toward a false persona belief. We test whether contamination predicts post-role-play factual errors, localize the responsible heads via activation patching, and derive a 'belief-ownership' steering direction (contrastive activation addition from own-voice vs. persona-voice activations) to test whether we can insulate the model's own belief while preserving faithful role-play. Metrics: joint probe accuracy/AUROC, subspace angle, contamination score, contamination-error AUROC, patching effect sizes, post-role-play factual accuracy, role-play faithfulness, and perplexity.
Experiments: 1) Dataset construction: Assemble ~5k real-world item-state facts the target models reliably know (e.g., 'The Earth is round', 'Vaccines do not cause autism', synthetic-but-model-known entity-attribute facts for control). For each, construct matched contexts: (a) OWN condition ('Answer in your own voice: is X true?'), (b) PERSONA-CONCORDANT ('Speak as a scientist. Is X true?'), (c) PERSONA-DISCORDANT ('Speak as a flat-earther / a 1850s physician / a user convinced X is false. Is X true?'). Include a critical LEAKAGE probe: after a discordant role-play turn, switch to the model's own voice ('Now, stepping out of character and speaking factually: is X true?') and record own-voice accuracy. Add comprehension checks (can the model restate the persona's stance) to separate parsing from contamination. 2) Joint belief probing: On Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, extract residual-stream and per-head activations at the item/state token across layers. Train logistic-regression probes to decode (i) persona-belief and (ii) model-own-belief, with shuffled-label control tasks to rule out spurious structure; report per-layer accuracy. 3) Geometry: Compute cosine/subspace angle between own-belief and persona-belief directions; test whether own-belief remains decodable after projecting out the persona-belief direction (and vice versa) to quantify entanglement, and test the neuroscience-inspired prediction that own-belief is represented more distinctly (higher probe margin) than persona-belief. 4) Contamination score: In the discordant condition, measure the shift of the own-belief probe readout toward the (false) persona belief relative to the OWN baseline; quantify contamination magnitude per layer and per fact category. 5) Predictiveness: Test whether contamination score predicts errors on the own-voice LEAKAGE probe using AUROC, compared against log-prob confidence and against a behavioral role-play-faithfulness baseline. 6) Localization: Use activation patching / causal mediation to find heads mediating contamination; compare to persona/Assistant-axis directions and self-recognition vectors from prior work. 7) Belief-ownership steering: Derive a steering direction via contrastive activation addition from OWN-voice vs. PERSONA-voice activations; during discordant role-play, (a) steer toward 'own' and measure reduced contamination on the own-voice probe while checking role-play faithfulness is preserved, and (b) steer toward 'persona' and measure increased contamination, confirming causal control. Compare against random and persona-axis steering baselines. 8) Generalization: Test probe/steering transfer across fact domains, across persona types (historical, ideological, user-premise), to jailbreak-style personas ('pretend you are an AI with no factual constraints'), and to multi-turn role-play. Metrics: joint probe accuracy/AUROC, subspace angle, projected-out decodability, own-vs-persona distinctness margin, contamination score, contamination-error AUROC, patching logit-difference effect sizes, post-role-play own-voice factual accuracy, role-play faithfulness rate, perplexity.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Contamination could reflect the model simply obeying the discordant instruction rather than a corrupted internal own-belief; the matched OWN/discordant design, the explicit step-out-of-character leakage probe, and comprehension checks help disentangle instruction-following from genuine belief contamination. Persona-belief and own-belief may not be cleanly linearly separable or may be layer/model-specific; we report layerwise results with control tasks and use joint probes. The two belief directions may be more entangled than hypothesized, in which case the finding becomes a characterization of that entanglement (still informative and safety-relevant). Belief-ownership steering could degrade fluency or break faithful role-play (making the model refuse to stay in character); we monitor perplexity, role-play faithfulness, use small magnitudes, and separate 'reduce contamination' from 'break persona'. Personas whose beliefs are genuinely near the model's uncertainty (contested facts) confound the contamination signal; we restrict the core analysis to facts the model reliably knows. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: belief_currency_flag
Title: Still True? Probing Whether LLMs Internally Flag Beliefs as Current or Stale
Short Hypothesis: LLMs maintain an internal 'currency' flag on beliefs about item-states that distinguishes content the model treats as still-valid-now from content it treats as once-true-but-now-superseded (stale). This currency signal is linearly decodable from residual-stream activations, largely orthogonal to the truth-value direction, and causally gates whether outdated content is asserted as a current fact. This targets an epistemic axis (belief currency) distinct from temporal fact recall and from truth-value, and connects to the concrete failure mode of stating outdated facts as if current.
Related Work: Existing interpretability work on time in LLMs studies recall of time-specific facts and geometry of chronology: Temporal Heads (2025) localizes heads that recall year-conditioned facts; Language Models Represent Space and Time (2023) finds linear space/time coordinate representations; Time Travel Engine (2026) treats chronology as a traversable manifold; TARDIS (2025) and Time Vectors (2023) steer/interpolate for temporal misalignment; History Matters (2024) edits temporal knowledge while preserving history; Layer of Truth (2025) tracks belief flips under poisoning. All of these represent *when a fact holds* or *how to recall/update it*, but none isolate an internal, decodable flag for the CURRENCY of a belief - i.e., whether the model tags a proposition as still-valid-now vs. once-true-but-now-stale - as an axis separate from the truth-value direction studied in Azaria & Mitchell (2023) and Truth-value judgment (2024). Prior belief work asks 'does the model believe X is true?' but not 'does the model believe X is still true?'. We introduce belief-currency as an orthogonal, steerable variable and link it causally to asserting outdated facts as current, which no prior work does.
Abstract: A fact can be true, false, or - crucially - it can have *been* true and since been superseded (a former capital, a retired record, a previous CEO). Humans robustly flag such content as stale rather than current. Large language models are notorious for confidently stating outdated facts as if they were current, yet prior interpretability work on time studies only how models recall time-specific facts or represent chronological coordinates, not whether models internally tag a belief by its currency. We ask a sharper, mechanistic question: does an LLM maintain an internal 'currency' flag that distinguishes beliefs it treats as still-valid-now from beliefs it treats as once-true-but-now-superseded? We hypothesize this flag is (i) linearly decodable from residual-stream activations, (ii) largely orthogonal to the well-studied truth-value direction, and (iii) causally gates whether stale content is asserted as a current fact. We construct a controlled dataset of item-state propositions in matched frames that vary currency (current vs. superseded) while holding proposition content and surface form as constant as possible, including synthetic entity-attribute facts with explicit update histories to control priors, plus a critical leakage probe that asks for the *current* value after a stale fact is present. We train linear probes on frozen open-weight models (Llama-3, Qwen2.5, Gemma-2, Pythia) to decode currency vs. truth, measure their geometric relationship, localize the responsible heads via activation patching (comparing to known Temporal Heads and truth heads), and test causal control: steering along the currency direction should modulate whether outdated content contaminates 'current-value' answers. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, subspace angle, projected-out decodability, patching effect sizes, and a staleness-leakage rate.
Experiments: 1) Dataset construction: Generate ~6k item-state propositions with an update structure. Two tracks: (a) real facts with known changes (e.g., 'The tallest building is the Burj Khalifa' after a later record, past vs. current world leaders, former vs. current company CEOs, retired vs. current sports records), each rendered as a CURRENT-valid variant and a SUPERSEDED (once-true-now-stale) variant; (b) synthetic entity-attribute facts with explicit in-context update histories (e.g., 'In 2020 Zorblax orbited Kelvath; in 2023 it was moved to orbit Vantor') to fully control priors and to specify ground-truth currency. Cross currency (current vs. superseded) with an unrelated true/false axis (some propositions are simply false, never-true) to separate 'stale-true' from 'false'. Add a critical LEAKAGE subset: after presenting a superseded fact in context, ask 'What is the CURRENT value of the attribute?' and record whether the model reports the stale value as current. Include comprehension checks (can the model restate the update history) to separate parsing failure from currency failure, and paraphrase/format perturbations to guard against surface-cue artifacts. 2) Probing: For Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Pythia-2.8B, extract residual-stream and per-head activations at the item/state token across layers. Train logistic-regression probes for (i) truth-value (true vs. never-true) and (ii) currency (current-valid vs. superseded-stale, restricted to true-at-some-point propositions). Report per-layer accuracy with shuffled-label control tasks to rule out spurious structure. 3) Geometry: Compute cosine/subspace angle between currency and truth directions; test whether currency is decodable after projecting out the truth direction (and vice versa) to establish orthogonality. Test whether currency is decodable across both real and synthetic tracks (generalization of the direction). 4) Localization: Use activation patching / causal mediation to find heads carrying the currency signal; compare to Temporal Heads (from prior work) and to truth/belief heads, testing whether currency is mediated by a distinct set. 5) Causal gating test: Derive a currency steering direction via contrastive activation addition (current vs. superseded activations). At inference on the leakage probe, (a) push toward 'current' on a superseded fact and measure increased staleness-leakage rate (stale value asserted as current); (b) push toward 'stale' on a current fact and measure whether the model hedges/marks it as possibly outdated. Compare against random-direction and truth-direction steering baselines to show specificity. Monitor perplexity and general benchmarks (MMLU subset) for collateral damage. 6) Predictiveness: Test whether the internal currency probe readout predicts behavioral staleness-leakage errors (AUROC) better than a log-prob confidence baseline. 7) Generalization: Test probe/steering transfer across domains (leaders, records, corporate, geographic) and from synthetic to real facts. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, subspace angle, projected-out decodability, patching logit-difference effect sizes, staleness-leakage rate delta, leakage-prediction AUROC, perplexity delta.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Currency may be entangled with surface temporal cues (words like 'former', 'used to', explicit years) rather than an abstract currency representation; we mitigate with diverse framings, paraphrases, matched-content controls, and by testing transfer to unseen cue types and to the synthetic track where currency is inferred from an update history rather than a keyword. The distinction may not be cleanly linearly separable or may be layer/model-specific; we report layerwise results with control tasks. Currency and truth directions may be less orthogonal than hypothesized, in which case the finding characterizes their entanglement (still informative). Leakage errors could stem from stale pretraining knowledge (the model never learned the update) rather than a currency-flag failure; the synthetic track with fully in-context update histories isolates the currency mechanism from stale parametric knowledge. For real facts, some 'current' values may drift after data collection; we timestamp the dataset and restrict claims accordingly. Steering could degrade fluency (off-manifold) or overshoot into indiscriminate hedging; we use small magnitudes, random/truth-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity and general benchmarks. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: belief_contestedness_flag
Title: Settled or Contested? Probing Whether LLMs Internally Flag Beliefs as Consensus vs. Genuinely Disputed
Short Hypothesis: LLMs maintain an internal 'contestedness' flag on beliefs about item-states that distinguishes propositions the model treats as settled/consensus (a single truth-value exists) from propositions it treats as genuinely contested (no single agreed truth-value). This contestedness signal is linearly decodable from residual-stream activations, largely orthogonal to the truth-value direction, and causally gates whether the model asserts a claim as settled fact vs. hedges/marks it as disputed.
Related Work: Prior interpretability work isolates a linear truth-value direction and treats propositions as binary true/false (Geometry of Truth 2023; Azaria & Mitchell 2023; Truth-value judgment: belief directions are context sensitive 2024). Belief-representation work studies self/other ToM beliefs (Language Models Represent Beliefs of Self and Others 2024; Brittle Minds 2024), representational stability of truth for fictional/synthetic content (Representational Stability of Truth 2025), and depth of implanted beliefs (Believe It or Not 2025). Political-perspective work finds a linear ideology direction usable to steer slant (Linear Representations of Political Perspective 2025). DynamicQA (2024) behaviorally distinguishes 'disputable dynamic facts' (viewpoint-dependent) and shows higher intra-memory conflict, but only at the output/persuasion level. Critically, NONE of these isolate an internal, decodable flag for whether a proposition is CONTESTED (has no single agreed truth) as an axis SEPARATE from the truth-value direction and from a partisan ideology direction. Existing truth probes force a true/false readout even on inherently contested claims; we ask instead whether the model internally represents 'this is genuinely disputed' as its own variable, and whether that variable causally controls unwarranted assertiveness vs. hedging. This is not a trivial extension: it reframes contested-topic overconfidence (and false balance) as a mechanistic, steerable epistemic signal orthogonal to truth-value.
Abstract: Not every proposition has a single truth-value: 'The capital of France is Paris' is settled, while 'Nuclear power is the best path to decarbonization' is genuinely contested. Humans robustly flag such claims as disputed and hedge accordingly, but LLMs are known to state contested claims with unwarranted confidence (or, conversely, to hedge on settled facts). Prior interpretability work isolates a linear truth-value direction and treats every claim as binary true/false; behavioral work notes that 'disputable' facts cause knowledge conflict, but no work has asked whether the model internally represents contestedness as its own variable. We hypothesize that LLMs maintain a 'contestedness' flag that distinguishes settled/consensus propositions from genuinely contested ones, and that this flag is (i) linearly decodable from residual-stream activations, (ii) largely orthogonal to both the truth-value direction and any partisan-ideology direction, and (iii) causally gates whether the model asserts a claim as settled fact vs. hedges. We construct a controlled dataset of item-state propositions labeled for contestedness (settled-true, settled-false, and genuinely-contested claims) balanced across topic domains, plus synthetic in-context 'consensus vs. dispute' framings to control priors. We train linear probes on frozen open-weight models (Llama-3, Qwen2.5, Gemma-2, Pythia) to decode contestedness vs. truth-value, measure their geometric relationship (subspace angles, projected-out decodability), and separate contestedness from the partisan-ideology direction. We localize responsible heads via activation patching and test causal control: steering along the contestedness direction should modulate assertiveness/hedging on a matched set of prompts. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, subspace angle, projected-out decodability, patching effect sizes, assertiveness/hedging-rate shifts, and perplexity.
Experiments: 1) Dataset construction: Build ~6k item-state propositions with three-way labels. (a) SETTLED-TRUE (uncontested facts, e.g., 'Water is composed of hydrogen and oxygen'), (b) SETTLED-FALSE (clearly false, uncontested, e.g., 'The Sun orbits the Earth'), (c) GENUINELY-CONTESTED claims that lack a single agreed truth-value across multiple domains: normative/policy ('X is the best economic policy'), unresolved empirical/scientific debates, aesthetic/taste, and moral-dilemma claims. Balance contested items across the political spectrum (pro/anti framings) and across non-political domains (aesthetics, ethics, unsettled science) to prevent conflation with a partisan direction. To control pretraining priors, add a SYNTHETIC track: novel entity-attribute claims embedded in matched in-context framings that stipulate either consensus ('All experts agree Zorblax orbits Kelvath') or dispute ('Experts disagree whether Zorblax orbits Kelvath'), holding proposition content constant. Add a critical ASSERTIVENESS probe: ask the model to answer each proposition and record whether it asserts a definitive answer vs. explicitly hedges/marks it disputed. Include comprehension/format perturbations (paraphrase, reorder) to guard against surface-cue artifacts. Human-validate contestedness labels on a sample. 2) Probing: For Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Pythia-2.8B, extract residual-stream and per-head activations at the item/state token across layers. Train logistic-regression probes for (i) truth-value (settled-true vs. settled-false) and (ii) contestedness (settled vs. genuinely-contested). Report per-layer accuracy with shuffled-label control tasks to rule out spurious structure. 3) Geometry: Compute cosine/subspace angle between the contestedness and truth-value directions; test whether contestedness remains decodable after projecting out the truth-value direction (and vice versa) to establish orthogonality. Separately compute a partisan-ideology direction (following Linear Representations of Political Perspective) and test whether contestedness is decodable after projecting out ideology, to show contestedness is not merely a political-slant signal (verified using non-political contested items). 4) Localization: Use activation patching / causal mediation to find heads carrying the contestedness signal; compare to truth/belief heads (from prior work) and to ideology-predictive heads, testing whether contestedness is mediated by a distinct set. 5) Causal gating test: Derive a contestedness steering direction via contrastive activation addition (contested vs. settled activations). At inference on the assertiveness probe, (a) push toward 'contested' on settled propositions and measure increased hedging rate; (b) push toward 'settled' on genuinely-contested propositions and measure increased unwarranted assertiveness. Compare against random-direction and truth-direction steering baselines to show specificity. Monitor perplexity and general benchmarks (MMLU subset) for collateral damage. 6) Predictiveness: Test whether the internal contestedness probe readout predicts behavioral over-assertiveness (asserting a contested claim as settled) better than a log-prob confidence baseline (AUROC). 7) Generalization: Test probe/steering transfer across domains (policy, science, ethics, aesthetics), from synthetic to real claims, and to naturalistic open-ended prompts. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, subspace angle, projected-out decodability (vs. both truth and ideology), patching logit-difference effect sizes, assertiveness/hedging-rate deltas, over-assertiveness prediction AUROC, perplexity delta.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Contestedness may be entangled with surface cues (words like 'debate', 'opinion', 'best') rather than an abstract epistemic representation; we mitigate with diverse framings, paraphrases, matched-content controls, and by testing transfer to unseen cue types and the synthetic in-context track where contestedness is stipulated rather than lexically signaled. The label 'genuinely contested' is partly subjective and may reflect the model's training-data distribution rather than an objective epistemic category; we human-validate labels, balance across domains, and treat the model's internal notion of contestedness as itself the object of study. Contestedness may partially overlap with the truth-value direction (contested items lack a clean truth-value) or with a partisan-ideology direction; the projected-out analyses and non-political contested items quantify and disentangle this, and even a characterization of entanglement is informative. The signal may not be cleanly linearly separable or may be layer/model-specific; we report layerwise results with control tasks. Steering could degrade fluency (off-manifold) or overshoot into indiscriminate hedging/assertiveness; we use small magnitudes, random/truth-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity and general benchmarks. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: belief_ripple_internal
Title: Does the Ripple Happen Inside? Probing Whether LLMs Internally Propagate In-Context Belief Updates Before Being Asked
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM reads a new fact stated in context, it internally updates its belief not only about that fact but, silently and before any query, about logically-entailed related facts. This internal 'ripple' is linearly decodable at the entailed-item representation, is graded and selective (some entailments propagate, others don't), and its magnitude at read-time predicts which downstream ripple queries the model will answer correctly. Ripple failures are thus visible internally at ingestion time, not just at output time.
Related Work: Ripple-effect work (RippleEdits 2023; ChainEdit 2025; PropMEND 2025; GradSim 2024; GIE/SIR 2024; KnowledgeSmith 2025; TRACK 2026) studies whether *edited* or in-context knowledge propagates to related facts, but measures propagation only behaviorally (multi-hop QA accuracy) or via gradient/hidden-space edit-side diagnostics; all require *querying* the related fact. 'Believe It or Not' (2025) and 'Do LMs Have Beliefs?' (2021) probe belief depth/consistency of implanted facts but again read beliefs by querying. None ask whether, upon merely *reading* a fact in context (no edit, no query), the model *spontaneously* updates the internal representation of logically-entailed items, whether that update is decodable at read-time, graded/selective per entailment type, and predictive of ripple success. We reframe the ripple as an internal, read-time representational-propagation phenomenon and provide a linear-probe + activation-patching handle on it, distinct from all output-level and edit-side prior work.
Abstract: Telling a language model 'Jack is Johnny's son' should, if the model reasons coherently, make it also believe 'Jack is Lily-Rose's sibling.' Prior work shows this ripple often fails, but always measures it by *asking* the related question. We ask a sharper, mechanistic question: when the model merely *reads* a new fact in context, does it silently update its internal belief about logically-entailed facts, before any query? We hypothesize that (i) such internal ripple updates are linearly decodable from residual-stream activations at the entailed item's representation, (ii) they are graded and selective across entailment types (e.g., symmetric relations, inverse relations, transitive/multi-hop, type-inheritance), and (iii) the read-time magnitude of the internal update predicts whether the model will answer the corresponding ripple query correctly. We construct controlled synthetic entity-relation graphs with novel entities (to bypass pretraining priors) plus a real-fact track. For each injected base fact, we enumerate entailed facts of known types and measure the internal belief about each entailed fact both before and after the base fact appears in context. We train linear belief probes on frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Pythia-2.8B), quantify per-entailment-type internal ripple magnitude, test whether it predicts downstream ripple-QA accuracy (AUROC) beyond a log-prob baseline, and localize the heads that carry propagation via activation patching. Finally, we test causal amplification: steering along a 'propagation' direction (contrastive activation addition from strong- vs. weak-ripple cases) to see if it increases both internal ripple magnitude and ripple-QA accuracy. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, internal-ripple magnitude by entailment type, ripple-success prediction AUROC, patching effect sizes, post-steering accuracy delta, perplexity.
Experiments: 1) Dataset construction: Build controlled synthetic entity-relation graphs with novel entities (e.g., invented people, places, companies) so entailed facts are not in pretraining. For each graph, designate a BASE fact to inject in context (e.g., 'Zorbot is the founder of Kelvara') and enumerate ENTAILED facts by type: (a) symmetric ('Kelvara was founded by Zorbot'), (b) inverse-relation ('Kelvara's founder is Zorbot' vs. 'Zorbot's company is Kelvara'), (c) transitive/multi-hop ('Kelvara is headquartered in city X' -> 'Zorbot works in X'), (d) type-inheritance ('Zorbot is a person' -> has properties of persons), and (e) NON-entailed distractor facts (should NOT ripple). Include a real-fact track adapted from RippleEdits for external validity. For each entailed/distractor fact, prepare a matched no-base-context control (fact never introduced). ~5k base facts with several entailments each. 2) Read-time internal belief probing: For Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Pythia-2.8B, extract residual-stream and per-head activations at the entailed-item's key tokens, in two conditions: (BASE-present) the base fact appears earlier in context, and (BASE-absent) it does not, WITHOUT ever asking the entailed question. Train linear belief probes (P(entailed fact holds)) on held-out data with shuffled-label control tasks. Define internal-ripple magnitude = probe belief(BASE-present) - probe belief(BASE-absent) at the entailed item, per layer, per entailment type. 3) Selectivity analysis: Test whether internal ripple magnitude is high for genuine entailments and near-zero for non-entailed distractors, and how it varies across entailment types (symmetric/inverse/transitive/inheritance). Report per-type ripple magnitude curves across layers. 4) Predictiveness: Separately query each entailed fact behaviorally (ripple-QA) to get ground-truth ripple success/failure. Test whether read-time internal-ripple magnitude predicts per-item ripple-QA success (AUROC), compared against a log-prob confidence baseline and against GradSim-style edit-side indicators adapted to in-context. 5) Localization: Use activation patching / causal mediation from BASE-present to BASE-absent runs to find the heads/layers that carry propagation to the entailed item; test whether distinct heads mediate different entailment types (e.g., symmetric vs. multi-hop). 6) Causal amplification: Derive a 'propagation' steering direction via contrastive activation addition from strong-ripple vs. weak-ripple base-present activations; inject it during reading and measure (a) increased internal ripple magnitude at entailed items, (b) increased ripple-QA accuracy, (c) that non-entailed distractors are NOT spuriously updated (specificity), (d) collateral effects on general benchmarks (MMLU subset) and perplexity. Compare against random-direction steering. 7) Generalization: Test probe/steering transfer across entailment types, from synthetic to real-fact track, and across graph depths (1-hop vs. multi-hop). Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, internal-ripple magnitude by entailment type and layer, ripple-success prediction AUROC, patching logit-difference effect sizes, post-steering accuracy and specificity deltas, perplexity delta.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Read-time internal ripple may be weak or absent (models may only compute entailments when queried), in which case a robust *negative* result is still highly informative for the ripple/editing literature and reframes ripple failures as a lack of spontaneous propagation. The entailed-item probe signal could reflect surface co-occurrence of tokens rather than a genuine belief update; matched BASE-absent controls, non-entailed distractors, and paraphrase perturbations mitigate this. Multi-hop entailments may not have a single clean probe target; we anchor probes at well-defined key tokens and report per-type results. Ripple magnitude and ripple-QA success could both be driven by a common confound (fact salience); we control salience and use partial-correlation analyses. Steering could degrade fluency or spuriously propagate to distractors; we monitor perplexity, specificity on distractors, and general benchmarks, and use small magnitudes with random-direction baselines. Synthetic novel entities may be represented differently from real knowledge; the real-fact track provides a check. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: aleatoric_epistemic_belief_split
Title: I Don't Know vs. Nobody Can Know: Do LLMs Internally Distinguish Epistemic from Aleatoric Uncertainty in Their Beliefs?
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM is uncertain about an item's state, it internally represents not just how uncertain it is (magnitude) but WHY: whether the uncertainty is epistemic (reducible - the model lacks information but a determinate answer exists) or aleatoric (irreducible - the outcome is genuinely random/indeterminate). This uncertainty-type signal is linearly decodable, largely orthogonal to the scalar uncertainty-magnitude direction studied in prior work, and causally gates the model's information-seeking/abstention behavior (it should defer or seek evidence under epistemic uncertainty but not under aleatoric uncertainty).
Related Work: Prior interpretability work treats uncertainty as a scalar magnitude: verbal uncertainty is a single linear feature (Calibrating Verbal Uncertainty / MUC 2025), semantic vs. verbal uncertainty mismatch predicts hallucination, calibration is a distributed low-dimensional direction (Calibration Across Layers 2025), entropy/token-frequency neurons regulate confidence (2024), models 'know the road not taken' (2025), belief manifolds encode a posterior's mean and variance (Shape of Beliefs 2026; Transformers Represent Belief State Geometry 2024), and models can verbalize calibrated confidence (Lin et al. 2022). Neuroscience distinguishes code-driven vs. correlational representations of uncertainty. Crucially, ALL of this treats uncertainty as one axis (how confident/wide the posterior is). NONE isolate the aleatoric-vs-epistemic DISTINCTION - whether the model represents the SOURCE of uncertainty (reducible ignorance vs. irreducible randomness) as its own internal variable, or links it causally to the correct downstream policy (seek-info/abstain under epistemic uncertainty; commit/report a distribution under aleatoric). We introduce uncertainty-type as an orthogonal, decodable, steerable belief attribute and connect it to a concrete failure mode: models that abstain or over-hedge on genuinely random questions, or confidently guess on answerable-but-unknown ones.
Abstract: A fair coin flip and a trivia question about an obscure fact both leave a language model unable to give a confident answer, but for fundamentally different reasons: the coin is irreducibly random (aleatoric uncertainty - no amount of information would help), while the trivia fact is merely unknown to the model (epistemic uncertainty - a determinate answer exists and could be looked up). Rational agents treat these differently: they seek information or abstain under epistemic uncertainty but simply report a distribution under aleatoric uncertainty. Prior interpretability work has thoroughly characterized uncertainty as a scalar magnitude (verbal-uncertainty features, calibration directions, entropy neurons, posterior-width manifolds) but has never asked whether LLMs internally represent WHY they are uncertain. We hypothesize that the aleatoric-vs-epistemic distinction is (i) linearly decodable from residual-stream activations, (ii) largely orthogonal to the scalar uncertainty-magnitude direction, and (iii) causally gates information-seeking/abstention behavior. We build a controlled dataset of item-state questions matched for uncertainty magnitude but varying in type: genuinely random/indeterminate (dice, coin flips, unknowable future events, ties) vs. answerable-but-unknown-to-the-model (obscure facts, redacted-but-determinate values, synthetic entity attributes withheld from context). We train linear probes on frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Pythia-2.8B) to decode uncertainty type vs. magnitude, measure their geometric relationship (subspace angle, projected-out decodability), localize responsible heads via activation patching, and test causal control: steering along the uncertainty-type direction should shift whether the model chooses to seek information/abstain vs. commit to a distribution. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, subspace angle, projected-out decodability, patching effect sizes, information-seeking/abstention-rate shifts, and perplexity.
Experiments: 1) Dataset construction: Build ~6k item-state questions grouped into three uncertainty types, matched for behavioral uncertainty magnitude (verified via the model's answer-distribution entropy). (a) ALEATORIC / irreducible: outcomes of fair random processes ('What number will this fair die show?'), genuinely indeterminate future/tie events, and questions with no fact of the matter; the correct epistemic stance is to report a distribution, not to seek more info. (b) EPISTEMIC-answerable-but-unknown: obscure real facts the model likely doesn't know ('What is the middle name of [obscure person]?'), and a controlled SYNTHETIC track where a novel entity's attribute is defined but deliberately WITHHELD from context ('Zorblax has a fixed birth-year, not stated here. What is it?') - here a determinate answer exists and information-seeking is warranted. (c) A SETTLED-KNOWN control (low uncertainty) to anchor the magnitude axis. Crucially, include MATCHED PAIRS with equal answer-entropy but different type (e.g., 'random die roll: 1-6' vs. 'the die was rolled behind a screen and its value is now fixed but unknown: 1-6') to dissociate type from magnitude. Add an INFORMATION-SEEKING probe: offer the model an action choice ('ANSWER now / SEEK more information (ask a question or call a lookup tool) / report a PROBABILITY DISTRIBUTION') and record its choice. Include comprehension checks and paraphrase/format perturbations to guard against surface-cue artifacts. 2) Probing: For Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Pythia-2.8B, extract residual-stream and per-head activations at the item/question representation across layers. Train logistic-regression probes for (i) uncertainty MAGNITUDE (low vs. high, using answer-entropy bins) and (ii) uncertainty TYPE (aleatoric vs. epistemic, restricted to high-uncertainty items). Report per-layer accuracy with shuffled-label control tasks. Also extract a scalar verbal-uncertainty feature (difference-in-means, following MUC) as a baseline magnitude direction. 3) Geometry: Compute cosine/subspace angle between the type direction and (a) the magnitude probe direction and (b) the MUC verbal-uncertainty feature; test whether type remains decodable after projecting out the magnitude direction (and vice versa) to establish orthogonality, using the matched-entropy pairs as the strongest test. 4) Localization: Use activation patching / causal mediation to find heads carrying the type signal; compare to entropy/confidence-regulation neurons and calibration directions from prior work, testing whether type is mediated by a distinct set. 5) Causal gating test: Derive an uncertainty-type steering direction via contrastive activation addition (aleatoric vs. epistemic activations, controlling for magnitude). On the information-seeking probe, (a) push toward 'epistemic' on aleatoric items and measure increased (irrational) information-seeking/abstention on genuinely random questions; (b) push toward 'aleatoric' on epistemic items and measure decreased information-seeking (over-committing to a guess/distribution when a lookup was warranted). Compare against random-direction and magnitude-direction steering baselines to show specificity; monitor perplexity and a general benchmark (MMLU subset) for collateral damage. 6) Predictiveness: Test whether the internal type probe readout predicts the model's information-seeking choice and its downstream abstention appropriateness (seeking on epistemic, reporting distribution on aleatoric) better than a scalar-uncertainty baseline (AUROC). 7) Generalization: Test probe/steering transfer across domains (games of chance, unknown facts, future events, synthetic withheld attributes) and from synthetic to real items. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, subspace angle, projected-out decodability (vs. magnitude and MUC feature), patching logit-difference effect sizes, information-seeking/abstention-rate deltas, type-prediction AUROC, perplexity delta.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Uncertainty type may be entangled with surface cues (words like 'random', 'roll', 'fair') rather than an abstract epistemic representation; we mitigate with diverse framings, paraphrases, matched-content controls, and the synthetic withheld-attribute track where 'epistemic' is inferred from a stated-but-hidden determinate value rather than a keyword. Type and magnitude may be less orthogonal than hypothesized (aleatoric items may cluster at specific magnitudes); the matched-entropy pairs are designed precisely to dissociate them, and even a characterization of entanglement is informative. The model may not actually possess a normative aleatoric/epistemic distinction, in which case a robust negative result (type is NOT decodable beyond magnitude) is itself a meaningful finding about the limits of LLM epistemic self-modeling. Information-seeking behavior depends on prompt scaffolding and may be instruction-following rather than driven by internal type representation; the matched design, comprehension checks, and predictiveness analysis relative to internal probes help disentangle these. Some 'aleatoric' items may be treated by the model as answerable and vice versa; we validate labels and use the model's own answer-entropy to define magnitude. Steering could degrade fluency (off-manifold) or overshoot into indiscriminate abstention; we use small magnitudes, random/magnitude-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity and general benchmarks. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: audience_knowledge_belief
Title: What Do You Already Know? Probing the LLM's Model of the User's Knowledge and How It Gates What Gets Said
Short Hypothesis: An LLM maintains an internal 'audience-knowledge' belief about what the current user already knows about an item, distinct from the model's own belief about that item's state, and this audience-knowledge signal is (i) linearly decodable, (ii) largely orthogonal to the model's own-belief/truth direction, and (iii) causally gates the model's pragmatic generation policy: whether it states, omits as redundant, or over-explains a piece of information.
Related Work: Interpretability of belief has focused on third-person Theory-of-Mind: decoding/steering the beliefs of story characters and an oracle (Language Models Represent Beliefs of Self and Others 2024; Language Models use Lookbacks to Track Beliefs 2025; Brittle Minds 2024; GridToM 2025; Common-ToM 2024), and on the truth-value/own-belief direction (Azaria & Mitchell 2023; Truth-value judgment 2024). Cognitive/pragmatic work (RSA-style listener/speaker modeling, common-ground benchmarks) studies inference about interlocutors behaviorally. Crucially, none isolate an internal, decodable representation of what the *current live user* already knows as a variable SEPARATE from the model's own factual belief, nor link it causally to the model's own *speaking* policy (state vs. omit-as-redundant vs. over-explain). We reframe the 'common ground' / audience model as an internal, steerable belief attribute that gates informativeness, connecting it to concrete failure modes: over-explaining to experts, condescension, unwarranted omission, and deceptive information withholding. This is not a trivial ToM extension: prior ToM decoding concerns a third party in a narrative; we concern the model's belief about its own conversational partner and how that belief controls the model's generation.
Abstract: Good communicators tailor what they say to what the listener already knows: they skip the obvious, explain the unfamiliar, and avoid condescension. To do this an LLM would need an internal model of the user's knowledge, held separately from its own knowledge of the facts. We ask whether LLMs maintain such an 'audience-knowledge' belief, whether it is a distinct internal variable, and whether it causally controls what the model chooses to say. We hypothesize that (i) the model's belief about what the user knows about an item is linearly decodable from residual-stream activations, (ii) this direction is largely orthogonal to the model's own-belief/truth direction, and (iii) steering it causally shifts the model's generation between stating, omitting-as-redundant, and over-explaining information. We build a controlled dataset of item facts embedded in conversational contexts that establish the user's knowledge state (user shown to already know the fact, shown not to know it, or unspecified) while holding the underlying fact and the model's own belief constant, plus matched pairs where the model believes an item but the user does or does not. We train linear probes on frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Pythia-2.8B) to decode audience-knowledge vs. own-belief, measure their geometric relationship, localize the responsible attention heads via activation patching (comparing to known ToM belief heads), and test causal control by steering along the audience-knowledge direction and measuring shifts in redundant-restatement, omission, and over-explanation rates. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, subspace angle, projected-out decodability, patching effect sizes, informativeness-behavior rate deltas, and perplexity.
Experiments: 1) Dataset construction: Generate ~6k item facts (real-world facts the target models reliably know, e.g., 'Paris is the capital of France', plus synthetic entity-attribute facts to control priors). For each, embed the fact in a short conversation that establishes the USER'S knowledge state about that item: (a) USER-KNOWS (the user earlier states or is described as knowing the fact / is an expert in the domain), (b) USER-DOESNT-KNOW (the user asks a naive question / is described as a novice), (c) UNSPECIFIED control. Hold the fact and the model's own belief constant across conditions; verify the model itself believes the fact via its own-belief probe. Add a critical BEHAVIOR probe: pose a downstream request whose ideal answer depends on the user's knowledge (e.g., 'Explain how to get from the airport to the city center' where the fact 'Paris is the capital' is relevant), and record whether the model states, omits-as-redundant, or over-explains the item. Include comprehension checks (can the model restate the user's knowledge state) to separate parsing from representation, and paraphrase/format perturbations to guard against surface-cue artifacts. 2) Probing: For Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Pythia-2.8B, extract residual-stream and per-head activations at the item token across layers. Train logistic-regression probes for (i) MODEL-OWN-BELIEF (does the model hold the fact as true) and (ii) AUDIENCE-KNOWLEDGE (does the model believe the USER knows the fact). Report per-layer accuracy with shuffled-label control tasks to rule out spurious structure. 3) Geometry: Compute cosine/subspace angle between the audience-knowledge and own-belief directions; test whether audience-knowledge remains decodable after projecting out the own-belief direction (and vice versa) to establish orthogonality, using matched pairs where own-belief is held constant but user-knowledge varies. 4) Localization: Use activation patching / causal mediation to find heads carrying the audience-knowledge signal; compare to third-person ToM belief heads reported in prior work (Beliefs of Self and Others; Lookbacks) and to own-belief/truth heads, testing whether audience-knowledge is mediated by a distinct or shared set. 5) Causal gating test: Derive an audience-knowledge steering direction via contrastive activation addition (user-knows vs. user-doesnt-know activations, controlling for own-belief). On the behavior probe, (a) push toward 'user-knows' and measure increased omission/redundancy-avoidance (the model treats the item as given), (b) push toward 'user-doesnt-know' and measure increased explanation/over-explanation of the item. Compare against random-direction and own-belief-direction steering baselines to show specificity; monitor perplexity and a general benchmark (MMLU subset) for collateral damage. 6) Predictiveness: Test whether the internal audience-knowledge probe readout predicts the model's actual state/omit/explain behavior better than a log-prob baseline (AUROC / accuracy). 7) Generalization: Test probe/steering transfer across domains (geography, science, procedures), from synthetic to real facts, and to multi-turn dialogues where the user's knowledge accrues over turns. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, subspace angle, projected-out decodability, patching logit-difference effect sizes, state/omit/over-explain rate deltas, behavior-prediction AUROC, perplexity delta.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Audience-knowledge may be entangled with surface cues (words like 'expert'/'novice'/'as you know') rather than an abstract representation; we mitigate with diverse framings, paraphrases, matched-content controls, and by testing transfer to unseen cue types and to knowledge states inferred from multi-turn accrual rather than a keyword. The audience-knowledge direction may overlap with the own-belief direction or with a generic third-person ToM belief direction; the projected-out analyses and matched pairs quantify and disentangle this, and even a characterization of entanglement is informative. The model may lack a genuine separate audience model, in which case a robust negative result (audience-knowledge not decodable beyond own-belief) is itself meaningful for pragmatics and alignment. Behavioral state/omit/explain choices depend on prompt scaffolding and may be instruction-following rather than driven by the internal representation; the matched design, comprehension checks, and predictiveness analysis relative to internal probes help disentangle these. Steering could degrade fluency or overshoot into indiscriminate omission or over-explanation; we use small magnitudes, random/own-belief-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity and general benchmarks. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: valenced_belief_update_asymmetry
Title: Good News, Bad News: Do LLMs Update Beliefs Asymmetrically Toward Desirable Evidence, and Is the Asymmetry Causally Steerable?
