Short Hypothesis: Like humans (Sharot et al.'s 'good news/bad news effect'), LLMs update their internal beliefs about an item's state MORE in response to desirable/favorable evidence than to equally-strong undesirable evidence — a valence-driven optimism asymmetry that is independent of evidence strength. We hypothesize this asymmetry is (i) present in the model's internally-decoded belief trajectory (not just its verbal output), (ii) mediated by an identifiable internal component (a valence-of-evidence direction / set of heads that gates how much an update is applied), and (iii) causally removable/reversible by intervening on that component, restoring symmetric (rational) updating.
Related Work: The human 'good news/bad news effect' (Sharot et al. 2011; Selectively altering belief formation, 2012; 198+ citations) shows humans discount undesirable evidence and over-weight desirable evidence when updating self-relevant beliefs, and that disrupting left IFG restores symmetry. In LLM interpretability, belief-state geometry and belief updating are studied (Transformers Represent Belief State Geometry 2024; The Shape of Beliefs 2026; Constrained Belief Updates 2025), and social-pressure overrides of belief are mechanistically characterized (When Truth Is Overridden: sycophancy 2025; Signal Competition / compliance subspace 2025). Behavioral work notes non-Bayesian updating (Martingale Score) but not valence-conditioned asymmetry. Crucially, NO prior work asks whether LLMs exhibit a *desirability/valence-driven* asymmetry in belief updating — over-updating toward favorable outcomes and under-updating toward unfavorable ones at equal evidence strength — nor localizes and causally reverses it. This differs from sycophancy work (which is about *social* signals from a user, not the intrinsic desirability of the evidence's content) and from my prior proposals (which concern epistemic attribute tags such as provenance/currency/contestedness, not valence-driven update magnitude). We transfer a canonical human-cognition finding into LLMs and give it a mechanistic, causal treatment.
Abstract: Humans famously update their beliefs asymmetrically: we readily absorb good news but discount bad news, an optimism bias whose neural basis has been isolated and even reversed with targeted brain stimulation. As LLMs increasingly form and revise beliefs about outcomes (a treatment will work, a plan will succeed, a risk is low), we ask whether they inherit an analogous valence-driven asymmetry — updating internal beliefs more toward desirable evidence than toward equally-strong undesirable evidence — and whether, unlike in humans, we can precisely locate and switch it off. We construct a controlled belief-updating paradigm in which an item's outcome probability is revised by a stream of evidence pieces whose *strength* (how much a rational Bayesian should update) is held constant while their *desirability* is varied: for self-relevant framings (the model's own predicted success, a user's health prognosis, a plan's payoff) some evidence is favorable and some unfavorable. We train linear belief probes on frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) to read the internal belief before and after each evidence piece, computing a per-update *asymmetry score* = (internal update to favorable evidence) − (internal update to matched unfavorable evidence). We test whether the asymmetry appears internally (not just verbally), whether it grows with self-relevance, and whether it correlates with behavioral over-optimism. We then localize a candidate 'evidence-valence gating' component via activation patching and derive a contrastive steering direction, testing whether ablating/steering it restores symmetric updating without harming overall evidence-integration accuracy or fluency. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, per-update asymmetry score, self-relevance modulation, asymmetry–optimism correlation, patching effect sizes, post-intervention symmetry restoration, integration accuracy, and perplexity.
Experiments: 1) Dataset/paradigm construction: Build ~5k belief-updating scenarios about an item's binary/continuous outcome (e.g., 'Will treatment T cure patient P?', 'Will project X hit its deadline?', 'Will candidate C pass the exam?'). Each scenario reveals a sequence of evidence pieces. Control EVIDENCE STRENGTH by specifying, in synthetic scenarios, explicit likelihood ratios / base rates so the rational Bayesian posterior update per piece is computable (an oracle trajectory), and by matching favorable vs. unfavorable pieces to identical |log-likelihood-ratio|. Vary DESIRABILITY of each piece (favorable vs. unfavorable to the hoped-for outcome) and vary SELF-RELEVANCE via framing: (a) model's own predicted success/competence, (b) a sympathetic user's outcome, (c) a neutral third party, (d) an outcome the model is framed to dis-prefer (to test whether asymmetry flips sign with valence rather than following a fixed direction). Include comprehension checks (can the model restate each evidence piece's direction/strength) and paraphrase/format perturbations to rule out surface cues; include a neutral-valence control set. 2) Internal belief probing: For Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B, at each evidence-token boundary extract residual-stream activations and train linear probes reading P(outcome) with shuffled-label control tasks; record the internal belief trajectory. Define per-update internal update = probe belief(after) − probe belief(before). 3) Asymmetry measurement: For matched favorable/unfavorable pieces of equal rational strength, compute asymmetry score = |internal update_favorable| − |internal update_unfavorable|; test asymmetry > 0 (optimism) against the rational-symmetric null, per model, per self-relevance level, and verify the asymmetry is *valence-conditioned* (flips with the dis-preferred framing) rather than a fixed directional drift. 4) Verbal-vs-internal & optimism link: Compare internal asymmetry to verbal-output asymmetry (stated posteriors), and test whether internal asymmetry predicts final over-optimistic answers (deviation from oracle posterior) via correlation/AUROC, vs. a log-prob baseline. 5) Self-relevance modulation: Test whether asymmetry increases from third-party → user → model-own-success framings, mirroring the human self-relevance effect. 6) Localization: Use activation patching / causal mediation to find heads/layers whose states carry the evidence-valence signal and gate update magnitude (patch favorable-evidence activations into unfavorable-evidence runs and vice versa); compare to sycophancy/compliance-subspace directions from prior work to establish distinctness from social-pressure mechanisms. 7) Causal intervention: Derive a contrastive 'valence-gating' steering direction (favorable vs. unfavorable matched-strength activations); test (a) ablating/projecting it out restores symmetric updating (asymmetry score → 0) and improves oracle-agreement, (b) amplifying it exaggerates optimism, (c) specificity: matched random directions and the truth direction do not restore symmetry, (d) collateral checks: overall evidence-integration accuracy on neutral scenarios, GSM8K/MMLU subset, and perplexity. 8) Generalization: Test probe/steering transfer across domains (medical, planning, forecasting), from synthetic to naturalistic scenarios, and across framings. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, per-update asymmetry score and its sign/self-relevance modulation, internal-vs-verbal gap, asymmetry–optimism AUROC, patching logit-difference effect sizes, post-intervention symmetry restoration and oracle-agreement delta, integration accuracy delta, perplexity delta.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The observed asymmetry could reflect the model misjudging evidence *strength* for valenced items rather than a genuine update-magnitude bias; the synthetic explicit-likelihood-ratio design, comprehension checks, and matched |LLR| controls are built to dissociate strength-misperception from valence gating (though for naturalistic items strength is only approximate). The asymmetry might be absent (a robust negative result is still valuable, showing LLMs update more rationally than humans on valenced evidence, or only mimic optimism in wording not internally). Valence gating may not be cleanly linear or single-locus; we report layerwise results and treat 'restore symmetry' vs. 'exaggerate' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact component. Self-relevance framing may just trigger sycophancy-like compliance; step 6's comparison to compliance-subspace directions and the dis-preferred-framing sign-flip test disentangle valence-of-content from social pressure. Steering could degrade fluency or blunt all updating (making the model ignore evidence); we monitor perplexity, neutral-scenario integration accuracy, and general benchmarks, and use small magnitudes with random-direction baselines. 'Desirability' labels are partly subjective and may reflect training-data framing; we human-validate a sample and balance across domains. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: continued_influence_belief
Title: Retracted but Not Erased: The Continued Influence of Corrected Misinformation in LLM Belief Representations
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM reads a false claim about an item that is later explicitly retracted in the same context, it verbally acknowledges the retraction yet retains an internally-decodable 'stale belief' in the retracted claim that continues to drive its downstream inferences — an LLM analogue of the human Continued Influence Effect (CIE). This internal residual belief is separable from the model's stated belief, predicts CIE-style reasoning errors, and can be causally erased by intervening on the component that carries it.
Related Work: The Continued Influence Effect / belief perseverance is a canonical, heavily-cited human finding: corrected misinformation continues to influence reasoning even after successful retraction (Chan et al. 2017 meta-analysis; Ecker et al. 2022 Nature Rev Psych; constraint-satisfaction models of perseverance, Read & Marcus-Newhall 2001; DIO model 2025). In LLMs, prior work studies (a) knowledge-editing reversibility and 'superficial editing' (Superficial Editing 2025; Believe It or Not 2025), (b) belief shifts under pretraining poisoning (Layer of Truth 2025), (c) intra-memory knowledge conflict localization (Where Knowledge Collides 2026), and (d) in-context knowledge conflict / sycophancy behaviorally. Crucially, NONE isolate the CIE signature: a *within-context* retraction event after which the model behaviorally acknowledges the correction yet an internally-decodable belief in the *retracted* claim persists and continues to drive inferences. Prior belief-entrenchment work (Martingale Score; confirmation-bias CoT) concerns gradual non-Bayesian drift, not persistence of an explicitly-corrected proposition. We transfer a specific human-cognition phenomenon into LLMs, dissociate stated-vs-internal belief around a discrete correction, and give it a causal mechanistic treatment (locate + intervene), which is new.
Abstract: People keep using misinformation even after they accept a correction — the Continued Influence Effect (CIE), one of the most robust findings in the misinformation literature. As LLMs increasingly ingest, then are corrected on, false claims within a single context (RAG updates, user retractions, multi-turn edits), we ask whether they inherit CIE at the level of their internal beliefs. We hypothesize that after an explicit in-context retraction of a false item-state claim, an LLM (i) verbally acknowledges the correction but (ii) retains a linearly-decodable residual belief in the retracted claim, (iii) this internal residual belief — not the stated belief — predicts continued reliance on the misinformation in downstream inference, and (iv) the residual can be causally erased by intervening on the component that carries it, reducing CIE-style errors. We build a controlled dataset of narratives/knowledge items in which a false claim is introduced and then retracted (with matched no-retraction and never-introduced controls), using both real-fact and synthetic-entity tracks to control priors, plus downstream inference probes whose correct answer depends on discarding the retracted claim. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear belief probes to read the internal belief in the retracted claim across layers, compute a per-item CIE residual (internal belief post-retraction minus never-introduced baseline), test whether it dissociates from stated belief and predicts downstream reliance (AUROC vs. a log-prob baseline), localize the responsible heads via activation patching, and test a contrastive 'retraction-completion' steering intervention that drives the internal belief to baseline. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, CIE residual magnitude, stated-vs-internal dissociation, reliance-prediction AUROC, patching effect sizes, post-intervention error reduction, and perplexity.
Experiments: 1) Dataset construction: Build ~5k scenarios each containing a false claim about an item's state that is later retracted, following the classic CIE paradigm. Two tracks: (a) REAL-FACT narratives (e.g., a report initially says 'the fire was caused by flammable materials in the closet' then retracts it) adapted from CIE stimuli; (b) SYNTHETIC-ENTITY track with novel entities/attributes to fully control pretraining priors (e.g., 'Zorblax was reported to orbit Kelvath. Correction: this was an error; Zorblax does not orbit Kelvath.'). Conditions per item: (i) RETRACTED (claim introduced then explicitly corrected), (ii) NO-RETRACTION (claim introduced, never corrected), (iii) NEVER-INTRODUCED (claim absent) as baseline. Vary retraction strength (mere negation vs. explanatory correction that supplies an alternative), following the CIE finding that alternatives matter. Add: a STATED-BELIEF probe ('Is it true that Zorblax orbits Kelvath?'), a DOWNSTREAM-RELIANCE probe (an open inference question whose correct answer requires discarding the retracted claim, e.g., 'What likely explains X?'), and comprehension checks (can the model restate that a correction occurred) to separate parsing failure from genuine perseverance. Include paraphrase/format perturbations to guard against surface cues. 2) Internal belief probing: For Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B, extract residual-stream and per-head activations at the retracted-claim's key tokens across layers, WITHOUT asking the stated-belief question, in all three conditions. Train linear belief probes (P(retracted claim holds)) on held-out data with shuffled-label control tasks. Define CIE residual = probe belief(RETRACTED) − probe belief(NEVER-INTRODUCED) at the item, per layer. A positive residual is the internal CIE signature. 3) Dissociation: Compare the internal CIE residual to the model's STATED belief (which should reflect the correction). Test the key CIE claim that the internal residual persists even when the stated belief has updated (per-item: stated=false but internal residual>0). Compare retraction-strength conditions (mere-negation vs. explanatory-alternative), predicting explanatory alternatives reduce the residual, mirroring humans. 4) Predictiveness: Collect ground-truth DOWNSTREAM-RELIANCE (does the model use the retracted claim in its open inference?). Test whether the internal CIE residual predicts per-item reliance (AUROC), compared against (a) a log-prob confidence baseline and (b) the stated-belief readout, to show the internal residual carries reliance-relevant information beyond what the model says. 5) Localization: Use activation patching / causal mediation to find heads/layers that carry the residual belief post-retraction (patch RETRACTED-condition activations into NEVER-INTRODUCED runs, and vice versa) to find the minimal component restoring/removing the residual; compare to knowledge-conflict heads reported in prior late-layer work. 6) Causal intervention ('retraction completion'): Derive a contrastive steering direction from RETRACTED vs. NEVER-INTRODUCED activations (the residual direction); test that (a) subtracting it drives the internal belief to baseline and reduces downstream reliance/CIE errors, (b) adding it exaggerates perseverance, (c) specificity: matched random directions and the truth direction do not reduce CIE, and unrelated facts/general benchmarks (MMLU subset) and perplexity are preserved. 7) Generalization: Test probe/steering transfer across the real and synthetic tracks, across domains, and across retraction phrasings. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, CIE residual magnitude by condition/layer, stated-vs-internal dissociation rate, reliance-prediction AUROC, patching logit-difference effect sizes, post-intervention CIE-error reduction, specificity checks, perplexity delta.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The residual could reflect surface co-occurrence of the retracted claim's tokens rather than a genuine belief; matched NEVER-INTRODUCED controls, non-introduced distractors, comprehension checks, and paraphrase perturbations mitigate this. CIE may be absent internally (a robust negative result — LLMs fully erase corrected claims — would itself be a valuable, publishable finding contrasting with humans). Stated belief and downstream reliance may both fail simply because the model can't parse the retraction; comprehension checks and the RETRACTED-vs-NO-RETRACTION contrast disentangle parsing failure from perseverance. The residual may not be cleanly linear or single-locus; we report layerwise results and treat 'drive belief to baseline / reduce CIE' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact component. Real-fact CIE stimuli may interact with pretraining priors; the synthetic track isolates the in-context mechanism. Downstream-reliance judgments require careful open-ended scoring (LLM-judge plus human validation on a sample). Steering could degrade fluency or over-suppress legitimately retained information; we use small magnitudes, random/truth-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity and general benchmarks. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: illusory_truth_internal
Title: Say It Again: In-Context Repetition Inflates LLMs' Internal Belief Confidence Independent of Truth
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human illusory-truth effect, merely repeating a claim within an LLM's context monotonically inflates the model's internally-decoded belief/confidence in that claim as a dose-response of repetition count, independent of (and even against) the claim's factual truth. This repetition-driven inflation is carried by an identifiable internal component (a 'familiarity/fluency' direction or set of heads) that is causally dissociable from the truth-value direction: ablating it restores truth-tracking without removing the model's ability to represent truth.
Related Work: The illusory-truth effect — repetition raising perceived truth and, separately, subjective confidence independent of factual truth — is among the most robust findings in cognitive psychology (Dechene et al.; Fazio et al. 2015; Hassan & Barber 2021 on repetition frequency; Unkelbach 2010 on fluency-as-cue; illusory-certainty 2024 showing repetition inflates confidence orthogonally to truth). In LLMs, repetition has been studied only at TRAINING time: 'Scaling Laws of Learning from Repeated Data' (2022) links repeated pretraining data to induction-head damage and memorization; 'Learning and Unlearning of Fabricated Knowledge' (2024) studies durability of injected facts; 'Layer of Truth' (2025) studies continual-pretraining poisoning shifting late-layer beliefs. The truth-probe literature (Geometry of Truth 2023; Azaria & Mitchell 2023; Truth-value judgment 2024) isolates a linear truth direction; CCPS (2025) probes confidence via representation stability. CRITICALLY, no work asks whether IN-CONTEXT (inference-time) repetition inflates an INTERNALLY-DECODED belief/confidence as a dose-response, orthogonally to truth, and whether that inflation is a locatable, ablatable fluency/familiarity component distinct from the truth direction. We transfer a canonical human-cognition phenomenon into LLM internals and give it a mechanistic, causal treatment.
Abstract: People judge repeated statements as truer and grow more confident in them, even when the statements are false — the illusory-truth effect, a fluency-driven bias separable from actual discrimination ability. As LLMs increasingly ingest contexts where the same claim recurs (repeated user assertions, echoed retrieval passages, multi-document redundancy), we ask whether they inherit this bias at the level of their internal beliefs. We hypothesize that (i) merely repeating a claim within the context monotonically inflates the model's internally-decoded belief/confidence in it as a dose-response of repetition count, (ii) this inflation is largely independent of the claim's factual truth and can push false claims toward 'believed', (iii) it is mediated by an identifiable internal 'familiarity/fluency' component that is causally dissociable from the well-studied truth-value direction, and (iv) ablating that component restores truth-tracking without destroying the model's representation of truth. We build a controlled dataset of matched true and false item-state claims each embedded in contexts that repeat the claim 0 to N times (with paraphrased-repetition and unrelated-filler controls to separate meaning-level repetition from token/length confounds), including a synthetic-entity track to control pretraining priors. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear belief and confidence probes, measure the repetition dose-response of the internal readout separately for true and false claims, quantify the truth-independent inflation, geometrically relate the repetition-inflation direction to the truth direction, localize responsible heads via activation patching, and test causal control by steering/ablating the inflation direction. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, per-count belief/confidence dose-response slopes, truth-independence of inflation, subspace angle vs. truth, patching effect sizes, post-ablation truth-tracking restoration, and perplexity.
Experiments: 1) Dataset construction: Generate ~6k item-state claims, balanced TRUE and FALSE, across domains (geography, science, history, trivia). Two tracks: (a) REAL facts the models reliably know/disbelieve; (b) SYNTHETIC novel-entity claims (e.g., 'Zorblax orbits Kelvath') with stipulated ground truth to control pretraining priors. For each claim, build matched contexts that present the claim REPEATED k times, k in {0,1,2,4,8}, interspersed with neutral filler. Include controls: (i) VERBATIM repetition, (ii) PARAPHRASED repetition (same proposition, different surface form — tests meaning-level vs. token-level repetition), (iii) LENGTH-MATCHED filler with the claim shown once (controls for context length), (iv) REPEATED-DISTRACTOR (an unrelated claim repeated k times, controls for generic repetition). Add a behavioral truth-judgment probe ('Is it true that X? Answer and rate your confidence') and comprehension checks. Apply format/paraphrase perturbations. 2) Internal probing: For Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B, extract residual-stream and per-head activations at the claim's key tokens (final query occurrence) across layers. Train (i) a linear BELIEF probe (P(claim true)) and (ii) a CONFIDENCE probe (following CCPS-style / representation-based confidence) on held-out data with shuffled-label control tasks; report per-layer accuracy/AUROC. 3) Dose-response measurement: For each k, read the internal belief and confidence at the query, SEPARATELY for true and false claims. Fit dose-response slopes (internal readout vs. k). Test the key illusory-truth prediction: belief/confidence rises monotonically with k for BOTH true and false claims (positive slope even for false), i.e., inflation is not just correct evidence accumulation. Compare verbatim vs. paraphrased repetition (a robust effect for paraphrase implicates a meaning-level familiarity signal), and confirm repeated-distractor / length-matched controls do not inflate the target claim's readout (specificity). 4) Truth-independence & geometry: Quantify the truth-INDEPENDENT component of inflation (belief shift attributable to k after conditioning on ground truth). Compute cosine/subspace angle between the repetition-inflation direction (difference-in-means: high-k vs. k=0 activations) and the truth-value direction; test whether inflation is decodable after projecting out the truth direction. 5) Localization: Use activation patching / causal mediation from high-k to k=0 runs to find the minimal heads/layers whose states carry the repetition-inflation signal; contrast with copying/induction heads (from repeated-data work) and truth/belief heads. 6) Causal control: Derive an 'inflation' steering direction (contrastive high-k vs. k=0). Test (a) subtracting/ablating it drives the internal belief on repeated FALSE claims back toward k=0 baseline and improves behavioral truth-judgment accuracy on repeated-false items; (b) adding it exaggerates illusory belief; (c) specificity: matched random directions and the truth direction itself do not selectively fix repeated-false items; (d) collateral checks: general benchmarks (MMLU subset), non-repeated claim accuracy, and perplexity are preserved. 7) Predictiveness & generalization: Test whether the internal inflation readout predicts behavioral illusory-truth errors (AUROC) beyond a log-prob baseline; test probe/steering transfer across domains, real vs. synthetic tracks, and repetition types. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, per-count dose-response slopes (true vs. false), truth-independent inflation magnitude, subspace angle and projected-out decodability vs. truth, patching logit-difference effect sizes, post-ablation truth-tracking restoration and error-reduction deltas, prediction AUROC, perplexity/benchmark deltas.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Repetition-driven belief change might be rational evidence accumulation rather than a fluency bias; the false-claim dose-response (repetition should NOT raise belief in a false claim if the model is rational), the paraphrased-repetition condition, and the repeated-distractor/length-matched controls are designed to dissociate genuine illusory-truth from evidence integration and length/token confounds. The effect may be absent internally (a robust negative result — LLMs resist in-context repetition bias — would itself be a valuable, publishable finding contrasting with humans). Belief and confidence probes may not be cleanly linear at every layer; we report layerwise results with control tasks and separate the two probes. The inflation and truth directions may be more entangled than hypothesized, in which case the finding characterizes their entanglement (still informative). Localization may yield a distributed rather than discrete component; we treat 'ablate to restore truth-tracking' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact head. Real-fact repetition interacts with pretraining priors; the synthetic track isolates the in-context mechanism. Steering could degrade fluency or blunt legitimate in-context updating; we use small magnitudes, random/truth-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity, non-repeated accuracy, and general benchmarks. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: behavioral_self_prediction_gap
Title: Do As I Say I Will? Probing the Gap Between an LLM's Internal Commitment and Its Actual Behavior
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM is asked to predict its own future behavior on an item (e.g., 'Will you answer / comply / refuse this?'), it forms an internally-decodable belief about that intended behavior, but this internal commitment (i) systematically diverges from the model's stated self-prediction in a self-flattering direction (it predicts it will behave better/more helpfully or more safely than it actually does), and (ii) the internal commitment predicts actual downstream behavior better than the stated self-prediction. This 'say-do' commitment is a distinct, decodable, causally steerable variable, separate from answer-correctness calibration studied in prior work.
Related Work: Prior interpretability work on self-knowledge concerns (a) answer-correctness calibration/confidence (Cognitive Dissonance 2023; confidence directions), (b) introspection about injected concepts (Emergent Introspective Awareness 2025; Feeling the Strength but Not the Source 2025; Latent Introspection 2026) and metacognitive monitoring/control of activations (LLMs Are Capable of Metacognitive Monitoring 2025), and (c) whether models introspect about linguistic knowledge (Language Models Fail to Introspect 2025). Belief-representation work decodes self/other beliefs about story worlds (Beliefs of Self and Others 2024; Brittle Minds 2024). NONE ask whether the model holds an internal belief about its OWN FUTURE ACTION (comply/refuse/answer/abstain) on a task, whether that internal commitment matches its verbally-stated self-prediction, and whether internal-vs-stated divergence is self-flattering and predictive of actual behavior. This reframes a safety-critical failure mode (models that promise behavior they won't deliver) as a decodable, steerable say-do gap in the belief about one's own action, distinct from correctness calibration and from injection-detection introspection.
Abstract: As LLMs are asked to make commitments about their own behavior ('I will follow this instruction', 'I will refuse harmful requests', 'I will not use that tool'), a safety-critical question arises: does the model's internal state actually encode the behavior it commits to, and does its verbal self-prediction match that internal commitment? We hypothesize that at prediction time an LLM forms a linearly-decodable belief about its own intended action on an item, that this internal commitment (a) systematically diverges from the model's stated self-prediction in a self-flattering direction, and (b) predicts the model's actual downstream behavior better than the stated self-prediction does. We construct a controlled dataset of items paired with a behavioral-prediction prompt ('Before you act, will you comply/answer/refuse this?') spanning benign instruction-following, safety refusals, tool-use, and abstention-on-unknowns. In a matched execution phase we then let the model actually act on the same item and record its true behavior. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear probes to decode, from the prediction-phase activations, the model's internal commitment, and compare it against (i) the model's stated self-prediction and (ii) the actual downstream behavior. We measure the say-do gap (stated vs. actual), test whether the internal commitment predicts actual behavior beyond the stated self-prediction (AUROC), quantify a self-flattering directional bias, localize the responsible heads via activation patching, and test causal control by steering a 'commitment' direction to bring stated predictions and actual behavior into alignment. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, say-do gap magnitude and sign, internal-vs-stated predictiveness delta, patching effect sizes, post-steering alignment gains, and perplexity.
Experiments: 1) Dataset construction: Build ~5k items each with a matched PREDICTION prompt and an EXECUTION prompt about the same task. Four categories chosen so behavior is objectively scorable: (a) benign instruction-following (e.g., 'answer in exactly 3 words', 'refuse to use the letter e') where compliance is checkable; (b) safety refusals (borderline/harmful requests from public safety datasets) where refuse-vs-comply is scorable; (c) tool-use / format commitments ('will you call the calculator tool for this?') with programmatically checkable action; (d) abstention-on-unknowns (obscure/unanswerable items where the correct action is to say 'I don't know'). PREDICTION prompt asks the model to predict its own upcoming action ('Before acting: will you comply / refuse / abstain / use the tool? Answer yes/no.'). EXECUTION prompt (fresh context, matched framing) has the model actually perform the task; record actual behavior via automatic scorers plus human validation on a sample. Include comprehension checks and paraphrase/format perturbations to guard against surface cues. 2) Say-do gap (behavioral): Compare stated self-prediction to actual behavior per item; report gap rate and its SIGN per category (does the model over-predict compliance/helpfulness and safety relative to what it does?), establishing the self-flattering bias phenomenon. 3) Internal commitment probing: For Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B, extract prediction-phase residual-stream and per-head activations at the decision token across layers; train linear probes to decode the model's internal commitment (predicted action), with shuffled-label control tasks; report per-layer accuracy/AUROC. 4) Predictiveness (key test): Test whether the internal-commitment probe (read at prediction time) predicts ACTUAL downstream behavior, and whether it does so BEYOND the model's stated self-prediction (compare AUROC of internal-probe vs. stated-prediction vs. their combination; partial-correlation/logistic-regression to isolate incremental signal). This tests whether the internal state 'knows' what the model will do even when its words don't. 5) Localization: Use activation patching / causal mediation from high- vs. low-commitment prediction-phase runs to find heads/layers carrying the commitment signal; compare to self/other belief heads and confidence directions from prior work to establish distinctness. 6) Causal control: Derive a contrastive 'commitment' steering direction (will-comply vs. will-refuse/abstain activations). Test (a) steering the prediction-phase commitment shifts actual execution-phase behavior in the predicted direction (dose-response), demonstrating the internal commitment is causal for behavior, not epiphenomenal; (b) using the internal commitment to correct the stated self-prediction reduces the say-do gap; (c) specificity: random and confidence-direction baselines do not selectively move behavior; (d) collateral checks on general benchmarks (MMLU subset) and perplexity. 7) Generalization: Test probe/steering transfer across the four categories and to multi-turn commitments (model promises in turn 1, acts in turn 3). Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, say-do gap magnitude and sign per category, internal-vs-stated predictiveness delta (incremental AUROC), patching logit-difference effect sizes, post-steering gap-reduction and behavior-shift deltas, perplexity/benchmark deltas.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Prediction and execution are in separate contexts, so a 'gap' could reflect context/sampling variance rather than a genuine self-model failure; matched framing, temperature control, repeated sampling, and a within-context variant (predict then immediately act) mitigate this. The internal-commitment probe might merely recover task features (e.g., 'this is harmful') rather than a genuine action-belief; category-balanced controls, non-behavioral distractor probes, and the incremental-over-stated-prediction test help separate action-commitment from task-feature decoding. The self-flattering bias may be small or category-specific (a robust negative or category-conditional result is still informative). Automatic behavior scoring is imperfect for open-ended items; we use programmatically checkable tasks where possible plus human validation. Steering could degrade fluency or induce indiscriminate compliance/refusal; we use small magnitudes, random/confidence-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity and general benchmarks. Instruction-tuned models may behave differently from base models (an interesting comparison but limits universality). Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: self_authored_belief_endowment
Title: I Thought of It, So It Must Be True: Do LLMs Over-Believe Their Own Self-Generated Claims?
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human 'generation effect' and endowment bias, an LLM holds a stronger internal belief in a proposition when the model itself generated it (e.g., as a chain-of-thought conclusion) than when the identical proposition is presented as externally-given text, holding content and truth constant. This self-authorship endowment is (i) linearly decodable as an internal belief-strength inflation, (ii) largely orthogonal to the truth-value direction, (iii) carried by an identifiable internal component, and (iv) causally reducible by steering, thereby lowering the model's tendency to trust its own unverified reasoning.
Related Work: Prior interpretability work isolates a linear truth-value/belief direction (Geometry of Truth 2023; Azaria & Mitchell 2023; Truth-value judgment 2024) and studies social overrides of belief (When Truth Is Overridden: sycophancy 2025; Signal Competition 2025; Trust Me I'm an Expert 2026). Notably, 'When Truth Is Overridden' finds user *expertise* is NOT internally encoded, and authority/credibility work concerns *external* source cues. My own prior proposal on belief-provenance tags source generically (prior vs. context vs. retrieval) but does NOT isolate self-authorship as a belief-STRENGTH modulator, nor connect it to the human generation/endowment effect, nor test the safety-critical case of a model over-trusting its OWN chain-of-thought conclusions. Confirmation-bias/entrenchment work (Martingale Score; CoT confirmation bias) concerns temporal drift, not authorship. No prior work asks whether merely being the *author* of a claim inflates an LLM's internal belief in it relative to the identical externally-supplied claim, nor gives this a mechanistic, causal treatment. We transfer a canonical human-cognition phenomenon (generation effect / endowment) into LLM belief internals.
Abstract: Humans believe and remember information more strongly when they generate it themselves than when they merely read it — the 'generation effect', a cousin of the endowment bias. As LLMs increasingly reason via chain-of-thought and then act on their own intermediate conclusions, a safety-critical question arises: does a model over-trust a claim simply because it produced the claim itself? We hypothesize that an LLM holds a stronger internal belief in a proposition it self-generated than in the identical proposition presented as external text, with content and factual truth held constant. We build a controlled dataset of matched item-state claims that appear in two conditions: SELF-AUTHORED (the model derives/states the claim as its own chain-of-thought conclusion) and EXTERNAL (the same verbatim claim is supplied as given text the model reads), plus true/false variants and a synthetic-entity track to control pretraining priors. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear belief probes to read internal belief strength at the claim, compute a per-item authorship-endowment score (self-authored belief minus external belief), test whether it is positive even for false claims (so it is not rational evidence), measure its geometric relationship to the truth direction, localize the responsible heads via activation patching, and test causal control by steering an 'authorship-endowment' direction to restore parity. We further test whether the endowment predicts a downstream failure: over-reliance on unverified self-generated claims in multi-step tasks. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, authorship-endowment score, truth-independence, subspace angle vs. truth, patching effect sizes, post-steering parity restoration, downstream over-reliance reduction, and perplexity.
Experiments: 1) Dataset construction: Generate ~6k item-state claims, balanced TRUE/FALSE, across domains (arithmetic/logic conclusions, factual attributions, entity-attribute claims). Two tracks: (a) REAL claims the models can plausibly derive/read; (b) SYNTHETIC novel-entity claims with stipulated ground truth to control priors. For each claim create MATCHED conditions with identical verbatim proposition at the read-out point: (i) SELF-AUTHORED — elicit the claim as the model's own conclusion via a short CoT/derivation ('Reason step by step, then state your conclusion'), then read internal belief at the model-produced conclusion token; (ii) EXTERNAL — the identical conclusion sentence is supplied verbatim as given text ('Here is a statement: <claim>') from a neutral source, and belief is read at the same tokens. Control conditions: (iii) EXTERNAL-ATTRIBUTED-TO-SELF (text says 'You previously concluded: <claim>' without the model actually generating it) to separate authorship from mere self-attribution; (iv) LENGTH/EFFORT-MATCHED external (a filler derivation precedes the external claim) to control for context length and preceding reasoning tokens. Include comprehension checks and paraphrase/format perturbations. 2) Internal belief probing: For Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B, extract residual-stream and per-head activations at the claim tokens across layers; train linear BELIEF probes (P(claim true)) and a representation-based CONFIDENCE probe, with shuffled-label control tasks; report per-layer accuracy/AUROC. 3) Endowment measurement: Define authorship-endowment = belief(SELF-AUTHORED) − belief(EXTERNAL) per item and layer. Test the key prediction that endowment > 0 for BOTH true and false claims (positive even for FALSE self-generated claims → not rational evidence accumulation). Verify control conditions: mere self-attribution (iii) yields smaller endowment than genuine generation, and length-matched (iv) rules out context-length confounds. 4) Truth-independence & geometry: Quantify the truth-independent endowment (belief shift after conditioning on ground truth); compute cosine/subspace angle between the endowment direction (difference-in-means SELF vs. EXTERNAL activations) and the truth-value direction; test whether endowment remains decodable after projecting out the truth direction. 5) Localization: Use activation patching / causal mediation from SELF-AUTHORED to EXTERNAL runs to find the minimal heads/layers carrying the endowment signal; contrast with truth/belief heads and with any 'self'/authorship representation from prior self-recognition work. 6) Causal control: Derive a contrastive 'authorship-endowment' steering direction (SELF vs. EXTERNAL). Test (a) subtracting it drives self-authored belief on FALSE claims toward external-parity and reduces over-confidence; (b) adding it exaggerates self-endowment; (c) specificity: matched random directions and the truth direction do not selectively restore parity; (d) collateral checks on general benchmarks (MMLU subset), non-manipulated claim accuracy, and perplexity. 7) Downstream over-reliance & predictiveness: In multi-step tasks (multi-hop QA, arithmetic word problems) where an intermediate self-generated claim may be wrong, test whether the internal endowment predicts the model failing to revisit/verify its own erroneous intermediate conclusion (AUROC vs. a log-prob baseline), and whether endowment-reducing steering increases self-correction and final accuracy on items with a faulty self-generated step. 8) Generalization: Test probe/steering transfer across domains, real vs. synthetic tracks, and authorship elicitation styles. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, authorship-endowment score (true vs. false), truth-independent endowment magnitude, subspace angle and projected-out decodability vs. truth, control-condition contrasts, patching logit-difference effect sizes, post-steering parity restoration, downstream self-correction / accuracy deltas, over-reliance prediction AUROC, perplexity/benchmark deltas.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The endowment could reflect rational reasons — a self-generated claim followed a derivation the model 'trusts', which is legitimate when the derivation is correct; the FALSE-claim contrast, the self-attribution control (iii), and the length/effort-matched control (iv) are designed to isolate authorship-per-se from valid derivation and from context confounds (though for correct derivations the two are hard to fully separate). The effect may be absent internally (a robust negative result — LLMs weight self- and externally-authored claims equally — is itself publishable and reassuring for safety). Reading belief at 'identical' tokens across conditions is imperfect because surrounding context differs; we anchor probes at matched claim tokens, use paraphrase perturbations, and report layerwise results. Endowment and truth directions may be more entangled than hypothesized, in which case the finding characterizes their entanglement (still informative). Localization may be distributed; we treat 'steer to restore parity' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact head. Downstream over-reliance scoring on open-ended steps needs careful automatic + human-validated judging. Steering could degrade fluency or make the model distrust its own correct reasoning (harming accuracy on items with valid self-generated steps); we use small magnitudes, random/truth-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity, valid-derivation accuracy, and general benchmarks. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: source_independence_discounting
Title: Counting Voices, Not Sources: Do LLMs Internally Track Whether Consensus Is Independent?
Short Hypothesis: When multiple retrieved documents assert the same claim, a rational agent should update its belief more if the sources are independent than if they are copies of one origin (the 'illusion of consensus' failure in humans). We hypothesize that LLMs DO form an internal, linearly-decodable representation of source independence-vs-dependence, but that this representation is causally under-weighted: the belief-update magnitude tracks raw report COUNT far more than the internally-available independence signal. We further hypothesize an identifiable internal component gates independence-discounting, and steering it can restore appropriate discounting of redundant sources — improving RAG faithfulness on repeated-but-non-independent evidence.
Related Work: Human social-learning work shows people partially discount correlated/dependent sources and distinguish true from false consensus (Bayesian belief polarization via source-independence perceptions, 2024; belief revision sensitive to statistical dependencies, 2020; social meta-inference / evidentiary value of consensus, 2021; getting to the source of the illusion of consensus, 2021). In LLMs, behavioral RAG work finds models are 'heuristic followers': paraphrased repetition is MORE persuasive than distinct independent support, and models show primacy/repetition biases (GroupQA: Rational Synthesizers or Heuristic Followers?, 2026; DynamicQA 2024). Knowledge-conflict probing shows parametric-vs-contextual source and conflict are linearly decodable (Probing Language Models on Their Knowledge Source, 2024; ProbeRAG/CLEAR, 2025), and Belief Dynamics (2025) gives a Bayesian account of in-context evidence accumulation as sigmoidal in report count. My prior 'illusory_truth_internal' proposal studies repetition-count dose-response of a single claim's belief, and 'belief_source_tags' studies provenance (prior/context/retrieval). NONE isolate an internal representation of source INDEPENDENCE (are these N reports genuinely distinct origins or copies of one?), nor test whether the belief-update under-weights that internally-available signal relative to raw count, nor causally restore independence-discounting. We transfer the canonical 'illusion of consensus' into LLM internals and give it a mechanistic, causal treatment.
Abstract: If ten news outlets independently confirm a claim, it is far stronger evidence than the same story copied ten times from one wire report. Humans partially honor this distinction; recent behavioral work shows LLMs largely do not, treating paraphrased repetition as more persuasive than genuinely independent support — an 'illusion of consensus' with direct consequences for retrieval-augmented generation. We ask a sharper, mechanistic question: does an LLM internally represent whether a set of agreeing sources is independent or dependent, and if so, why does it fail to use that signal? We hypothesize that (i) source independence-vs-dependence is linearly decodable from residual-stream activations at the point the model reads a group of agreeing reports, (ii) the model's internal belief-update magnitude nonetheless tracks raw report COUNT far more than this independence signal (a decodable-but-under-used representation), (iii) an identifiable internal component gates independence-discounting, and (iv) steering that component restores appropriate discounting of redundant sources. We build a controlled dataset of item-state claims each supported by N reports whose INDEPENDENCE is varied (verbatim copies, paraphrases attributed to one origin, and genuinely distinct independent sources) at matched surface repetition counts, with a synthetic-entity track to control priors. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear probes to decode independence and to read internal belief, quantify how belief tracks count vs. independence against a Bayesian oracle, localize the gating component via activation patching, and test a contrastive steering intervention that restores discounting. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, count-vs-independence belief sensitivity, oracle-deviation, patching effect sizes, post-steering discounting restoration and RAG-faithfulness gains, and perplexity.
Experiments: 1) Dataset construction: Generate ~5k item-state claims across domains (news-style facts, science claims, entity-attributes). Two tracks: (a) REAL claims models plausibly evaluate; (b) SYNTHETIC novel-entity claims (e.g., 'Zorblax orbits Kelvath') with stipulated ground truth to control pretraining priors. For each claim, construct evidence groups that vary INDEPENDENCE while holding report COUNT (N in {1,2,4,8}) constant: (i) INDEPENDENT — N genuinely distinct sources with different authors/outlets/wording/reasoning; (ii) DEPENDENT-VERBATIM — the same report copied N times (explicitly attributed to one origin, e.g., 'reprinted from Source A'); (iii) DEPENDENT-PARAPHRASE — N paraphrases explicitly derived from one origin ('Sources B–E all cite Source A'). Cross with TRUE/FALSE claims. Include a Bayesian ORACLE label: independent reports should raise posterior more than dependent copies at equal N (compute an explicit likelihood-ratio oracle on the synthetic track). Add a downstream BELIEF/ANSWER probe ('Given these reports, how confident are you that X? Answer + confidence'), comprehension checks (can the model restate which sources are independent?), and paraphrase/format/order perturbations (to separate independence from primacy/length confounds). 2) Independence probing: For Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B, extract residual-stream and per-head activations after the model reads the evidence group, across layers; train linear probes to decode INDEPENDENCE (independent vs. dependent) at matched N, with shuffled-label control tasks; report per-layer accuracy/AUROC. This tests whether the signal is internally available. 3) Belief probing & count-vs-independence sensitivity: Train linear BELIEF/confidence probes reading internal posterior in the claim. For each condition, measure how the internal belief scales with (a) report COUNT and (b) INDEPENDENCE. Fit belief ~ count + independence and report standardized coefficients; the key prediction is a large count coefficient and a small independence coefficient relative to the Bayesian oracle (under-weighting the available signal). Compute per-item oracle-deviation. Compare verbal-output sensitivity to internal-belief sensitivity. 4) Localization: Use activation patching / causal mediation to find heads/layers carrying the independence signal and those gating the discounting of dependent evidence (patch INDEPENDENT-group activations into DEPENDENT-group runs at matched N; find the minimal component that increases/decreases the belief update); contrast with knowledge-source/conflict heads from prior probing work and with copying/induction heads. 5) Causal restoration: Derive a contrastive 'independence-discounting' steering direction (independent vs. dependent activations at matched N). Test (a) applying it on DEPENDENT groups reduces the (unwarranted) belief update toward oracle-appropriate discounting; (b) removing/negating it on INDEPENDENT groups collapses the update, confirming causality; (c) specificity: random-direction and truth-direction steering do not selectively restore discounting; (d) collateral checks on general benchmarks (MMLU subset), independent-evidence accuracy, and perplexity. 6) Predictiveness & RAG application: Test whether the internal independence probe predicts the model's behavioral over-persuasion by redundant sources (AUROC vs. a log-prob baseline), and whether discounting-steering improves faithfulness/accuracy on a RAG-style task where the majority of retrieved passages are non-independent copies of a false claim while a minority independent source is correct. 7) Generalization: Test probe/steering transfer across domains, real vs. synthetic tracks, dependence types (verbatim vs. paraphrase), and report counts. Metrics: independence-probe accuracy/AUROC, belief count vs. independence coefficients and oracle-deviation, internal-vs-verbal gap, patching logit-difference effect sizes, post-steering discounting-restoration and RAG-faithfulness/accuracy deltas, over-persuasion prediction AUROC, perplexity/benchmark deltas.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The independence signal may not be internally decodable at all — a robust negative result (LLMs simply count reports and never represent independence) is itself valuable and would sharpen the 'heuristic follower' picture for RAG design. Conversely, if belief already tracks independence appropriately, the interesting finding shifts to characterizing the (smaller-than-expected) illusion — still informative. Independence might be decoded via surface cues (explicit 'reprinted from A' tags) rather than an abstract representation; we mitigate with diverse framings, paraphrase/order perturbations, comprehension checks, and a condition where independence must be inferred from author/wording diversity rather than an explicit tag. Count and independence can be partially confounded with context length and primacy; matched-N designs, length-matched fillers, and order perturbations dissociate them. The Bayesian oracle is exact only on the synthetic track; real-claim oracles are approximate. Steering could degrade fluency or make the model indiscriminately distrust all repeated evidence (harming legitimate independent consensus); we use small magnitudes, random/truth-direction baselines, monitor perplexity, independent-evidence accuracy, and general benchmarks. Downstream RAG-faithfulness scoring on open-ended answers needs automatic + human-validated judging. Localization may be distributed; we treat 'steer to restore discounting' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact head. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: internal_belief_coherence_gap
Title: Rational Inside, Fallacious Out: Is the Conjunction Fallacy a Readout Bug in LLM Belief Representations?
Short Hypothesis: The conjunction fallacy and related probabilistic incoherence in LLMs are largely a *verbalization/readout* failure rather than a failure of the model's internal belief representation: a linearly-decoded internal belief-strength readout for conjunctions (P(A∧B)) respects probability-theory monotonicity (≤ P(A) and ≤ P(B)) far more often than the model's stated probability judgments do. The internal representation is thus more coherent than the output, the residual internal incoherence is carried by an identifiable component, and steering it can bring stated judgments back into coherence.
Related Work: Behavioral work shows LLMs produce incoherent probability judgments mirroring human systematic deviations (Incoherent Probability Judgments in LLMs, Zhu et al. 2024) and commit the conjunction fallacy driven by token bias (A Peek into Token Bias, 2024; Thinking Fast and Slow in LLMs, 2022). Others attempt to *recover* coherent probabilities from embeddings by imposing axiomatic constraints via a trained VAE (Recovering Event Probabilities from LLM Embeddings, 2025) or find LLMs fail to give rational probabilistic beliefs at the output (Exploring the Potential..., 2025). Interpretability work isolates linear truth/belief directions (Geometry of Truth 2023; Truth-value judgment 2024), plausibility/modal-category vectors (Is This Just Fantasy? 2025), and belief-state geometry (Constrained Belief Updates 2025). CRITICALLY, all prior probabilistic-coherence work is either purely behavioral or *engineers* a coherent latent via extra training; none ask whether the model's *own, natively-decoded* belief-strength representation already respects the conjunction rule while its verbal output violates it — i.e., whether the fallacy is representational or a readout artifact — nor localize/causally steer the incoherence. We reframe a canonical human-cognition bias as a decodable internal-vs-stated coherence gap and give it a mechanistic, causal treatment, distinct from all my prior single-belief attribute proposals (this concerns *coherence relations among multiple beliefs*).
Abstract: People judge 'Linda is a bank teller and a feminist' as more probable than 'Linda is a bank teller' — the conjunction fallacy, a signature violation of probability theory. LLMs reproduce this and related incoherences in their stated judgments, and prior work either documents this behaviorally or trains auxiliary models to squeeze coherent probabilities out of embeddings. We ask a sharper, mechanistic question: is the fallacy a bug in the model's internal belief representation, or a bug in how that representation is read out into words? We hypothesize that a linearly-decoded internal belief-strength readout for a conjunction P(A∧B) respects the conjunction rule (it is ≤ the readouts for P(A) and P(B)) substantially more often than the model's verbalized probability judgments do; that the internal representation is therefore more coherent than the output; that the residual internal incoherence is carried by an identifiable component; and that steering it restores coherence in the stated judgments. We construct a controlled dataset of item propositions and their conjunctions/disjunctions (Linda-style representativeness pairs, plus neutral and synthetic-entity conjunctions to control priors and token-bias confounds). On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear belief-strength probes, compute per-triple internal vs. stated conjunction-rule violation rates, geometrically relate a 'coherence-violation' direction to the truth/plausibility directions, localize the responsible heads via activation patching, and test whether steering reduces both internal and stated violations. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, internal vs. stated violation-rate gap, monotonicity error, subspace angle, patching effect sizes, post-steering coherence gains, and perplexity.
Experiments: 1) Dataset construction: Build ~5k proposition triples (A, B, A∧B), spanning: (a) REPRESENTATIVENESS pairs in the Linda style where B is representative/typical (the classic fallacy trigger), (b) NEUTRAL pairs where A and B are unrelated (weak representativeness pull), (c) a SYNTHETIC-ENTITY track with novel entities/attributes (e.g., 'Zorblax is a miner' / 'Zorblax is a miner and a poet') to control pretraining priors and to make base rates stipulable, and (d) DISJUNCTION triples (A, B, A∨B) to test the dual monotonicity (P(A∨B) ≥ P(A)). Include matched controls that swap which conjunct is representative to separate token/representativeness bias from genuine incoherence, plus paraphrase/format/order perturbations. For synthetic items, stipulate base rates so a ground-truth coherent ordering exists. 2) Stated-judgment baseline: Elicit the model's verbal probability for each of A, B, A∧B (and A∨B) via direct probability prompts and via forced binary comparison ('which is more probable, A or A∧B?'); compute the STATED conjunction-rule violation rate (P(A∧B) > P(A)) and disjunction violation rate. Include comprehension checks. 3) Internal belief-strength probing: For Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B, present each proposition and extract residual-stream and per-head activations at the proposition's key tokens across layers; train a linear belief-STRENGTH probe (regressing a graded belief/plausibility score, calibrated on a held-out set of propositions with known relative probabilities, with shuffled-label control tasks). Read the internal belief-strength for A, B, and A∧B WITHOUT asking the comparison question. Define INTERNAL conjunction-rule violation = readout(A∧B) > min(readout(A), readout(B)). 4) Key test — internal vs. stated coherence gap: Compare per-triple internal violation rate to stated violation rate. The core prediction: internal violation rate is significantly LOWER than stated (the representation is more coherent than the output), especially on representativeness pairs. Report the gap per model, per condition (representativeness/neutral/synthetic), and per layer, and test whether the internal readout preserves monotonicity even when the verbal output flips. 5) Geometry: Compute the 'coherence-violation' direction (difference-in-means between violating vs. non-violating conjunctions after controlling for representativeness) and its subspace angle to the truth/plausibility direction (following Is This Just Fantasy? modal vectors); test whether violation is decodable after projecting out plausibility, isolating incoherence from mere typicality. 6) Localization: Use activation patching / causal mediation to find heads/layers whose states inject the representativeness pull that converts a coherent internal readout into an incoherent stated judgment (patch representativeness-pair activations into neutral-pair runs and vice versa); contrast with token-bias-related heads and plausibility/belief heads. 7) Causal control: Derive a contrastive 'coherence' steering direction (coherent vs. violating conjunction activations). Test (a) steering reduces the STATED conjunction/disjunction violation rate toward the internally-implied coherent ordering; (b) negating it exaggerates the fallacy; (c) specificity: random and plausibility-direction steering do not selectively fix coherence; (d) collateral checks on general benchmarks (MMLU subset), non-conjunction judgment accuracy, and perplexity. 8) Predictiveness & generalization: Test whether the internal readout predicts, per triple, when the model will emit an incoherent stated judgment (AUROC vs. a log-prob baseline); test probe/steering transfer across representativeness/neutral/synthetic tracks and to disjunctions and simple base-rate-neglect items. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, internal vs. stated violation-rate gap, monotonicity error, subspace angle and projected-out decodability vs. plausibility, patching logit-difference effect sizes, post-steering violation-rate reduction and specificity, incoherence-prediction AUROC, perplexity/benchmark deltas.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The internal belief-strength probe requires a calibrated graded readout, which is harder than a binary truth probe; miscalibration could artificially inflate or deflate the internal violation rate. We mitigate by calibrating on held-out propositions with known relative probabilities, reporting layerwise results with control tasks, and focusing on the *relative* ordering (monotonicity) rather than absolute probabilities. It is possible the internal representation is *equally* incoherent as the output — a robust null (no internal-vs-stated gap) would still be a valuable, publishable finding, showing the fallacy is representational, not a readout artifact, and constraining the 'recover coherent probabilities from embeddings' program. The coherence-violation signal may be entangled with the representativeness/plausibility direction (violating conjunctions are exactly the typical ones); the swapped-conjunct controls, neutral pairs, synthetic track, and projected-out analyses are designed to dissociate representativeness pull from genuine incoherence, though full separation is difficult. Reading belief at 'matched' tokens across A, B, and A∧B is imperfect since the conjunction is longer; we anchor probes at shared conjunct tokens and use paraphrase perturbations. Localization may be distributed; we treat 'steer to restore coherence' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact head. Steering could degrade fluency or make the model indiscriminately rank conjunctions as improbable (harming cases where a conjunction is legitimately near a conjunct); we use small magnitudes, random/plausibility-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity, non-conjunction accuracy, and general benchmarks. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: belief_halo_contamination
Title: The Halo Inside: Does One Valenced Trait Silently Contaminate an LLM's Beliefs About Logically-Independent Traits?
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human halo effect, asserting a single valenced trait about an item (e.g., a person is 'attractive', a company is 'ethical') causally shifts an LLM's internally-decoded belief about logically-independent traits of that same item in a valence-congruent direction, holding evidence for those other traits constant. We hypothesize this halo is (i) an internal belief-contamination effect visible before any query, (ii) graded with the strength/valence of the seed trait and larger for traits stereotypically associated with the seed, and (iii) mediated by a dominant valence axis, so that steering along a single valence direction reproduces and removing it abolishes the contamination.
Related Work: The halo effect - a single valenced attribute biasing judgments of unrelated attributes of the same target - is a canonical, heavily-cited human finding (attractiveness halo; 'A Constant Error, Revisited' 2024 on shared lexical context; halo-update effect 2023; confluence theory on irrelevant beliefs 2012; inferred-contagion dispositional bias 2016). In LLMs, prior work documents cognitive biases behaviorally (BiasBuster 2024) and, most relevantly, finds a single dominant 'Valence-Assent Axis' (VAA) jointly encoding 'what is good' and 'what is true' that steers reasoning (A Unified Representation Underlying the Judgment of LLMs 2025). Belief-probing work isolates truth/belief directions (Truth-value judgment 2024; Brittle Minds 2024; Shape of Beliefs 2026), and hallucination-spillover work shows learned knowledge contaminates other tasks via lexical similarity (New-Knowledge-Induced Hallucinations 2025; knowledge overshadowing 2025). CRITICALLY, none isolate the halo effect as an internal belief-contamination phenomenon: whether asserting one valenced trait shifts the internally-decoded belief about *logically-independent* traits of the same item, whether that contamination is graded/stereotype-selective, and whether it rides on the VAA valence axis or on trait-specific spreading. We transfer a canonical human bias into LLM belief internals and give it a mechanistic, causal treatment, distinct from behavioral bias benchmarks and from prior single-belief-attribute proposals.
Abstract: People who learn one good thing about someone assume other unrelated good things too - the halo effect, one of the most robust biases in social cognition. As LLMs increasingly form beliefs about entities (people, products, companies, treatments) from fragments of valenced information, we ask whether they inherit this bias at the level of their internal beliefs, and by what mechanism. We hypothesize that asserting a single valenced trait about an item causally shifts the model's internally-decoded belief about logically-independent traits of that same item in a valence-congruent direction, with the underlying evidence for those other traits held constant. We further hypothesize this halo is graded (larger for stronger/more extreme seed traits and for traits stereotypically linked to the seed) and that, consistent with recent evidence for a dominant Valence-Assent Axis, it is mediated by a single valence direction rather than trait-specific spreading. We build a controlled dataset of items each described by a seed trait (positive/negative/neutral) plus a set of logically-independent target traits, using synthetic entities to control priors. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear belief probes to read each target-trait belief before and after the seed appears (no query), compute a per-item halo-contamination score, test stereotype-selectivity and dose-response, extract a valence direction, and test whether steering it reproduces the halo and projecting it out abolishes it, localizing the responsible heads via activation patching. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, halo-contamination magnitude, stereotype and dose modulation, valence-axis mediation share, patching effect sizes, post-intervention halo change, and perplexity.
Experiments: 1) Dataset construction: Generate ~5k items across domains where halo effects matter (people described by traits, products, companies, medical treatments). Two tracks: (a) REAL-plausible entities; (b) SYNTHETIC novel entities (e.g., invented people/brands 'Zorel Corp') to control pretraining priors. Each item has a SEED trait rendered at valence levels {strongly-positive, mildly-positive, neutral, mildly-negative, strongly-negative} (e.g., 'Zorel is extremely honest' vs. 'Zorel is deeply dishonest'), plus a set of TARGET traits that are logically independent of the seed but vary in STEREOTYPE association with it (e.g., for 'honest': high-assoc 'trustworthy-adjacent', low-assoc 'good at math'). Include a NO-SEED baseline (targets described alone) and matched EVIDENCE-controlled targets (an explicit, valence-neutral fact about each target trait so genuine evidence is held constant across seed conditions). Add comprehension checks and paraphrase/order perturbations to guard against surface-cue/priming-of-tokens confounds. 2) Internal belief probing: For Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B, extract residual-stream and per-head activations at each TARGET-trait's key tokens across layers, WITHOUT asking about the target, in SEED and NO-SEED conditions. Train linear belief probes (P(target trait holds), and a graded valence-of-target readout) on held-out data with shuffled-label control tasks; report per-layer accuracy/AUROC. Define halo-contamination = belief(target | seed) - belief(target | no-seed), signed by seed valence. 3) Phenomenon tests: (a) Test halo > 0 (valence-congruent shift) across models and domains, versus the rational null (no shift, since target evidence is held constant). (b) Dose-response: does halo magnitude scale monotonically with seed valence extremity? (c) Stereotype-selectivity: is halo larger for high-association than low-association targets (mirroring the human finding), and does it appear even for low/zero-association targets (the 'irrelevant belief' contamination)? (d) Verbal-vs-internal: compare internal halo to the model's stated trait judgments. 4) Mechanism - valence-axis mediation: Extract a valence direction via difference-in-means on positive vs. negative seed activations (and compare to a VAA-style axis). Test the key mechanistic hypothesis: (i) how much of the halo contamination is explained by movement along this single valence direction (mediation share); (ii) does projecting out the valence direction at the target representation abolish the halo while preserving evidence-based target belief; (iii) is residual (off-axis) contamination trait-specific? 5) Localization: Use activation patching / causal mediation from SEED to NO-SEED runs to find heads/layers that transport the seed's valence to the target representation; contrast with truth/belief heads and copying heads. 6) Causal control: Derive a contrastive 'halo/valence' steering direction. Test (a) adding it reproduces/exaggerates the halo on NO-SEED items; (b) subtracting it on SEED items abolishes the halo and restores evidence-based target beliefs; (c) specificity: random and truth-direction steering do not selectively move independent targets; (d) collateral checks on general benchmarks (MMLU subset), non-target belief accuracy, and perplexity. 7) Predictiveness & downstream: Test whether the internal halo predicts biased behavioral judgments (e.g., inflated hiring/loan/quality ratings on independent criteria) via AUROC vs. a log-prob baseline, and whether halo-reducing steering reduces such biased ratings while preserving evidence-based accuracy - probed in a high-stakes track (hiring, product safety, clinical prognosis). 8) Generalization: transfer of probes/steering across domains, real vs. synthetic tracks, and stereotype-association levels. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, halo-contamination magnitude, dose and stereotype modulation slopes, internal-vs-verbal gap, valence-axis mediation share, patching logit-difference effect sizes, post-intervention halo change and evidence-preservation, biased-judgment prediction AUROC, downstream bias-reduction and accuracy deltas, perplexity/benchmark deltas.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The halo shift could reflect rational inference from correlated real-world trait co-occurrence rather than an irrelevant-belief bias; the synthetic-entity track, the evidence-controlled targets (with explicit neutral facts), and the low/zero-association target condition are designed to isolate genuine contamination from legitimate correlational inference (though for real entities the two are hard to fully separate). The effect may be absent internally - a robust negative result (LLMs keep independent traits uncontaminated) would itself be a valuable, publishable finding contrasting with humans and with the VAA account. The contamination could arise from token-level priming/co-occurrence rather than a valence belief; paraphrase/order perturbations, comprehension checks, and reading belief at target tokens distinct from the seed mitigate this. The single-valence-axis mediation hypothesis may only partially hold; if residual trait-specific spreading dominates, the finding shifts to characterizing distributed vs. unified halo mechanisms (still informative and directly engages the VAA claim). Belief probes may not be cleanly linear at every layer; we report layerwise results with control tasks. Steering could degrade fluency or indiscriminately flatten all evaluative structure; we use small magnitudes, random/truth-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity, evidence-based accuracy, and general benchmarks. Downstream high-stakes ratings need automatic plus human-validated scoring. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: negation_suppression_lag
Title: Believe It Before You Deny It: A Transient Affirmed-Belief Signature in How LLMs Process Negation
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the psycholinguistic 'two-step simulation' theory of negation (humans first mentally represent the affirmed proposition, then suppress it), an LLM processing a negated claim 'X is not the case' transiently forms an internally-decodable belief in the AFFIRMED proposition X at earlier layers/token positions before that belief is suppressed at later layers. This affirmed-belief-then-suppress trajectory is layer-localized, larger under processing load, predicts negation-comprehension errors, and is carried by an identifiable suppression component that can be causally strengthened to reduce negation-induced errors.
Related Work: Prior LLM negation work is behavioral or engineering: 'Strong hallucinations from negation and how to fix them' (2024) proves LMs mishandle negation and proposes treating negation as an operation constraining latent evolution; BERT-attention work (2020) finds shallow negation-scope heads; benchmarks document negation failures. Belief-probing work isolates linear truth/belief directions (Geometry of Truth 2023; Truth-value judgment 2024) and belief-state geometry (Transformers Represent Belief State Geometry 2024; Shape of Beliefs 2026), and ToM work decodes true/false-belief status (Beliefs of Self and Others 2024; Lookbacks 2025). Human psycholinguistics robustly shows a 'two-step' negation process: comprehenders first simulate the affirmed state and only later suppress/invert it (Kaup et al.; neuroscience shows negation reuses inhibitory control and demands effortful conscious processing, e.g., Inhibitory Mechanisms 2021; Dogs Cannot Bark ERP 2011). NONE of this asks whether an LLM's *internal belief representation* transiently endorses the affirmed proposition before suppressing it, whether that suppression is a layer-localized dynamic, whether it predicts negation errors, or whether a suppression component can be causally strengthened. We transfer a canonical human-cognition finding into LLM belief internals and give it a mechanistic, causal treatment, distinct from prior scope/hallucination work and from my earlier epistemic-tag proposals.
Abstract: When people read 'the door is not open,' they first mentally simulate an open door and only afterward suppress that representation to arrive at the intended meaning — the two-step simulation account of negation, one of the most reproduced findings in psycholinguistics. LLMs are notoriously error-prone on negation, yet prior interpretability work treats negation only as a scope-detection or hallucination-fixing problem, never asking whether the model inherits the human two-step signature at the level of its internal beliefs. We hypothesize that when an LLM processes a negated claim, its linearly-decoded belief in the AFFIRMED proposition is transiently high at early layers/token positions and is then suppressed at later layers — a decodable affirmed-belief-then-suppress trajectory. We further hypothesize this suppression (i) is layer-localized, (ii) grows with processing load (nested/double negation, time pressure via early-exit read-outs), (iii) predicts behavioral negation-comprehension errors when suppression is incomplete, and (iv) is carried by an identifiable suppression component such that strengthening it reduces negation errors while ablating it exaggerates residual affirmed belief. We build a controlled dataset of matched affirmative and negated item-state claims (plus double-negation and synthetic-entity tracks to control priors), train linear belief probes across layers on frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B), trace the affirmed-belief trajectory across layers/positions, quantify residual affirmed belief and its relation to errors, localize the suppression component via activation patching, and test causal control by steering it. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, layerwise affirmed-belief trajectory, residual-belief magnitude, load modulation, residual-belief–error AUROC, patching effect sizes, post-intervention error change, and perplexity.
