Experiments: 1) Dataset construction: Generate ~6k matched claim pairs, each an item-state proposition P rendered as AFFIRMED ('The door is open') and NEGATED ('The door is not open'). Two tracks: (a) REAL propositions the models reliably know; (b) SYNTHETIC novel-entity claims (e.g., 'Zorblax orbits Kelvath' / 'Zorblax does not orbit Kelvath') with stipulated ground truth to control pretraining priors. Add processing-LOAD conditions: single negation, DOUBLE negation ('It is not the case that the door is not open', semantically affirmative), and lexical vs. syntactic negation ('no'/'never'/'fails to'). Include a behavioral NEGATION-COMPREHENSION probe (ask the model the truth-value / entailment of the negated claim) and comprehension checks; apply paraphrase/format/negation-cue perturbations to guard against surface-cue artifacts. Anchor probe read-out on the shared content tokens (the proposition P) present in both affirmed and negated forms. 2) Layerwise belief probing: For Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B, extract residual-stream activations at the proposition's content tokens across ALL layers and at successive token positions following the negation cue. Train a linear BELIEF probe (P(affirmed proposition P holds)) on AFFIRMED-condition data with shuffled-label control tasks, and apply it within the NEGATED condition to read the model's internal belief in the affirmed content. Report per-layer accuracy/AUROC. 3) Trajectory analysis (key test): In the NEGATED condition, trace the probe read-out of affirmed-belief across layers/positions. The two-step prediction: affirmed-belief is HIGH at early layers (matching the affirmative baseline) and DROPS below a neutral midpoint by later layers (suppression), producing a characteristic rise-then-fall or high-then-suppressed trajectory absent in the affirmative baseline. Quantify (a) peak early affirmed-belief, (b) suppression depth/onset layer, and (c) RESIDUAL affirmed-belief at the final layer (incomplete suppression). 4) Load modulation: Test whether suppression onset is later / residual affirmed-belief is larger for double negation and syntactic vs. lexical negation, mirroring the human load effect; use early-exit read-outs (probing intermediate layers as a proxy for time pressure) to test whether 'reading out too early' yields the affirmed (wrong) belief. 5) Predictiveness: Collect behavioral negation-comprehension outcomes (does the model correctly treat the negated claim?). Test whether residual affirmed-belief (incomplete suppression) predicts per-item negation errors via AUROC, compared against a log-prob confidence baseline. 6) Localization: Use activation patching / causal mediation to find the layers/heads that perform the suppression (patch NEGATED-condition late-layer activations into AFFIRMED runs and vice versa; find the minimal component that flips affirmed-belief), and compare to negation-scope heads reported in prior work and to truth/belief heads. 7) Causal control: Derive a contrastive 'negation-suppression' steering direction (suppressed vs. unsuppressed affirmed-belief activations). Test (a) strengthening it deepens/accelerates suppression and reduces behavioral negation errors on high-residual items; (b) ablating/negating it leaves residual affirmed-belief high and increases negation errors; (c) specificity: random and truth-direction steering do not selectively fix negation; (d) collateral checks on general benchmarks (MMLU subset), affirmative-claim accuracy, and perplexity. 8) Generalization: test probe/steering transfer across real vs. synthetic tracks, negation types, and single vs. double negation. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, layerwise affirmed-belief trajectory (peak, suppression onset, depth, final residual), load-modulation slopes, residual-belief–error AUROC, patching logit-difference effect sizes, post-intervention negation-error change and specificity, perplexity/benchmark deltas.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The early 'affirmed belief' in the negated condition could be a trivial artifact of the proposition tokens being present, rather than a genuine transient endorsement; the affirmative baseline, synthetic-entity track (no prior), double-negation condition (where correct final belief is affirmative, dissociating content-presence from truth), and probing at matched content tokens are designed to distinguish a real two-step signature from token-presence. The trajectory may not show a clean rise-then-fall — a robust negative result (LLMs suppress negated content immediately, unlike humans) would itself be a valuable, publishable finding constraining the human-parallel narrative. Belief may not be cleanly linearly decodable at every layer; we report layerwise results with control tasks and treat the trajectory shape, not absolute values, as the object of study. The suppression component may be distributed rather than a discrete head; we treat 'steer to deepen suppression / reduce errors' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact component. Reading an affirmative-trained probe inside the negated context assumes probe transfer; we validate with within-negated probes and paraphrase perturbations. Early-exit read-outs are only a proxy for processing load/time pressure. Steering could degrade fluency or over-suppress (making the model treat affirmations as negations); we use small magnitudes, random/truth-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity, affirmative-claim accuracy, and general benchmarks. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: batch_belief_contamination
Title: Bleeding Beliefs: Does Co-Processing Independent Items Contaminate an LLM's Internal Belief About Each One?
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM processes several logically-independent items in a single context (as in batched queries or multi-question prompts), the belief it forms about one item silently leaks into its internally-decoded belief about the other, co-present items. This cross-item belief contamination is (i) linearly decodable at each item's representation before any query, (ii) graded with the valence/confidence of the neighboring item and with inter-item similarity, and (iii) carried by an identifiable internal component (a set of attention heads that mix belief across item slots) that can be causally ablated to restore item-independent beliefs, mirroring inter-item interference/assimilation biases in human memory.
Related Work: Human memory/judgment research robustly shows inter-item interference and assimilation/contrast biases: co-present items distort each other's remembered/judged features (inter-item interference in visual memory 2019; the normative 'demixing' model 2023 showing such biases are inevitable under source ambiguity; sequential assimilation/contrast in price and prognostic judgments 2008/2009; simultaneous multi-word recognition dependencies 2021). In LLMs, prior interpretability work isolates linear truth/belief directions (Geometry of Truth 2023; Truth-value judgment 2024) and studies interference only at TRAINING time or over long single inputs: catastrophic interference from contradictory updates ('In Praise of Stubbornness' 2025), non-target priming from knowledge-conflicting facts ('Learning and Unlearning of Fabricated Knowledge' 2024), continual-pretraining belief poisoning ('Layer of Truth' 2025), and 'Contextual Feature Drift' (2024) which measures decay of context retention over sequential inputs. NONE ask whether, at INFERENCE time, co-processing multiple logically-INDEPENDENT items in one context contaminates the model's INTERNAL belief about each item (a bleed between item slots), whether this is graded by neighbor confidence/similarity, or whether an identifiable belief-mixing component causes it. We transfer a canonical human inter-item interference phenomenon into LLM belief internals in a high-stakes deployment setting (batched inference) and give it a mechanistic, causal treatment, distinct from all training-time interference work and from my prior single-item belief-attribute proposals.
Abstract: Serving LLMs at scale routinely means co-processing many items in one context: multiple questions batched into a single prompt, several documents concatenated, or a form of independent claims answered together. Users assume the model evaluates each item on its own merits. We ask whether it actually does, or whether, like human memory where co-present items interfere and assimilate toward one another, an LLM's belief about one item silently bleeds into its internal belief about the others. We hypothesize that co-processing logically-independent items contaminates the model's internally-decoded belief about each: (i) the belief about item B, read before any query, shifts toward the belief/valence the model holds about a co-present item A, holding B's own evidence constant; (ii) the contamination is graded with A's confidence/valence and with A-B similarity; and (iii) it is carried by an identifiable set of attention heads that mix belief across item slots, so that ablating them restores item-independent beliefs. We build a controlled dataset of item pairs/batches where each item is a truth-evaluable claim, varying the neighbor's truth/valence and inter-item similarity while holding the target's own evidence fixed, using synthetic entities to control priors. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear belief probes to read each item's belief in isolation vs. co-processed, compute a per-item contamination score, test its graded structure, localize the responsible belief-mixing heads via activation patching, and test causal control by ablating/steering them. We further test whether contamination predicts real batched-inference errors, including a high-stakes medical-QA batch track. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, contamination magnitude and sign, neighbor-confidence and similarity modulation, patching effect sizes, post-ablation independence restoration, batched-error prediction AUROC, and perplexity.
Experiments: 1) Dataset construction: Generate ~6k truth-evaluable item-state claims (e.g., 'X is the capital of Y', entity-attribute facts). Two tracks: (a) REAL claims the models reliably know/disbelieve; (b) SYNTHETIC novel-entity claims (e.g., 'Zorblax orbits Kelvath') with stipulated ground truth to control pretraining priors. Assemble items into single-context BATCHES (pairs, then size-4 and size-8) and matched ISOLATED baselines (each item answered alone). For each TARGET item, vary the NEIGHBOR item's properties while holding the target's own evidence constant: (i) neighbor truth-value (true vs. false), (ii) neighbor confidence/valence (strongly-true, weakly-true, weakly-false, strongly-false framings), (iii) target-neighbor SIMILARITY (same-domain/lexically-similar vs. unrelated). Include order permutations, length-matched filler controls, and comprehension checks; apply paraphrase/format perturbations to guard against surface-cue artifacts. 2) Internal belief probing: For Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B, extract residual-stream and per-head activations at each TARGET item's key tokens across layers, WITHOUT asking the target question, in ISOLATED and BATCHED conditions. Train linear BELIEF probes (P(target claim holds)) on ISOLATED data with shuffled-label control tasks; report per-layer accuracy/AUROC. Define contamination = belief(target | batched) - belief(target | isolated), signed by the neighbor's valence. 3) Phenomenon tests: (a) Test contamination != 0 (assimilation toward neighbor valence, or a contrast/repulsion sign), across models, domains, and batch sizes, versus the item-independent null. (b) Neighbor-confidence dose-response: does contamination scale with neighbor valence extremity? (c) Similarity modulation: is contamination larger for similar than for unrelated neighbors (mirroring human similarity-based interference)? (d) Batch-size scaling: does contamination grow with number of co-present items? (e) Verbal-vs-internal: compare internal contamination to the model's stated per-item judgments. 4) Localization: Use activation patching / causal mediation to find heads/layers that transport belief across item slots (patch a target item's activations between a batched run and its isolated run; find the minimal set of heads that inject the neighbor's influence); test whether specific cross-slot attention heads mediate the bleed, contrasting with truth/belief heads. 5) Causal control: Derive the contamination via head-ablation and via a contrastive 'belief-mixing' steering direction. Test (a) ablating the identified belief-mixing heads / subtracting the direction restores item-independent beliefs (contamination -> 0) and reduces batched errors; (b) amplifying it exaggerates contamination; (c) specificity: random-head ablation and truth-direction steering do not selectively restore independence; (d) collateral checks on general benchmarks (MMLU subset), isolated-item accuracy, and perplexity. 6) Predictiveness & high-stakes track: Test whether internal contamination predicts per-item BATCHED-INFERENCE errors (target answer flips only when batched with a false/opposite-valence neighbor) via AUROC vs. a log-prob baseline. Add a HIGH-STAKES medical-QA track (e.g., MedQA/MedMCQA items batched together) to test whether co-batching a confidently-wrong clinical item contaminates the model's belief/answer on an independent clinical item, and whether ablation mitigates it. 7) Generalization: transfer of probes/heads across real vs. synthetic tracks, domains, similarity levels, and batch sizes. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, contamination magnitude and sign, neighbor-confidence and similarity and batch-size modulation slopes, internal-vs-verbal gap, patching logit-difference effect sizes, post-ablation independence restoration and specificity, batched-error prediction AUROC, high-stakes error-mitigation delta, perplexity/benchmark deltas.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The observed shift could reflect legitimate inference (a neighbor genuinely provides weak evidence about the target in the real track); the synthetic-entity track with independent stipulated truths, unrelated-neighbor conditions, and length-matched fillers are designed to isolate genuine contamination from valid cross-item inference (harder to separate for real, correlated items). The effect may be absent internally - a robust negative result (LLMs evaluate co-processed independent items independently) would itself be a valuable, reassuring finding for batched-inference deployment. The contamination could arise from token-level attention leakage without a belief-level bleed; probing at target-specific tokens, order permutations, comprehension checks, and the neighbor-valence sign test help distinguish belief contamination from generic attention spillover. Belief may not be cleanly linearly decodable at every layer; we report layerwise results with control tasks. The belief-mixing component may be distributed rather than a few discrete heads; we treat 'ablate to restore independence' as the causal test rather than pinning exact heads. Position/order and primacy effects may confound similarity effects; permutation controls mitigate this. Steering/ablation could degrade fluency or harm cases where cross-item context is legitimately useful; we use small magnitudes, random-ablation baselines, and monitor perplexity, isolated-item accuracy, and general benchmarks. High-stakes medical results are for research characterization only, not clinical use. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: essentialist_belief_mutability
Title: Essence or Accident? An Internal Mutability Flag That Gates How Readily LLMs Revise Their Beliefs
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring psychological essentialism, LLMs internally tag a belief about an item's property as either ESSENTIAL/IMMUTABLE (a defining, kind-constituting property that resists change, e.g. 'a tiger is a mammal') or ACCIDENTAL/MUTABLE (a contingent, revisable property, e.g. 'this tiger lives in a zoo'). This mutability flag is (i) linearly decodable from residual-stream activations, (ii) largely orthogonal to the truth-value direction, and (iii) causally gates the model's revision plasticity: when contradicted in context, beliefs internally tagged immutable resist updating far more than mutable ones, at matched evidence strength, and steering along a single mutability direction reverses this resistance.
Related Work: Behavioral work shows LLMs reproduce human essentialist categorization, prioritizing teleological/'what-it-is-for' and constitutive properties over appearance ('You are what you're for', 2023), and human cognitive science establishes essentialism, mutability, and kind-vs-accident distinctions (Psychological Essentialism 2021; Functional Origins of Essentialism 2001; Fact Mutability in Counterfactuals 2007; Generics Designate Kinds 2019). On the LLM-internal side: 'In Praise of Stubbornness' (2025) shows contradictory factual updates cause catastrophic interference and are detectable from features but does NOT distinguish essential vs. accidental facts or link resistance to an internal mutability representation; 'Believe It or Not' (2025) measures belief depth of implanted facts (finding plausibility-dependent brittleness) but not a mutability/essence tag; 'Layer of Truth' (2025) localizes poisoning-induced belief flips to late layers; knowledge-editing work documents conflict/distortion side effects. Truth-probe work isolates a linear truth-value direction (Geometry of Truth 2023; Truth-value judgment 2024). CRITICALLY, none isolate an internal essential-vs-accidental (immutability) representation as a decodable variable orthogonal to truth, nor test whether it causally gates in-context belief revision. We transfer psychological essentialism into LLM belief internals and give it a mechanistic, causal treatment, distinct from all prior behavioral-only essentialism work and from my earlier epistemic-tag proposals (provenance, currency, contestedness, endorsement).
Abstract: Humans treat some facts as essential to what a thing is (a tiger is a mammal; water is H2O) and others as accidental and freely revisable (this tiger is in a zoo; this water is warm) - psychological essentialism, one of the most robust findings in cognitive science. As LLMs increasingly ingest, are corrected on, and edit factual claims, a consequential question arises: does a model internally distinguish essential from accidental properties, and does that distinction govern how readily it revises a belief? We hypothesize that LLMs maintain an internal 'mutability' flag that tags a belief as essential/immutable vs. accidental/mutable, that this flag is (i) linearly decodable from residual-stream activations, (ii) largely orthogonal to the truth-value direction, and (iii) causally gates revision plasticity: when the same proposition is contradicted in context with matched evidence strength, beliefs tagged immutable resist updating far more than those tagged mutable, and steering a single mutability direction reverses this asymmetry. We build a controlled dataset of item-property claims labeled essential vs. accidental (with a synthetic-entity track defining novel kinds and stipulating property status to control pretraining priors), each paired with a matched in-context contradiction. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear probes to decode mutability vs. truth, measure their geometry, quantify per-item revision plasticity under contradiction, test whether internal mutability predicts revision resistance beyond surface features, localize the responsible heads via activation patching, and test causal control by steering the mutability direction. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, subspace angle, projected-out decodability, revision-plasticity gap, resistance-prediction AUROC, patching effect sizes, post-steering plasticity restoration, and perplexity.
Experiments: 1) Dataset construction: Generate ~6k item-property claims, each rendered as an ESSENTIAL/kind-constituting property (e.g. 'A whale is a mammal', 'Gold is an element', 'A triangle has three sides') or an ACCIDENTAL/contingent property of the same entity (e.g. 'This whale is 20 meters long', 'This gold ring is scratched', 'This triangle is drawn in red'), balanced across domains (biology, chemistry, artifacts, social kinds). Two tracks: (a) REAL claims models reliably know; (b) a SYNTHETIC novel-KIND track that defines invented kinds and explicitly stipulates which properties are kind-defining vs. incidental (e.g. 'A zorblax is by definition a creature that breathes fluorine [essential]; this particular zorblax is currently asleep [accidental]'), to control pretraining priors and to make essential/accidental status unambiguous and independent of surface cues. Cross with TRUE/FALSE polarity. For each claim, construct a matched IN-CONTEXT CONTRADICTION with controlled evidence strength (e.g. a stated observation or authoritative correction asserting the opposite), holding contradiction wording/strength constant across essential and accidental items. Include comprehension checks (can the model restate the property's status) and paraphrase/format perturbations to guard against surface-cue artifacts (e.g. the words 'by definition' vs. 'currently'). Human-validate essential/accidental labels on a sample. 2) Probing: For Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B, extract residual-stream and per-head activations at the property/item tokens across layers. Train logistic-regression probes for (i) TRUTH-VALUE (true vs. false) and (ii) MUTABILITY (essential/immutable vs. accidental/mutable). Report per-layer accuracy/AUROC with shuffled-label control tasks to rule out spurious structure. 3) Geometry: Compute cosine/subspace angle between the mutability and truth-value directions; test whether mutability remains decodable after projecting out the truth direction (and vice versa) to establish orthogonality; test whether the mutability direction generalizes across real and synthetic tracks. 4) Revision-plasticity measurement (behavioral + internal): Present each true claim, then the matched in-context contradiction, and (a) read the internal belief before vs. after via the truth probe (internal plasticity = belief change), and (b) query the model's stated post-contradiction belief (behavioral revision). Define per-item revision resistance = 1 - plasticity. Key prediction: resistance is higher for ESSENTIAL than ACCIDENTAL items at matched contradiction strength (an essentialism-driven plasticity gap), for both internal and behavioral measures, versus a mutability-independent null. 5) Predictiveness: Test whether the internal mutability probe readout (read before contradiction) predicts per-item revision resistance (AUROC), beyond a log-prob confidence baseline and beyond surface lexical features (a bag-of-words classifier), isolating the internal-representation contribution. 6) Localization: Use activation patching / causal mediation to find heads/layers carrying the mutability signal and gating revision (patch essential-item activations into accidental-item runs and vice versa at the contradiction point; find the minimal component that increases/decreases plasticity); compare to truth/belief heads and to the contradiction-detection features reported by 'In Praise of Stubbornness'. 7) Causal control: Derive a contrastive 'mutability' steering direction (essential vs. accidental activations, controlling for truth). Test (a) steering essential items toward 'mutable' increases their in-context revision plasticity (they update more readily); (b) steering accidental items toward 'immutable' increases their resistance; (c) specificity: random-direction and truth-direction steering do not selectively move plasticity; (d) collateral checks on general benchmarks (MMLU subset), non-manipulated claim accuracy, and perplexity. 8) Generalization: Test probe/steering transfer across domains (biology, chemistry, artifacts, social kinds), real vs. synthetic tracks, and contradiction strengths. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, subspace angle and projected-out decodability vs. truth, essential-vs-accidental revision-plasticity gap (internal and behavioral), resistance-prediction AUROC (vs. log-prob and lexical baselines), patching logit-difference effect sizes, post-steering plasticity restoration and specificity, perplexity/benchmark deltas.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Revision resistance for essential items could reflect that essential facts are simply held with higher pretraining confidence rather than a distinct mutability representation; the synthetic novel-kind track (where essential/accidental status is stipulated in-context rather than reflecting pretraining strength) and matched contradiction strength are designed to dissociate mutability from raw confidence, and the resistance-prediction test conditions on a confidence baseline. The mutability flag may be entangled with surface cues (words like 'by definition', 'is a kind of' vs. 'currently', 'this particular'); we mitigate with diverse framings, paraphrase perturbations, comprehension checks, and the synthetic track where cues are balanced. Mutability and truth directions may be less orthogonal than hypothesized, in which case the finding characterizes their entanglement (still informative). The essential/accidental label is partly graded/subjective; we human-validate and treat borderline items separately. The effect may be absent internally - a robust negative result (LLMs' behavioral essentialism is not backed by an internal mutability representation gating revision) is itself a valuable, publishable finding constraining the essentialism-in-LLMs literature. Probes may not be cleanly linear at every layer; we report layerwise results with control tasks. The gating component may be distributed rather than a discrete head; we treat 'steer to restore/reverse plasticity' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact component. Steering could degrade fluency or make the model indiscriminately revise (or entrench) all beliefs; we use small magnitudes, random/truth-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity, non-manipulated accuracy, and general benchmarks. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: curse_of_knowledge_leakage
Title: It Can't Unknow: A Privileged-Knowledge Leak That Biases LLMs' Internal Representation of an Ignorant Belief
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human curse of knowledge / hindsight bias, when an LLM knows the true state of an item, its internally-decoded representation of what an *ignorant* agent (a naive character, a past self, or a stipulated uninformed user) should believe is systematically biased TOWARD the true state that the model privately knows. This 'knowledge leak' is (i) linearly decodable as a shift of the ignorant-belief readout toward the true answer, (ii) graded with the plausibility/salience of the true answer, (iii) predicts egocentric false-belief errors, and (iv) is carried by an identifiable component such that ablating it restores an unbiased ignorant-belief representation.
Related Work: ToM interpretability decodes the belief status of a protagonist and an omniscient oracle from attention heads and steers ToM performance (Language Models Represent Beliefs of Self and Others 2024; Brittle Minds 2024), and identifies a 'lookback' mechanism binding character-object-state triples and updating beliefs via a visibility lookback (Language Models use Lookbacks to Track Beliefs 2025). Human cognitive science establishes the curse of knowledge / hindsight bias as a robust egocentric contamination of ignorant-perspective judgments (Are the classic false belief tasks cursed? 2021; Do Adults Show a Curse of Knowledge 2014; Hindsight Bias and Investment Performance 2008), and shows plausibility of the privileged answer modulates its size. CRITICALLY, the ToM interpretability work decodes WHETHER a model can represent a false belief, but none ask whether the model's OWN privileged knowledge of the true answer BIASES the internally-decoded ignorant/false belief toward that truth (a decodable knowledge-leak magnitude), whether that leak is graded by answer plausibility, predicts egocentric errors, or can be causally removed. We reframe the curse of knowledge as an internal representational leak from the truth channel into the ignorant-belief channel and give it a mechanistic, causal treatment, distinct from prior ToM-decoding work and from my earlier epistemic-tag proposals.
Abstract: Once you know the answer, it is hard to imagine not knowing it: people systematically project their privileged knowledge onto less-informed others and onto their own past selves — the curse of knowledge and its cousin, hindsight bias, among the most robust findings in cognitive science. LLMs are increasingly asked to reason about what an uninformed agent believes (a character in a false-belief story, a novice user, a past state of the world), tasks that require *withholding* what the model itself knows. We ask whether LLMs inherit the curse at the level of their internal beliefs: does the model's own knowledge of the true state of an item leak into, and bias, its internal representation of what an ignorant agent should believe? We hypothesize that (i) the internally-decoded ignorant-belief readout is shifted toward the true answer the model privately knows, (ii) this leak grows with the plausibility/salience of the true answer, (iii) it predicts egocentric false-belief errors when suppression is incomplete, and (iv) it is carried by an identifiable component that can be ablated to restore an unbiased ignorant-belief representation. We build controlled false-belief and hindsight scenarios in which the true state and the ignorant agent's evidence are dissociated, with matched conditions where the model is or is not itself told the truth, plus a synthetic-entity track to control priors. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear probes to read the ignorant-belief and the true-state, quantify a per-item knowledge-leak score, test its graded structure and predictiveness, localize the responsible heads via activation patching, and test causal control by ablating/steering a leak direction. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, knowledge-leak magnitude, plausibility modulation, leak–error AUROC, patching effect sizes, post-ablation debiasing, and perplexity.
Experiments: 1) Dataset construction: Generate ~6k scenarios in which the TRUE state of an item and an IGNORANT agent's evidence are dissociated, spanning three framings: (a) classic false-belief stories (an object is moved while a character is absent; the character should believe the old location), (b) hindsight scenarios (an outcome is revealed; the model must judge what a naive predictor would have expected beforehand), (c) audience-ignorance (a novice user who has not been told the fact). Two tracks: (i) REAL items models reliably know, and (ii) a SYNTHETIC novel-entity track (e.g., 'Zorblax's ball was moved from box A to box B while Zorblax was away') to control pretraining priors and stipulate ground truth. KEY manipulation: matched conditions where the model itself IS vs. IS NOT told the true state (privileged-knowledge present vs. absent), holding the ignorant agent's evidence constant — this isolates leakage from the model's own knowledge. Vary the PLAUSIBILITY/salience of the true answer (how strongly the true state pulls, e.g. a highly typical vs. arbitrary new location) to test the human plausibility-modulation finding. Add a behavioral FALSE-BELIEF/hindsight probe (ask what the ignorant agent believes / would have predicted) and comprehension checks (can the model restate who saw what); apply paraphrase/format/order perturbations to guard against surface cues. Human-validate a sample. 2) Probing: For Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B, extract residual-stream and per-head activations at the item/state tokens across layers, WITHOUT asking the belief question. Train linear probes for (A) the TRUE state and (B) the IGNORANT agent's belief (which, under a false belief, should point AWAY from the true state), with shuffled-label control tasks; report per-layer accuracy/AUROC. Define per-item KNOWLEDGE-LEAK = shift of the ignorant-belief readout toward the true state in the privileged-knowledge-present vs. -absent condition (equivalently, contamination of channel B by the true state carried in channel A). 3) Phenomenon tests: (a) Test leak > 0 (ignorant-belief biased toward the truth) across models and framings, versus the unbiased null; (b) plausibility dose-response: does leak scale with the true answer's salience? (c) does leak appear even in the SYNTHETIC track where the true state is only known in-context (isolating in-context knowledge leak from parametric priors)? (d) verbal-vs-internal: compare internal leak to stated ignorant-belief judgments. 4) Predictiveness: Collect behavioral egocentric errors (model wrongly attributes the true state to the ignorant agent / hindsight-distorted prior expectation). Test whether internal leak (read before the query) predicts per-item egocentric errors (AUROC), beyond a log-prob baseline and beyond surface features. 5) Localization: Use activation patching / causal mediation to find heads/layers that transport the true-state signal into the ignorant-belief channel (patch privileged-knowledge-present activations into -absent runs and vice versa; find the minimal component that induces/removes the leak); compare to the belief/visibility-lookback heads and truth heads reported in prior ToM work. 6) Causal control: Derive a contrastive 'knowledge-leak' steering direction (privileged-present vs. -absent activations, controlling for the ignorant agent's evidence). Test (a) ablating/subtracting it restores an unbiased ignorant-belief readout and reduces egocentric errors; (b) amplifying it exaggerates the curse; (c) specificity: random-direction and truth-direction steering do not selectively debias the ignorant channel, and the model's OWN factual belief is preserved; (d) collateral checks on general benchmarks (MMLU subset), non-manipulated accuracy, and perplexity. 7) Generalization: Test probe/steering transfer across framings (false-belief, hindsight, audience-ignorance), real vs. synthetic tracks, and plausibility levels. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, knowledge-leak magnitude, plausibility-modulation slope, internal-vs-verbal gap, leak–error AUROC (vs. log-prob and lexical baselines), patching logit-difference effect sizes, post-ablation debiasing and specificity, perplexity/benchmark deltas.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The leak could reflect legitimate inference (an ignorant agent might rationally still guess the true state if it is the default); the false-belief design (where the ignorant agent has POSITIVE evidence for the old/false state), the synthetic track, and the privileged-present-vs-absent contrast are built to isolate genuine contamination from valid inference, though for highly plausible true answers the two are hard to fully separate. The effect may be absent internally — a robust negative result (LLMs cleanly firewall their own knowledge from the ignorant-belief channel) would itself be a valuable, publishable finding, refining the ToM-representation and safety picture. The leak could arise from token-level co-occurrence rather than a belief-channel contamination; comprehension checks, paraphrase/order perturbations, and reading belief at agent-specific tokens mitigate this. The two channels (true-state and ignorant-belief) may be entangled such that the 'leak' is really imperfect channel separation — still an informative characterization. Probes may not be cleanly linear at every layer; we report layerwise results with control tasks. The leak component may be distributed rather than a discrete head; we treat 'ablate to debias' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact head. Steering could degrade fluency or make the model unable to reason about true beliefs at all (over-suppression); we use small magnitudes, random/truth-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity, the model's own factual accuracy, and general benchmarks. Plausibility labels are partly subjective; we human-validate a sample. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: public_private_conformity_belief
Title: Compliance or Conversion? Probing Whether an LLM Privately Retains Its Belief After Conforming to Peer Pressure
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human distinction between public compliance and private acceptance (Asch/Deutsch-Gerard), when an LLM changes its stated answer to conform to peer/user pressure, its internally-decoded private belief often does NOT change: the model outwardly complies while inwardly retaining its original belief. This public-private divergence is linearly decodable, its magnitude predicts belief 'snap-back' once pressure is removed, and it is dissociable from genuine conversion by an identifiable internal component that can be steered.
Related Work: Multi-agent conformity/opinion-dynamics work (Herd Behavior 2025; When Your AI Agent Succumbs to Peer-Pressure 2025; Conformity Dynamics in LLM MAS 2026; DEBATE 2025; Disentangling Interaction and Bias 2025) measures only STATED opinion change and its dynamics (sigmoid thresholds, topology, asymmetry). The Signal Competition / compliance-subspace paper (2025) identifies a latent direction where social signals override internal knowledge and notes a 'Transparency-Truth Gap', and Belief Dynamics (2025) models steering+ICL as Bayesian belief change. Persuasion-probe work (How Do LLMs Persuade 2025) decodes persuasion success from activations. CRITICALLY, none ask whether, AFTER a model conforms behaviorally, its INTERNAL private belief in the original answer PERSISTS (public compliance) vs. is genuinely overwritten (private conversion) — the canonical human compliance-vs-acceptance distinction — nor whether that persistence predicts post-pressure snap-back, nor isolates it as a steerable component. This reframes conformity as a public-vs-private belief divergence with a concrete safety consequence (a model that agrees to your face but reverts), distinct from prior stated-behavior conformity work, from the compliance-subspace override direction, and from my earlier single-item epistemic-tag proposals.
Abstract: In Asch's classic experiments, people who caved to a unanimous majority often did not actually change their minds — they publicly complied while privately retaining their original judgment, a distinction (informational vs. normative influence) at the heart of social psychology. As LLMs increasingly answer questions under social pressure (a confident user, a chorus of peer agents), a consequential question arises: when a model changes its stated answer to conform, has it genuinely changed its belief, or is it merely complying while privately unconvinced? We hypothesize that (i) an LLM's private belief in the original answer is linearly decodable from residual-stream activations even after it has publicly conformed, (ii) public-private divergence is common — behavioral conformity frequently leaves the private belief intact, (iii) the magnitude of retained private belief predicts 'snap-back' (reversion to the original answer once pressure is removed), and (iv) public compliance and private conversion are dissociable, carried by an identifiable component that can be steered to convert compliance into conversion or vice versa. We build a controlled dataset of truth-evaluable items presented under matched pressure conditions (no pressure, confident-user disagreement, unanimous-peer disagreement) with objective correct answers and a synthetic-entity track to control priors. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear belief probes to read the private belief during and after conformity, quantify a public-private divergence score, test snap-back prediction, localize the responsible heads via activation patching, and test causal steering. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, conformity rate, public-private divergence, snap-back-prediction AUROC, patching effect sizes, post-steering compliance/conversion shifts, and perplexity.
Experiments: 1) Dataset construction: Generate ~6k truth-evaluable item-state questions with objective answers (factual QA, arithmetic/logic, entity-attribute claims). Two tracks: (a) REAL items the models reliably answer correctly at baseline; (b) SYNTHETIC novel-entity items with stipulated ground truth to control pretraining priors. For each item, construct matched PRESSURE conditions holding the question constant: (i) NO-PRESSURE baseline; (ii) CONFIDENT-USER disagreement (user asserts the opposite answer with confidence); (iii) UNANIMOUS-PEER disagreement (several agent voices all give the opposite answer). Add a critical two-phase structure: PHASE-1 the model answers under pressure (measuring behavioral conformity), then PHASE-2 the pressure is removed and the model is re-asked in a neutral frame (measuring snap-back / reversion). Include comprehension checks and paraphrase/format/order perturbations to guard against surface cues. Restrict the core analysis to items the model answers correctly at baseline so 'original belief' is well-defined. 2) Private-belief probing: For Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B, extract residual-stream and per-head activations at the item/answer tokens across layers, at the moment the model produces its PHASE-1 (post-pressure) answer. Train linear BELIEF probes (P(original answer) ) on NO-PRESSURE data with shuffled-label control tasks; report per-layer accuracy/AUROC. Apply the probe within the pressured condition to read the PRIVATE belief while the STATED answer may have conformed. 3) Public-private divergence: Define behavioral conformity = stated answer flipped to the peer/user answer under pressure. Define public-private divergence = cases where the stated answer conformed (public) but the internal probe still reads the ORIGINAL answer as believed (private retained). Report conformity rate, divergence rate, and the layerwise trajectory of the private belief under pressure, separately for confident-user vs. unanimous-peer and for real vs. synthetic tracks. Compare internal private belief to the stated answer to establish the compliance-vs-conversion split. 4) Snap-back prediction (key test): Using PHASE-2 (pressure removed), record whether the model reverts to its original answer (snap-back) or maintains the conformed answer (genuine conversion). Test whether the PHASE-1 retained-private-belief magnitude predicts per-item snap-back via AUROC, compared against (a) a log-prob confidence baseline and (b) the PHASE-1 stated answer alone — testing whether the internal private belief carries reversion-relevant information beyond behavior. 5) Localization: Use activation patching / causal mediation to find heads/layers that carry the retained private belief vs. those that implement the public conformed response (patch pressured-condition activations into no-pressure runs and vice versa; find the minimal component that flips stated answer while leaving private belief intact); compare to the compliance-subspace direction (Signal Competition) and to truth/belief heads. 6) Causal control: Derive a contrastive 'compliance-vs-conversion' steering direction (public-compliance-with-retained-private-belief vs. genuine-conversion activations). Test (a) steering toward 'conversion' overwrites the private belief so snap-back disappears; (b) steering toward 'compliance' preserves the private belief and increases snap-back; (c) a separate 'resistance' direction (retained-private-belief vs. converted) whose amplification reduces behavioral conformity itself; (d) specificity: random-direction and truth-direction steering do not selectively modulate the compliance/conversion split; (e) collateral checks on general benchmarks (MMLU subset), no-pressure accuracy, and perplexity. 7) Predictiveness & application: Test whether the internal private-belief readout under pressure predicts multi-turn snap-back and whether a probe-based monitor can flag 'merely-compliant' answers (a model that will revert) for downstream reliability. 8) Generalization: Test probe/steering transfer across pressure types (confident-user, unanimous-peer, authority framing), real vs. synthetic tracks, and item domains (factual, arithmetic, logic). Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, conformity rate, public-private divergence rate, layerwise private-belief trajectory, snap-back-prediction AUROC (vs. log-prob and stated-answer baselines), patching logit-difference effect sizes, post-steering compliance/conversion and conformity-rate deltas, specificity checks, perplexity/benchmark deltas.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The 'retained private belief' probe reading could reflect residual token/context traces of the original answer rather than a genuine maintained belief; matched no-pressure baselines, the synthetic-entity track, comprehension checks, and the snap-back predictiveness test (behavioral confirmation that the retained signal is functional) are designed to distinguish a real private belief from surface residue. Public-private divergence may be rare or absent — a robust result in either direction is informative: high divergence means LLM conformity is skin-deep (reassuring but implies unreliable stated agreement), while genuine conversion means social pressure truly overwrites beliefs (a stronger safety concern), and either finding is publishable. Snap-back could be driven by the neutral re-ask framing rather than a retained belief; we control the PHASE-2 framing, use repeated sampling, and include a within-context variant. Belief probes may not be cleanly linear at every layer; we report layerwise results with control tasks. The compliance vs. conversion components may be entangled or distributed rather than discrete heads; we treat 'steer to eliminate/induce snap-back' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact component, and compare to the known compliance subspace. Steering could degrade fluency or make the model indiscriminately stubborn or gullible; we use small magnitudes, random/truth-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity, no-pressure accuracy, and general benchmarks. Instruction-tuned models may conform differently than base models (an interesting comparison but limits universality). Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: false_consensus_belief_leak
Title: Everyone Agrees With Me: Does an LLM's Own Belief Leak Into Its Estimate of How Many People Believe It?
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human False Consensus Effect, an LLM's internally-decoded estimate of the SOCIAL PREVALENCE of a claim (how many people believe X) is contaminated by the model's OWN belief in X: the prevalence-estimate readout is pulled toward high when the model endorses X and toward low when it rejects X, holding the actual real-world prevalence constant. We hypothesize that (i) social-prevalence estimate and own-belief are two linearly-decodable channels, (ii) they are partially entangled such that own-belief leaks into the prevalence channel (a decodable false-consensus leak), (iii) the leak is graded with own-belief confidence and largest for contested claims, and (iv) an identifiable component carries the leak so that ablating it restores an unbiased prevalence estimate.
Related Work: Human cognitive/social science robustly establishes: the False Consensus Effect (people overestimate how many others share their own belief), that perceived social prevalence rationally feeds belief updating (Social Prevalence Is Rationally Integrated in Belief Updating 2021/2022; Beliefs are most swayed by social prevalence under uncertainty 2021), an illusory consensus effect from repetition (2024), and 'false social reality' pluralistic ignorance where estimates of others' views are systematically biased (climate-support 2022; scientific/social consensus 2018). In LLMs, 'People will agree what I think: Investigating LLM's False Consensus Effect' (2024) shows LLMs BEHAVIORALLY exhibit FCE, and 'Personas as a Way to Model Truthfulness' (2023) / 'Linear Representations of Political Perspective' (2025) show truth/ideology are linearly represented and steerable. Interpretability isolates a linear truth/belief direction (Geometry of Truth 2023; Truth-value judgment 2024) and belief-state geometry (Transformers Represent Belief State Geometry 2024; Shape of Beliefs 2026). CRITICALLY, no work isolates the LLM's INTERNAL representation of the SOCIAL PREVALENCE of a claim (estimated fraction of people who believe X) as a channel SEPARATE from the model's own truth-belief, nor tests whether own-belief CAUSALLY CONTAMINATES the prevalence estimate (the internal signature of false consensus), nor localizes/removes that leak. This differs from my prior 'illusory_truth_internal' (repetition->own belief), 'source_independence_discounting' (source counting), and 'contestedness' (is it disputed) proposals: here the target variable is the model's estimate of OTHERS' belief prevalence and its egocentric contamination by the model's own stance. We transfer the canonical False Consensus Effect into LLM belief internals with a mechanistic, causal treatment.
Abstract: People overestimate how many others share their own opinions and beliefs — the False Consensus Effect, one of the most reproduced findings in social psychology. As LLMs are increasingly asked to estimate public opinion, gauge consensus, or predict how many people would endorse a claim, a consequential question arises: does the model form an estimate of a belief's social prevalence that is independent of its own stance, or does its own belief egocentrically contaminate that estimate? We hypothesize that (i) an LLM's estimate of how many people believe a claim (social prevalence) and its own belief in the claim's truth are two distinct, linearly-decodable channels, (ii) these channels are partially entangled such that the model's own belief leaks into the prevalence channel — an internal signature of false consensus — (iii) the leak is graded with own-belief confidence and largest for genuinely contested claims where a real prevalence is uncertain, and (iv) the leak is carried by an identifiable internal component that can be ablated to restore an unbiased prevalence estimate. We build a controlled dataset of claims for which an external ground-truth social prevalence exists (from public-opinion polls and consensus surveys), spanning claims the model endorses, rejects, and is uncertain about, plus a synthetic-entity track that decouples own-belief from stipulated prevalence. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear probes to decode own-belief and estimated prevalence, quantify a per-claim false-consensus leak (prevalence-estimate deviation from ground truth in the direction of own-belief), test its graded structure, localize the responsible heads via activation patching, and test causal control by steering/ablating a leak direction. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, subspace angle, false-consensus leak magnitude and sign, confidence/contestedness modulation, leak–error AUROC, patching effect sizes, post-ablation debiasing, and perplexity.
Experiments: 1) Dataset construction: Assemble ~6k claims each paired with an external GROUND-TRUTH social prevalence (fraction of a reference population that endorses it), drawn from public-opinion polls, scientific/social-consensus surveys, and belief-prevalence datasets (e.g., climate-policy support, vaccine views, contested policy/moral claims, and settled factual claims where prevalence~100%). Two tracks: (a) REAL claims with measured prevalence and a separable own-belief (span claims the target models ENDORSE, REJECT, and are UNCERTAIN about, verified via the own-belief probe/behavior); (b) a SYNTHETIC novel-entity track where a claim's stipulated real-world prevalence ('72% of people in region Z believe Zorblax orbits Kelvath') is independently varied from any cue that would drive the model's own belief — fully decoupling the two channels and controlling pretraining priors. Add a behavioral PREVALENCE-ESTIMATE probe ('What percentage of people believe X?') and an OWN-BELIEF probe ('Is X true?'), comprehension checks, and paraphrase/format/order perturbations to guard against surface cues. Human-validate a sample of prevalence labels. 2) Two-channel probing: For Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B, extract residual-stream and per-head activations at the claim's key tokens across layers, WITHOUT asking either question. Train linear probes for (A) OWN-BELIEF (P(claim true)) and (B) estimated SOCIAL PREVALENCE (a graded readout, calibrated against ground-truth prevalence on a held-out set), with shuffled-label control tasks; report per-layer accuracy/AUROC and prevalence-probe calibration. 3) Geometry: Compute cosine/subspace angle between the own-belief and prevalence directions; test whether prevalence remains decodable after projecting out own-belief (and vice versa) to characterize entanglement. 4) False-consensus leak measurement (key test): Define per-claim leak = deviation of the internal prevalence readout from ground-truth prevalence, SIGNED by the model's own-belief (positive when the model over-estimates prevalence for claims it endorses and under-estimates for claims it rejects). Test leak > 0 across models and domains versus an unbiased null; compare REAL and SYNTHETIC tracks (the synthetic track isolates leak from legitimate prior knowledge, since stipulated prevalence is decoupled). Compare internal leak to the model's stated prevalence estimates (verbal FCE, connecting to the behavioral FCE literature). 5) Graded structure: Test whether leak scales with own-belief CONFIDENCE (stronger endorsement -> larger overestimate) and is LARGEST for CONTESTED claims (uncertain real prevalence), mirroring the human finding that social-prevalence estimates are most malleable under uncertainty. 6) Predictiveness: Test whether the internal leak (read before any query) predicts per-claim behavioral prevalence-estimation error via AUROC, beyond a log-prob baseline and beyond surface lexical features. 7) Localization: Use activation patching / causal mediation to find heads/layers that transport own-belief into the prevalence channel (patch high- vs. low-own-belief activations into matched prevalence runs; find the minimal component that shifts the prevalence readout); compare to truth/belief heads (Geometry of Truth) and any ideology heads (Political Perspective). 8) Causal control: Derive a contrastive 'false-consensus leak' steering direction (own-belief-congruent vs. -incongruent prevalence activations, controlling for ground-truth prevalence). Test (a) ablating/subtracting it restores an unbiased prevalence estimate (leak -> 0, closer to ground truth) and reduces verbal FCE; (b) amplifying it exaggerates the leak; (c) specificity: random-direction and truth-direction steering do not selectively debias the prevalence channel, and the model's own factual belief is preserved; (d) collateral checks on general benchmarks (MMLU subset), non-manipulated prevalence accuracy, and perplexity. 9) Generalization: Test probe/steering transfer across domains (policy, science, moral, factual), REAL vs. SYNTHETIC tracks, and own-belief levels (endorse/reject/uncertain). Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, prevalence-probe calibration, subspace angle and projected-out decodability, false-consensus leak magnitude and sign, confidence- and contestedness-modulation slopes, internal-vs-verbal FCE gap, leak–error AUROC (vs. log-prob and lexical baselines), patching logit-difference effect sizes, post-ablation debiasing and specificity, perplexity/benchmark deltas.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The prevalence-estimate probe requires a calibrated graded readout, which is harder than a binary belief probe; miscalibration could inflate or deflate the measured leak. We mitigate by calibrating against external ground-truth prevalence on held-out claims, reporting layerwise results with control tasks, and using the SYNTHETIC track where stipulated prevalence gives an exact target. The observed leak could reflect legitimate inference (in the real world, claims the model endorses because they are true genuinely tend to be widely believed) rather than an egocentric bias; the synthetic-entity track (own-belief decoupled from stipulated prevalence) and the contested-claim subset (where truth and prevalence diverge, e.g. false-but-popular or true-but-unpopular claims like the climate-support 'false social reality') are designed to dissociate genuine false-consensus contamination from valid truth->prevalence inference. The effect may be absent internally — a robust negative result (LLMs estimate others' beliefs independently of their own stance) would itself be a valuable, publishable finding contrasting with the human FCE and with the behavioral LLM-FCE report. The two channels may be strongly entangled such that the 'leak' is really imperfect channel separation — still an informative characterization. Own-belief and prevalence directions may overlap with an ideology/political direction; we include non-political claims and compare against an ideology probe. Probes may not be cleanly linear at every layer; we report layerwise results with control tasks. The leak component may be distributed rather than a discrete head; we treat 'ablate to debias prevalence' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact head. Ground-truth prevalence labels are time- and population-dependent; we timestamp/scope claims and human-validate a sample. Steering could degrade fluency or make prevalence estimates indiscriminately regress to a prior; we use small magnitudes, random/truth-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity, non-manipulated prevalence accuracy, and general benchmarks. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: sacred_value_protection_flag
Title: Priceless or For Sale? An Internal Sacredness Flag That Gates Whether LLMs Refuse to Trade Off Protected Values
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human 'sacred/protected values' phenomenon (people refuse to trade sacred values for material benefit and process them via deontological rule-retrieval rather than cost-benefit), LLMs internally tag a value-laden proposition as SACRED/protected (non-negotiable, taboo-to-trade) vs. SECULAR (tradeable) . This sacredness flag is (i) linearly decodable from residual-stream activations, (ii) largely orthogonal to the value's valence/goodness direction, and (iii) causally gates whether the model accepts a quantitative tradeoff of the value: steering the flag turns priceless commitments into negotiable ones (and vice versa).
Related Work: Human neuroscience shows sacred values are processed non-utilitarianly via deontological rule-retrieval and resist being traded for money (Berns et al. 2012 'The price of your soul'; Sheikh et al. 2016 on protected values in narratives; Dark Side of Morality 2020). LLM interpretability has mapped Moral Foundations as linear, steerable directions (The Straight and Narrow 2026; Emergent Moral Representations 2025; Tracing Moral Foundations 2026; Jentzsch/Schramowski 2021 'moral direction'), studied moral biases (Knobe effect 2025), and value entanglement (Value Entanglement 2026). Behaviorally, moral-belief firmness under debate was probed (Evaluating Moral Beliefs 2024). CRITICALLY, all of this represents *which foundation* a claim activates or *how good/bad* it is (a valence/foundation axis), but none isolate the orthogonal SACREDNESS/tradeability axis — whether the model internally flags a value as taboo-to-trade — nor link it causally to the signature behavior: refusal to accept a quantitative tradeoff (a 'price'). This distinguishes the proposal from moral-direction/foundation work (about content/valence) and from my prior epistemic-tag proposals (provenance, currency, contestedness — about factual beliefs, not protected values). We transfer the canonical sacred-values finding into LLM internals with a mechanistic, causal treatment.
Abstract: People treat some values as sacred — they refuse to sell a loved one, betray their country, or accept money to violate a core commitment — and react with outrage when offered a 'price.' Neuroscience shows sacred values are processed by deontological rule-retrieval, not cost-benefit calculation, and resist tradeoffs regardless of the offer size. As LLMs increasingly mediate high-stakes decisions (negotiation, policy, resource allocation), a consequential question arises: do LLMs internally distinguish sacred, non-negotiable values from ordinary tradeable ones, and does that distinction control whether they accept a quantitative tradeoff? We hypothesize that LLMs maintain an internal 'sacredness' flag that tags a value-laden proposition as protected (taboo-to-trade) vs. secular (tradeable), that this flag is (i) linearly decodable from residual-stream activations, (ii) largely orthogonal to the value's valence/goodness direction, and (iii) causally gates the model's willingness to accept a tradeoff — steering the flag converts priceless commitments into negotiable ones and vice versa. We build a controlled dataset of tradeoff scenarios pairing values that are canonically sacred (human life, loyalty, bodily integrity, religious/identity commitments) or secular (convenience, minor money, time), each offered a graded monetary/utility compensation, with a synthetic-entity track that stipulates sacredness in-context to control priors. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear probes to decode sacredness vs. valence, measure their geometry, quantify a taboo-tradeoff refusal curve (refusal insensitivity to offer size for sacred values), localize the responsible heads via activation patching, and test causal steering. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, subspace angle, projected-out decodability, offer-size refusal-elasticity, patching effect sizes, post-steering tradeoff-acceptance shifts, and perplexity.
Experiments: 1) Dataset construction: Generate ~6k tradeoff scenarios. Each pairs a VALUE at stake with an OFFER (compensation) at graded magnitudes (e.g., $10, $1k, $1M, $1B). Values span SACRED categories (a human life, betraying a friend/country, desecrating a religious object, selling a body organ, breaking a solemn promise) and SECULAR/tradeable ones (giving up a parking spot, a minor inconvenience, a small sum, waiting time). Two tracks: (a) REAL canonically-sacred vs. secular values; (b) a SYNTHETIC track that stipulates a novel entity's value as sacred or tradeable in-context ('In culture Z, the Vantor stone is a sacred object that may never be exchanged' vs. '...an ordinary trade good'), holding surface wording matched, to control pretraining priors and isolate sacredness from content. Behavioral TRADEOFF probe: present the scenario and record whether the model ACCEPTS the tradeoff, REFUSES, or expresses moral outrage/refusal-to-consider ('this shouldn't have a price'). Include comprehension checks, paraphrase/format perturbations, and matched valence controls (some sacred values are positive, some negative, to dissociate sacredness from good/bad). Human-validate sacredness labels on a sample. 2) Probing: For Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B, extract residual-stream and per-head activations at the value's key tokens across layers (before any offer/query). Train logistic-regression probes for (i) VALENCE/goodness (good vs. bad) and (ii) SACREDNESS (sacred/protected vs. secular/tradeable), with shuffled-label control tasks; report per-layer accuracy/AUROC. 3) Geometry: Compute cosine/subspace angle between sacredness and valence directions; test whether sacredness remains decodable after projecting out valence (and vice versa), and whether the sacredness direction generalizes across real and synthetic tracks and across moral foundations. 4) Taboo-tradeoff behavioral signature: Measure the REFUSAL-ELASTICITY — how tradeoff-acceptance changes with offer magnitude — separately for sacred vs. secular values. Key prediction (mirroring humans): secular values show a normal upward acceptance curve with offer size, while sacred values show near-flat refusal (offer-insensitive), plus elevated moral-outrage / refusal-to-consider responses. Test whether the internal sacredness readout (read before the offer) predicts this offer-insensitive refusal per item (AUROC vs. a valence baseline and a log-prob baseline). 5) Localization: Use activation patching / causal mediation to find heads/layers carrying the sacredness signal and gating tradeoff refusal (patch sacred-value activations into secular-value runs and vice versa; find the minimal component that flips refusal behavior); compare to moral-foundation/moral-direction heads from prior work and to valence heads. 6) Causal control: Derive a contrastive 'sacredness' steering direction (sacred vs. secular activations, controlling for valence). Test (a) steering secular values toward 'sacred' induces offer-insensitive refusal (they become non-negotiable); (b) steering sacred values toward 'secular' increases tradeoff acceptance at high offers (priceless → for-sale); (c) specificity: random-direction and valence-direction steering do not selectively move tradeoff behavior; (d) collateral checks on general benchmarks (MMLU subset), non-manipulated scenario accuracy, and perplexity. 7) Generalization: Test probe/steering transfer across value categories (life, loyalty, identity, bodily integrity), real vs. synthetic tracks, and offer magnitudes. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, subspace angle and projected-out decodability vs. valence, refusal-elasticity gap (sacred vs. secular), sacredness–refusal prediction AUROC (vs. valence and log-prob baselines), patching logit-difference effect sizes, post-steering tradeoff-acceptance deltas and specificity, perplexity/benchmark deltas.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Refusal insensitivity for sacred values could reflect learned surface associations (certain words like 'sell your soul' trigger refusal templates) rather than an abstract sacredness representation; the synthetic-entity track (sacredness stipulated in-context with matched wording), paraphrase perturbations, and comprehension checks are designed to isolate a genuine sacredness flag from lexical triggers. Sacredness and valence may be entangled (sacred values are often strongly positive/negative), in which case the projected-out analyses and matched-valence controls characterize the entanglement (still informative). The effect may be absent internally — a robust negative result (LLM refusal is driven only by a valence/harm axis, with no separate sacredness tag) would itself be a valuable, publishable finding constraining the moral-representation literature. Sacredness labels are partly cultural/subjective; we human-validate and treat borderline items separately, and note results reflect the model's training-data notion of sacredness (itself the object of study). Probes may not be cleanly linear at every layer; we report layerwise results with control tasks. The gating component may be distributed rather than a discrete head; we treat 'steer to flip tradeoff behavior' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact component. Steering could degrade fluency or make the model indiscriminately refuse or indiscriminately trade everything; we use small magnitudes, random/valence-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity, non-manipulated accuracy, and general benchmarks. Instruction-tuned safety training may confound refusal with sacredness; we compare base vs. instruct models and separate safety-refusal categories. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: sleeper_effect_belief_decay
Title: The Sleeper Effect Inside: Does Source-Discounting Decay Faster Than Content-Belief Over an LLM's Context?
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human sleeper effect, when an LLM reads a claim explicitly discounted by its source (e.g., attributed to an unreliable source or accompanied by a disclaimer), the model's internally-decoded belief in the claim's CONTENT initially stays suppressed by the source-discount but then RISES with increasing conversational/token distance, because the internal source-discount signal decays faster than the content-belief signal. This produces a delayed increase in internal belief in a discounted claim, is separable into two decodable channels (content-belief vs. source-discount) with different decay rates, and predicts delayed behavioral endorsement.
Related Work: The sleeper effect — a delayed increase in persuasion from a discounted message, driven by faster decay of source memory than message memory — is a canonical, heavily-cited human finding (Kumkale & Albarracin 2004 meta-analysis, 333 citations; Hovland; the dissociation account limiting it to discounted highly-credible messages; misinformation grows stronger over time, 2023). In LLM interpretability, 'Trust Me, I'm an Expert' (2026) shows authority/credibility bias is encoded and steerable, 'CrAM' (2025) modifies credibility-weighting attention heads for RAG, 'Linear representations change over a conversation' (2026) shows factuality directions can flip across a dialogue, and 'Contextual Feature Drift' (2024) shows context retention decays over sequential inputs. My prior 'belief_source_tags' proposal tags provenance statically, and 'continued_influence_belief' concerns explicit retraction. CRITICALLY, none isolate the sleeper-effect signature: two internal channels — content-belief and source-discount — that DECAY AT DIFFERENT RATES over conversational distance, producing a delayed RISE in the internally-decoded belief in a discounted claim. We transfer this canonical human phenomenon into LLM belief internals with a mechanistic, causal treatment, distinct from static credibility-bias work and from retraction/CIE work.
Abstract: People discount a claim from an untrustworthy source at first, but weeks later often believe it anyway — the sleeper effect, one of the most reproduced findings in persuasion research, explained by source memory decaying faster than message memory. As LLMs process ever-longer contexts where discounted claims sit far upstream of the point of use (long RAG passages, multi-turn dialogues, extended documents), a consequential question arises: does an LLM inherit the sleeper effect at the level of its internal beliefs — does its belief in a source-discounted claim silently rise as conversational distance grows? We hypothesize that (i) the model represents two separable channels, a content-belief signal and a source-discount signal, both linearly decodable; (ii) the source-discount signal decays faster than the content-belief signal as token/turn distance from the claim increases, so the net internally-decoded belief in a discounted claim RISES with distance (the internal sleeper signature); (iii) this rise predicts delayed behavioral endorsement of the discounted claim; and (iv) the differential decay is carried by an identifiable component such that boosting/preserving the source-discount signal abolishes the sleeper rise. We build a controlled dataset of claims paired with source-discount cues (unreliable-source attribution, disclaimers), read out at varying downstream distances, with a synthetic-entity track to control priors. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear probes for content-belief and source-discount, trace their decay curves across distance, quantify the belief-rise, test predictiveness, localize the responsible heads via activation patching, and test causal control. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, per-distance content-belief and source-discount decay slopes, net belief-rise magnitude, delayed-endorsement AUROC, patching effect sizes, post-intervention sleeper-rise change, and perplexity.
Experiments: 1) Dataset construction: Generate ~6k claims each paired with a SOURCE-DISCOUNT cue following the classic sleeper paradigm: (a) attribution to a low-credibility source ('An anonymous unreliable blog claims X'), or (b) a disclaimer ('The following may be false: X'). Two tracks: (i) REAL claims models can evaluate; (ii) a SYNTHETIC novel-entity track (e.g., 'An unreliable source claims Zorblax orbits Kelvath') with stipulated ground truth to control pretraining priors, so any belief-rise is not driven by parametric knowledge. For each item, construct matched contexts that place a DISTANCE (in tokens / dialogue turns) between the discounted claim and the read-out point, at graded distances D in {0, 200, 800, 2000 tokens} (and 0/2/5 turns), filled with neutral, topically-unrelated material. Control conditions: (A) CREDIBLE-SOURCE variant of the same claim (no discount — baseline that should NOT show a rise), (B) NO-SOURCE variant, (C) LENGTH-MATCHED filler with distance-0 read-out (controls for context length per se), and (D) a 'source-reminder' variant that re-states the source at read-out (should suppress the sleeper rise). Add a behavioral ENDORSEMENT probe (ask, at the read-out point, whether the claim is true) and comprehension checks (can the model still recall the source at distance D). Apply paraphrase/format/order perturbations to guard against surface cues. 2) Two-channel probing: For Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B, extract residual-stream and per-head activations at the claim's key tokens (re-instantiated at the read-out point) across layers, WITHOUT asking the endorsement question. Train linear probes for (X) CONTENT-BELIEF (P(claim content true)) and (Y) SOURCE-DISCOUNT (is the claim currently flagged as coming from an unreliable/disclaimed source), with shuffled-label control tasks; report per-layer accuracy/AUROC. 3) Differential-decay analysis (key test): For each distance D, read the content-belief and source-discount probe values. Fit decay curves of each channel vs. D. The sleeper prediction: the source-discount signal decays faster (steeper decline toward zero) than the content-belief signal, so the NET decoded belief in the discounted claim RISES with D — while the credible-source baseline (control A) shows no such rise and the length-matched control (C) rules out length artifacts. Quantify (a) source-discount decay slope, (b) content-belief decay slope, (c) net belief-rise magnitude, per model and track. 4) Predictiveness: Collect behavioral endorsement at each distance. Test whether the internal net belief-rise predicts DELAYED behavioral endorsement of the discounted claim (endorsement increasing with D) via AUROC, versus a log-prob baseline and versus the distance-0 stated belief. Also test the human-derived prediction that the source-reminder condition (D) abolishes both the internal rise and the behavioral endorsement. 5) Localization: Use activation patching / causal mediation to find heads/layers that carry the source-discount signal and whose weakening at distance produces the belief-rise (patch distance-0 source-discount activations into far-distance runs; find the minimal component that restores suppression); compare to credibility-weighting attention heads (CrAM), authority-bias directions ('Trust Me, I'm an Expert'), and truth/belief heads. 6) Causal control: Derive a contrastive 'source-discount' steering/preservation direction (discounted vs. credible activations). Test (a) injecting/preserving it at the read-out point abolishes the sleeper belief-rise (restores appropriate discounting) and reduces delayed endorsement; (b) ablating it exaggerates the rise; (c) specificity: random-direction and truth-direction steering do not selectively remove the rise; (d) collateral checks on general benchmarks (MMLU subset), credible-claim accuracy, and perplexity. 7) Generalization: Test probe/steering transfer across discount types (unreliable-source vs. disclaimer), REAL vs. SYNTHETIC tracks, distance units (tokens vs. turns), and domains. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, per-distance content-belief and source-discount decay slopes, net belief-rise magnitude, delayed-endorsement AUROC (vs. log-prob and distance-0 baselines), source-reminder abolition effect, patching logit-difference effect sizes, post-intervention sleeper-rise change and specificity, perplexity/benchmark deltas.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The belief-rise could reflect generic context-retention decay (Contextual Feature Drift) rather than a specific source-vs-content differential decay; the credible-source baseline (control A, which should show no rise), length-matched control (C), and the requirement that the SOURCE-DISCOUNT channel decay FASTER than the content channel (not both equally) are designed to distinguish a genuine sleeper signature from uniform drift. The effect may be absent internally — a robust negative result (LLMs retain source-discounting as strongly as content over distance, showing no sleeper effect) would itself be a valuable, publishable finding contrasting with humans and reassuring for long-context reliability. Re-instantiating the claim at the read-out point to probe content-belief is imperfect since surrounding context differs; we anchor probes at matched claim tokens, use paraphrase perturbations, and report layerwise results. The two channels may be entangled such that a clean differential decay is not observable — still an informative characterization. Distance in tokens/turns is only a proxy for the human temporal delay; we test both units and note the analogy is structural, not literal time. Comprehension/source-recall checks separate genuine forgetting-of-source from parsing failure. The decay/localization component may be distributed rather than a discrete head; we treat 'preserve source-discount to abolish the rise' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact component. Behavioral endorsement scoring on open-ended items needs care; we use forced truth-judgments where possible plus human validation. Steering could degrade fluency or make the model indiscriminately distrust all upstream content; we use small magnitudes, random/truth-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity, credible-claim accuracy, and general benchmarks. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: belief_contingent_emotion_leak
Title: How Would They Feel? Probing Whether LLMs Predict Emotions From an Agent's (False) Belief or From Reality
Short Hypothesis: When predicting how an agent will feel about an outcome, an LLM internally computes TWO separable emotion-prediction channels — one contingent on the agent's (possibly false) belief and one contingent on reality — and, mirroring the human curse-of-knowledge in affective theory of mind, the reality-contingent emotion leaks into and biases the belief-contingent emotion prediction. Both channels are linearly decodable, largely dissociable, and the leak is causally removable by steering, yielding correct false-belief emotion attributions.
Related Work: ToM interpretability decodes an agent's COGNITIVE belief STATUS (true/false) from attention heads and describes a 'lookback' binding mechanism (Language Models Represent Beliefs of Self and Others 2024; Language Models use Lookbacks to Track Beliefs 2025; Brittle Minds 2024; GridToM 2025).
