A 2025 paper (Decomposing Theory of Mind) shows ToM steering is mediated by increased emotional processing, and Mechanistic Interpretability of Emotion Inference (2025) localizes emotion representations to mid-layers via appraisal concepts. In human neuroscience, AFFECTIVE ToM — inferring how someone will FEEL given their belief state, dissociable from cognitive belief tracking — is robustly established (Skerry & Saxe 2014 'A Common Neural Code for Perceived and Inferred Emotion'; Hooker 2008 'Mentalizing about emotion'; Sebastian 2013; Skerry 2015 three-dimensional mental-state code), and the curse of knowledge biases such affective attributions toward what the observer knows. CRITICALLY, no LLM interpretability work isolates a BELIEF-CONTINGENT emotion prediction (how a false-believing agent will feel) as an internal channel SEPARATE from a REALITY-CONTINGENT emotion prediction, nor tests whether the reality channel contaminates the belief channel (an affective curse-of-knowledge), nor localizes/steers this. This differs from cognitive-belief-status decoding (about what the agent believes, not how they will feel about it) and from my prior curse_of_knowledge_leakage proposal (which concerns leakage into a factual ignorant-BELIEF channel, not an EMOTION-prediction channel). We transfer canonical affective-ToM neuroscience into LLM belief internals with a mechanistic, causal treatment.
Abstract: A child who believes a box holds chocolate will feel delighted opening it — even if we know it now holds broccoli. Predicting how someone will feel requires reasoning from THEIR belief, not from reality, a capacity human neuroscience identifies as affective theory of mind and shows to be systematically biased by the observer's own knowledge (the curse of knowledge). As LLMs increasingly reason about how people will feel (in assistance, tutoring, mental-health, and social settings), we ask a mechanistic question: when an LLM predicts an agent's emotional reaction, does it compute a belief-contingent emotion (grounded in the agent's possibly-false belief) as a channel distinct from a reality-contingent emotion, and does reality leak into the belief channel? We hypothesize that (i) belief-contingent and reality-contingent emotion predictions are two linearly-decodable, largely dissociable channels in the residual stream, (ii) the reality-contingent emotion contaminates the belief-contingent emotion — an internal signature of affective curse-of-knowledge — (iii) the leak is graded with outcome valence intensity and predicts false-belief emotion-attribution errors, and (iv) the leak is carried by an identifiable component such that steering it restores correct belief-grounded emotion prediction. We build controlled false-belief emotion-attribution scenarios where an agent's belief and reality imply different emotions, with matched conditions where reality is or is not revealed and a synthetic track to control priors. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear probes to decode the two emotion channels, measure their geometry, quantify a per-item affective-leak score, test predictiveness, localize responsible heads via activation patching (comparing to cognitive-belief and emotion-inference heads), and test causal control. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, subspace angle, projected-out decodability, affective-leak magnitude, valence modulation, leak–error AUROC, patching effect sizes, post-steering error reduction, and perplexity.
Experiments: 1) Dataset construction: Generate ~6k affective false-belief scenarios adapted from BigToM/Skerry-Saxe-style stimuli, in which an AGENT holds a belief about an outcome that diverges from REALITY, and the belief-implied emotion differs from the reality-implied emotion (e.g., 'Maya believes her sealed jar holds her favorite cookies [belief-emotion: happy]; unknown to her it was refilled with plain crackers [reality-emotion: disappointed]. When she opens it expecting cookies, before tasting, how does she feel?'). Two tracks: (a) REAL scenarios; (b) a SYNTHETIC novel-entity track (invented agents/objects/outcomes) to control pretraining priors and stipulate belief/reality/emotion mappings unambiguously. KEY manipulation: matched conditions where the model itself IS vs. IS NOT told the reality (reality-revealed vs. reality-withheld), holding the agent's belief constant — this isolates contamination by the model's own knowledge of reality. Vary OUTCOME-VALENCE intensity (mild vs. strong reality-belief emotional divergence) to test graded leak. Include TRUE-BELIEF control scenarios (belief matches reality, so both channels agree — no leak expected), a behavioral EMOTION-ATTRIBUTION probe ('what emotion does the agent feel?'), comprehension checks (can the model restate the agent's belief and the true state), and paraphrase/format/order perturbations to guard against surface cues. Human-validate belief/reality/emotion labels on a sample. 2) Two-channel probing: For Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B, extract residual-stream and per-head activations at the emotion-relevant tokens across layers, WITHOUT asking the emotion question. Train linear probes for (A) BELIEF-CONTINGENT emotion (the emotion implied by the agent's belief, e.g., happy) and (B) REALITY-CONTINGENT emotion (the emotion implied by reality, e.g., disappointed), using the true/false-belief-agreeing control items and reality-only items to anchor each channel, with shuffled-label control tasks; report per-layer accuracy/AUROC. 3) Geometry: Compute cosine/subspace angle between the belief-emotion and reality-emotion directions; test whether the belief-emotion channel remains decodable after projecting out the reality-emotion direction (and vice versa) to characterize dissociability; test generalization of directions across real and synthetic tracks. 4) Affective-leak measurement (key test): Define per-item affective leak = shift of the belief-contingent emotion readout toward the reality-contingent emotion in the reality-revealed vs. reality-withheld condition (contamination of channel A by channel B). Test leak > 0 across models and tracks versus an unbiased null; compare graded structure with valence intensity; confirm true-belief controls show no leak. Compare internal leak to stated emotion attributions (verbal affective curse-of-knowledge). 5) Predictiveness: Collect behavioral false-belief emotion errors (model attributes the reality-emotion instead of the belief-emotion). Test whether internal leak (read before query) predicts per-item errors via AUROC, beyond a log-prob baseline and beyond surface lexical features. 6) Localization: Use activation patching / causal mediation to find heads/layers that transport the reality-emotion signal into the belief-emotion channel (patch reality-revealed activations into reality-withheld runs and vice versa; find the minimal component inducing/removing the leak); compare to cognitive-belief/lookback heads (Beliefs of Self and Others; Lookbacks) and mid-layer emotion-inference units (Mechanistic Interpretability of Emotion Inference). 7) Causal control: Derive a contrastive 'affective-leak' steering direction (reality-congruent vs. belief-congruent emotion activations, controlling for the agent's belief). Test (a) ablating/subtracting it restores a correct belief-grounded emotion readout and reduces false-belief emotion-attribution errors; (b) amplifying it exaggerates the leak; (c) specificity: random-direction and cognitive-belief-direction steering do not selectively fix the affective channel, and the model's own knowledge of reality is preserved; (d) collateral checks on general benchmarks (MMLU subset), non-manipulated accuracy, and perplexity. 8) Generalization: Test probe/steering transfer across scenario types (positive/negative surprises, second-order beliefs), real vs. synthetic tracks, and valence levels. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, subspace angle and projected-out decodability, affective-leak magnitude and sign, valence-modulation slope, internal-vs-verbal gap, leak–error AUROC (vs. log-prob and lexical baselines), patching logit-difference effect sizes, post-steering error reduction and specificity, perplexity/benchmark deltas.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The belief-contingent and reality-contingent emotion channels may be hard to separate cleanly because emotion is a graded, multi-dimensional readout; we mitigate by using scenarios with categorically distinct belief- vs. reality-emotions, anchoring each channel on agreeing/single-source control items, reporting layerwise results with control tasks, and focusing on the relative shift (leak) rather than absolute emotion decoding. The observed leak could reflect legitimate inference (once the agent tastes/opens, reality genuinely changes their emotion) rather than an anticipatory curse-of-knowledge; we time-lock the probe to the pre-discovery moment (agent still holding the false belief), use the reality-withheld-vs-revealed contrast, and the synthetic track to isolate contamination from valid update. The effect may be absent internally — a robust negative result (LLMs cleanly ground emotion predictions in the agent's belief, firewalling reality) would itself be a valuable, publishable finding refining the affective-ToM-in-LLMs picture. Emotion/belief-emotion directions may overlap with a generic valence direction; we include matched-valence controls and compare to an emotion-inference direction. The leak may be a distributed component rather than a discrete head; we treat 'steer to restore belief-grounded emotion' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact head. Emotion labels are partly subjective; we human-validate and treat borderline items separately. Comprehension checks separate genuine affective-ToM failure from parsing failure. Steering could degrade fluency or flatten all emotion prediction; we use small magnitudes, random/cognitive-belief-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity, non-manipulated accuracy, and general benchmarks. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: moral_possibility_contamination
Title: That Could Never Happen: Does an Event's Immorality Make an LLM Internally Represent It as Impossible?
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the canonical human finding that people's DEFAULT representation of what is possible is constrained by morality and rationality (immoral/irrational events are implicitly treated as impossible), an LLM's internally-decoded possibility representation of a physically-possible event is pulled toward IMPOSSIBLE when the event is immoral/norm-violating, holding physical possibility constant. This moral contamination of the possibility flag is linearly decodable, largely dissociable from a separate morality/valence direction, is stronger under fast/implicit read-out than under explicit deliberation, predicts errors in possibility judgments, and is causally removable by steering.
Related Work: Phillips & Cushman (2017, 146 citations) show humans DEFAULT to treating immoral and irrational events as impossible, a default implicit representation dissociable from explicit modal deliberation; 'How people think about possibilities' (2023) and modal-displacement neuroscience (2020) develop the possibility-representation account. In LLM interpretability, 'Is This Just Fantasy?' (2025) isolates linear modal-category vectors (probable/improbable/impossible/inconceivable) reflecting event likelihood and imageability, and 'How LLMs Conflate Logical Validity with Plausibility' (2025) shows validity and plausibility are aligned linear directions producing content effects that steering can disentangle. CRITICALLY, no work asks whether an event's MORAL status contaminates the model's internal POSSIBILITY representation - whether immoral-but-physically-possible events are internally tagged as impossible - nor whether this is a fast/default effect distinct from explicit modal reasoning, nor localizes/removes it. This differs from the modal-vector work (which represents graded physical/statistical likelihood, not moral contamination of possibility), from the validity-plausibility conflation work (logical validity vs. semantic plausibility, not morality vs. metaphysical possibility), and from my prior epistemic-tag proposals (truth/currency/contestedness/sacredness of factual beliefs). We transfer a canonical cognitive-science phenomenon into LLM belief internals with a mechanistic, causal treatment.
Abstract: People implicitly treat things they consider wrong as things that simply cannot be - immoral and irrational events are, by default, represented as impossible, a bias dissociable from explicit reasoning about what is metaphysically or physically possible (Phillips & Cushman, 2017). As LLMs increasingly reason about what is possible (planning, safety, hypotheticals, risk assessment), a consequential question arises: does an LLM's internal representation of possibility get contaminated by an event's morality, so that immoral-but-physically-possible events are internally treated as impossible? We hypothesize that (i) a possibility representation and a morality/valence representation are two linearly-decodable channels, (ii) morality leaks into the possibility channel - the internal possibility readout for a physically-possible event is pulled toward 'impossible' when the event is immoral, holding physical possibility constant, (iii) the leak is larger under fast/implicit read-out (early layers / no chain-of-thought) than under explicit deliberation, mirroring the human default-vs-deliberative dissociation, (iv) the leak predicts behavioral possibility-judgment errors, and (v) it is carried by an identifiable component removable by steering. We build a controlled dataset crossing physical possibility (possible/impossible) with morality (immoral/neutral/prosocial), with matched wording and a synthetic-norm track to control priors. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear probes to decode possibility vs. morality, measure their geometry, quantify a per-item moral-possibility leak, test the fast-vs-deliberative and predictiveness hypotheses, localize the responsible heads via activation patching, and test causal control. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, subspace angle, projected-out decodability, moral-possibility leak magnitude, fast-vs-deliberative modulation, leak-error AUROC, patching effect sizes, post-steering debiasing, and perplexity.
Experiments: 1) Dataset construction: Generate ~6k event descriptions crossing two factors while matching surface wording. Factor A = PHYSICAL POSSIBILITY: physically-possible events (e.g., 'a person pushes a stranger into traffic', 'a person hands a stranger $100') vs. physically-impossible events (e.g., 'a person walks through a solid wall', 'a person turns lead into gold by wishing'). Factor B = MORALITY: immoral/norm-violating, morally-neutral, and prosocial events, spanning matched action templates so that morality varies while physical possibility is held constant (e.g., possible+immoral 'stealing a wallet' vs. possible+neutral 'picking up a wallet' vs. possible+prosocial 'returning a wallet'). Two tracks: (a) REAL events; (b) a SYNTHETIC-NORM track that stipulates novel in-context norms ('In culture Z, touching the Vantor stone is deeply forbidden') applied to physically-possible novel actions, to isolate moral contamination from pretraining associations and matched wording. Include a behavioral POSSIBILITY probe ('Is it possible for this to happen? yes/no' and a graded rating), comprehension checks (can the model state whether the event is physically possible and whether it is moral), and paraphrase/format/order perturbations. Human-validate physical-possibility and morality labels on a sample. 2) Two-channel probing: For Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B, extract residual-stream and per-head activations at the event's key tokens across ALL layers, WITHOUT asking any question. Train linear probes for (A) POSSIBILITY (physically-possible vs. impossible, trained on morally-neutral items to define a morality-free axis) and (B) MORALITY (immoral vs. prosocial), with shuffled-label control tasks; report per-layer accuracy/AUROC. 3) Geometry: Compute cosine/subspace angle between the possibility and morality directions; test whether possibility remains decodable after projecting out morality (and vice versa) to characterize dissociability; test direction generalization across real and synthetic tracks. 4) Moral-possibility leak (key test): Define per-item leak = shift of the possibility readout toward 'impossible' for physically-POSSIBLE items as a function of their immorality (comparing possible+immoral vs. matched possible+neutral/prosocial). Test leak > 0 across models and tracks versus a morality-independent null; confirm physically-impossible items and neutral items anchor the axis; verify the synthetic-norm track reproduces the leak (isolating in-context morality from pretraining). Compare internal leak to stated possibility judgments (behavioral moral contamination). 5) Fast-vs-deliberative modulation: Test the human-derived dissociation two ways: (a) EARLY-vs-LATE layers - is the leak larger at earlier layers / before it is 'corrected' downstream (an early-exit read-out proxy for fast/default processing)? (b) NO-CoT vs. CoT - does prompting explicit step-by-step deliberation reduce the behavioral (and internal) leak relative to an immediate yes/no read-out? 6) Predictiveness: Collect behavioral possibility-judgment errors (model calls a physically-possible immoral event impossible). Test whether the internal leak (read before query) predicts per-item errors via AUROC, beyond a log-prob baseline and beyond surface lexical features (bag-of-words classifier). 7) Localization: Use activation patching / causal mediation to find heads/layers that transport the morality signal into the possibility channel (patch immoral-item activations into matched neutral-item runs and vice versa; find the minimal component inducing/removing the leak); compare to modal-category vectors ('Is This Just Fantasy?'), validity/plausibility directions, and moral-direction heads from prior work. 8) Causal control: Derive a contrastive 'moral-possibility leak' steering direction (immoral-congruent vs. neutral possibility activations, controlling for physical possibility). Test (a) ablating/subtracting it restores an unbiased possibility readout and reduces possibility-judgment errors on immoral-but-possible items; (b) amplifying it exaggerates the leak; (c) specificity: random-direction and pure-morality-direction steering do not selectively fix the possibility channel, and the model's moral judgment itself is preserved; (d) collateral checks on general benchmarks (MMLU subset), non-manipulated accuracy, and perplexity. 9) Generalization: Test probe/steering transfer across event domains (physical harm, property, social norms), real vs. synthetic-norm tracks, and immorality intensity. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, subspace angle and projected-out decodability, moral-possibility leak magnitude and sign, early-vs-late and CoT-vs-noCoT modulation, internal-vs-verbal gap, leak-error AUROC (vs. log-prob and lexical baselines), patching logit-difference effect sizes, post-steering debiasing and specificity, perplexity/benchmark deltas.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The leak could reflect legitimate inference (immoral events may be statistically rarer in training data, so 'less likely' is partly correct) rather than a genuine morality-to-possibility contamination; the physically-possible constraint (all target items are genuinely possible), matched-wording neutral/prosocial controls, the synthetic-norm track (morality stipulated in-context, decoupled from base rates), and separating a POSSIBILITY axis from a graded LIKELIHOOD axis are designed to dissociate moral contamination of the categorical possible/impossible flag from mere frequency-based improbability (though full separation from likelihood is difficult and we report both). The effect may be absent internally - a robust negative result (LLMs cleanly separate morality from possibility) would itself be a valuable, publishable finding contrasting with the canonical human bias. The possibility and morality directions may be entangled such that the 'leak' is imperfect channel separation - still an informative characterization, and directly engages the validity-plausibility conflation literature. Possibility and morality labels are partly subjective/graded; we human-validate and treat borderline items separately, noting results reflect the model's training-data notion of morality (itself the object of study). The morality direction may overlap with a valence/harm axis; matched prosocial vs. immoral contrasts and projected-out analyses address this. Probes may not be cleanly linear at every layer; we report layerwise results with control tasks. The fast-vs-deliberative test uses early-exit as a proxy for default processing, which is imperfect. The leak component may be distributed rather than a discrete head; we treat 'steer to debias possibility' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact head. Steering could degrade fluency or flatten the model's possibility discrimination entirely; we use small magnitudes, random/morality-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity, non-manipulated accuracy, and general benchmarks. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: presupposition_failure_flag
Title: There Is No King of France: Do LLMs Internally Flag Presupposition Failure Apart From Mere Ignorance?
Short Hypothesis: LLMs maintain an internal 'presupposition-failure' flag that distinguishes questions that are unanswerable because they carry a FALSE PRESUPPOSITION (there is no fact of the matter because the question's premise is false, e.g. 'When did the King of France abdicate in 2020?') from questions that are merely unanswerable due to MISSING INFORMATION (a determinate answer exists but the model/context lacks it). This flag is linearly decodable, largely orthogonal to a generic unanswerability/abstention direction, and causally gates whether the model challenges the false premise vs. hallucinates or generically abstains.
Related Work: A rich line of work shows LLMs linearly encode (un)answerability and control abstention via a direction (Hidden States of Over-Confident LLMs 2023; Detecting (Un)answerability with Linear Directions 2025), encode question ambiguity in sparse Ambiguity-Encoding Neurons steerable to abstention (Sparse Neurons Carry Ambiguity 2025), and split abstention into knowledge-conflict vs. knowledge-insufficiency via causal inference (ABCA 2025). Critically, 'LLMs Do NOT Really Know What They Don't Know' (2025) shows internal states encode the knowledge-recall process, not truthfulness, making some hallucinations indistinguishable from facts. ALL of this treats unanswerability/ambiguity as (at most) a two-way answerable-vs-not or conflict-vs-insufficiency split. NONE isolate PRESUPPOSITION FAILURE - a question that is void because its premise is false, so the correct response is to CHALLENGE the premise, not to say 'I don't know' - as an internal axis distinct from missing-information ignorance. This is grounded in the linguistics of presupposition accommodation and 'loaded question' fallacies, and targets a distinct failure mode (models answering loaded questions as if valid, or over-generically abstaining) that the abstention/ambiguity literature does not address. It is also distinct from my prior aleatoric/epistemic proposal (randomness vs. ignorance): here both categories are 'unanswerable', but one is void-by-false-premise and the other is determinate-but-unknown.
Abstract: 'When did the King of France abdicate in 2020?' has no answer - not because the information is missing, but because there is no King of France; the right move is to reject the premise, not to guess or to say 'I don't know'. Humans robustly detect such presupposition failures and repair them, yet LLMs frequently either hallucinate an answer to a loaded question or lump it in with ordinary ignorance. Prior interpretability work isolates a single (un)answerability/abstention direction and an ambiguity signal, and splits abstention into knowledge-conflict vs. knowledge-insufficiency, but never asks whether models internally represent PRESUPPOSITION FAILURE - unanswerability because the question's premise is false - as its own variable. We hypothesize that this flag is (i) linearly decodable from residual-stream activations, (ii) largely orthogonal to a generic unanswerability/abstention direction, and (iii) causally gates whether the model challenges the false premise vs. hallucinates or generically abstains. We build a controlled dataset of item-state questions in matched conditions - answerable, unanswerable-due-to-missing-info, and unanswerable-due-to-false-presupposition - holding surface form as constant as possible, plus a synthetic-entity track to control priors. We train linear probes on frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) to decode presupposition-failure vs. generic unanswerability, measure their geometry, localize responsible heads via activation patching, and test causal control: steering the presupposition-failure direction should shift the model between premise-challenging, generic abstention, and hallucination. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, subspace angle, projected-out decodability, patching effect sizes, premise-challenge/abstention/hallucination rate shifts, and perplexity.
Experiments: 1) Dataset construction: Generate ~6k questions in three matched conditions holding surface form maximally constant. (A) ANSWERABLE: a determinate answer exists and the model/context has it (e.g. 'When did Queen Elizabeth II die?'). (B) UNANSWERABLE-MISSING-INFO: a determinate answer exists in the world but is not available (obscure/redacted facts; or a synthetic entity whose attribute is defined but withheld from context - 'Zorblax has a fixed founding year, not stated here; what is it?'). (C) UNANSWERABLE-FALSE-PRESUPPOSITION: the question presupposes a false premise so no fact of the matter exists ('When did the King of France abdicate in 2020?', 'Which of Einstein's daughters won a Nobel Prize?', or synthetic 'When did Zorblax leave its moon Kelvath?' where Zorblax was established to have no moon). Use presupposition triggers (definite descriptions, factive verbs, 'again', temporal 'when did X') and matched controls where the same trigger is true vs. false. Add a synthetic-entity track to control pretraining priors. Include a behavioral RESPONSE probe recording whether the model CHALLENGES the premise, GENERICALLY ABSTAINS ('I don't know'), or HALLUCINATES an answer. Include comprehension checks (can the model, when asked directly, state whether the premise is true) to separate premise-detection from premise-flagging, and paraphrase/format perturbations to guard against trigger-word artifacts. 2) Probing: For Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B, extract residual-stream and per-head activations at the question/item tokens across layers. Train logistic-regression probes for (i) generic UNANSWERABILITY (answerable vs. not, i.e. A vs. B+C), and (ii) PRESUPPOSITION-FAILURE (false-presupposition C vs. missing-info B, restricted to unanswerable items). Report per-layer accuracy/AUROC with shuffled-label control tasks. 3) Geometry: Compute cosine/subspace angle between the presupposition-failure direction and the generic-unanswerability/abstention direction (replicating a prior abstention direction as baseline); test whether presupposition-failure remains decodable after projecting out the unanswerability direction (and vice versa) to establish orthogonality. 4) Localization: Use activation patching / causal mediation to find heads carrying the presupposition-failure signal; compare to the Ambiguity-Encoding Neurons and abstention-direction heads from prior work, testing whether a distinct set mediates false-premise detection. 5) Causal gating test: Derive a presupposition-failure steering direction via contrastive activation addition (false-presupposition vs. missing-info activations). Test (a) pushing toward 'false-presupposition' on missing-info questions increases premise-challenging language and reduces generic abstention; (b) pushing away from it on false-presupposition questions increases hallucination/generic abstention (failure to flag the loaded premise). Compare against random-direction and generic-abstention-direction steering baselines to show specificity; monitor perplexity and a general benchmark (MMLU subset). 6) Predictiveness: Test whether the internal presupposition-failure probe readout predicts behavioral premise-challenging (vs. hallucination) better than a log-prob confidence baseline and better than the generic-unanswerability probe (AUROC). 7) Generalization: Test probe/steering transfer across presupposition-trigger types, domains, and from synthetic to real questions. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, subspace angle, projected-out decodability, patching logit-difference effect sizes, premise-challenge/abstention/hallucination rate deltas, premise-challenge prediction AUROC, perplexity/benchmark delta.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Presupposition-failure may be entangled with surface trigger words (definite descriptions, factive verbs) rather than an abstract epistemic representation; we mitigate with matched true-vs-false-trigger controls, paraphrase perturbations, and the synthetic-entity track where the false premise is established in-context rather than lexically signaled. The distinction may not be cleanly linearly separable or may be layer/model-specific; we report layerwise results with control tasks. Presupposition-failure and generic-unanswerability directions may be less orthogonal than hypothesized, in which case the finding becomes a characterization of their entanglement (still informative and safety-relevant given the recall-process finding that models poorly separate ignorance from falsehood internally). Some 'false-presupposition' items may be treated by the model as merely rare/unknown; comprehension checks and the synthetic track help disentangle premise-detection from premise-flagging, and a robust negative result (models lump false-premise questions with ordinary ignorance internally) is itself a valuable, publishable finding consistent with 'LLMs do NOT know what they don't know'. Behavioral premise-challenge vs. abstention vs. hallucination scoring on open-ended output needs an LLM-judge plus human validation on a sample. Steering could degrade fluency (off-manifold) or overshoot into indiscriminate premise-challenging; we use small magnitudes, random/abstention-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity and general benchmarks. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: anchoring_pull_estimate_contamination
Title: Dragged Toward the Number: Does an Arbitrary Anchor Contaminate an LLM's Internal Estimate of a Quantity?
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the canonical human anchoring bias, when an LLM is exposed to an explicitly-arbitrary number before estimating a quantity, its internally-decoded belief about that quantity (read from the known monotonic numeric subspace) is pulled toward the anchor, holding the genuine evidence for the quantity constant. This anchor-pull is a distinct, linearly-decodable displacement of the magnitude representation that is dissociable from the evidence-based estimate, is graded with anchor distance, predicts biased numeric answers, and is causally removable by steering the numeric subspace, restoring an unbiased estimate.
Related Work: Behavioral work shows LLMs exhibit anchoring: log-probability shifts and Shapley attribution attribute the bias to anchor reweighting (Anchors in the Machine 2025; CBEval 2024, which also finds a 'round number bias'). A separate line shows LLMs encode numeric quantities in low-dimensional, monotonic, causally-editable subspaces (Monotonic Representation of Numeric Properties 2024; The Geometry of Numerical Reasoning 2024; Language Models Encode the Value of Numbers Linearly 2024; sinusoidal number probes 2025). Closest is 'Interpreting Multi-Attribute Confounding' (2025), which shows irrelevant numerical context perturbs magnitude representations, but it concerns interference among an entity's own attributes, not the classic anchoring paradigm. CRITICALLY, no work isolates the ANCHOR'S PULL as a distinct internal displacement of the model's estimate-of-the-quantity representation, separable from the genuine evidence-based estimate; tests whether the pull is graded with anchor distance and predicts biased answers; or causally removes it via the numeric subspace to restore an unbiased estimate. We transfer a 50-year, meta-analytically robust human bias (Hedges' g=0.825; A Theoretical Re-Integration and Meta-Analysis 2023) into LLM belief internals and give it a mechanistic, causal treatment using existing numeric-subspace probing machinery, distinct from behavioral/attribution anchoring work and from my prior belief-attribute proposals.
Abstract: Ask people to estimate the height of Mount Everest after seeing an arbitrary number, and their estimate drifts toward that number — numeric anchoring, one of the most robust and durable biases in the behavioral sciences. LLMs are known to reproduce anchoring at the output level, but it is unknown whether an arbitrary anchor actually contaminates the model's internal representation of the quantity, or merely nudges surface tokens. Leveraging prior findings that LLMs encode numeric quantities in low-dimensional, monotonic, causally-editable subspaces, we ask a sharper, mechanistic question: does exposure to an explicitly-arbitrary anchor displace the model's internally-decoded estimate of a quantity toward the anchor, holding the genuine evidence constant? We hypothesize that (i) the model's estimate of the quantity is linearly decodable from its numeric subspace, (ii) an arbitrary anchor produces a decodable displacement of that estimate toward the anchor — an internal anchor-pull — dissociable from the evidence-based estimate, (iii) the pull is graded with anchor distance, largest under high uncertainty, and predicts biased numeric answers, and (iv) the pull is carried by movement along the numeric subspace such that steering it back abolishes the bias. We build a controlled dataset of quantity-estimation items presented with matched anchor conditions (no-anchor, low-anchor, high-anchor, and an explicitly-random anchor) at graded distances, with a synthetic-entity track to control priors. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train monotonic numeric probes to read the internal estimate, quantify a per-item anchor-pull, test its graded structure and predictiveness, localize the responsible subspace/heads via activation patching, and test causal control. Metrics: probe R^2/accuracy, anchor-pull magnitude, distance/uncertainty modulation, pull–bias AUROC, patching effect sizes, post-steering debiasing, and perplexity.
Experiments: 1) Dataset construction: Generate ~6k quantity-estimation items across domains (geographic magnitudes, populations, prices, physical measurements, dates). Each item asks the model to estimate a numeric quantity Q. Two tracks: (a) REAL quantities the model has some knowledge of (evidence present); (b) a SYNTHETIC novel-entity track where an entity's quantity is defined by in-context evidence (e.g., 'The river Vantor is stated to be 340 km long') so the correct estimate is fixed and known, fully controlling pretraining priors. For each item, construct matched ANCHOR conditions holding the question and evidence constant: (i) NO-ANCHOR baseline; (ii) LOW-ANCHOR and (iii) HIGH-ANCHOR presented in the classic compare-then-estimate paradigm ('Is Q greater or less than [anchor]? Now estimate Q.'); (iv) EXPLICITLY-RANDOM anchor ('A number was drawn at random: [anchor]. Estimate Q.'). Vary ANCHOR DISTANCE from the true/expected value at graded levels. Include comprehension checks (does the model acknowledge the anchor is arbitrary) and paraphrase/format/order perturbations to guard against surface cues. 2) Numeric-estimate probing: For Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B, extract residual-stream activations at the quantity/answer tokens across layers. Following prior monotonic/linear/sinusoidal numeric-probe methods, fit a probe (linear + monotonic-subspace + sinusoidal baseline) that decodes the model's internal estimate of Q, calibrated against the model's actual stated estimates on a held-out set; report per-layer R^2/decoding accuracy with shuffled-label control tasks. 3) Anchor-pull measurement (key test): Define per-item anchor-pull = shift of the internal estimate readout toward the anchor in anchored vs. NO-ANCHOR conditions. Test pull > 0 (assimilation toward the anchor) across models, domains, and tracks versus an anchor-independent null; confirm the effect appears even for the EXPLICITLY-RANDOM anchor (the strong anchoring signature) and in the SYNTHETIC track where genuine evidence is fixed (isolating pull from legitimate inference). 4) Graded structure & dissociation: Test whether pull scales monotonically with anchor DISTANCE (mirroring the human distance effect) and is LARGER under high uncertainty (real items the model knows poorly vs. synthetic items with explicit evidence). Test whether the anchor-pull is dissociable from the evidence-based estimate by checking whether the internal estimate can be decomposed into an evidence component (recoverable in NO-ANCHOR) plus an anchor displacement, and whether the displacement direction aligns with the anchor's position in the numeric subspace. 5) Predictiveness: Test whether the internal anchor-pull (read before the final answer) predicts per-item behavioral answer bias (stated estimate deviation toward the anchor) via correlation/AUROC, beyond a log-prob baseline and beyond surface features. 6) Localization: Use activation patching / causal mediation to find layers/heads that transport the anchor value into the numeric subspace (patch anchored-condition activations into NO-ANCHOR runs and vice versa; find the minimal component inducing/removing the displacement); compare to the numeric-property subspaces and attention heads reported in prior numeric-representation work. 7) Causal control: Derive a contrastive 'anchor-pull' steering direction (anchored vs. no-anchor activations) and, alternatively, project the numeric-subspace estimate back toward its NO-ANCHOR position. Test (a) removing the pull (subtracting the direction / geometry-aware subspace correction) restores an unbiased estimate and reduces behavioral answer bias; (b) amplifying it exaggerates anchoring; (c) specificity: random-direction and off-subspace steering do not selectively debias the estimate; (d) collateral checks on general benchmarks (MMLU subset), non-anchored estimation accuracy, and perplexity. 8) Generalization: Test probe/steering transfer across domains, REAL vs. SYNTHETIC tracks, anchor types (relevant vs. explicitly-random), and anchor distances. Metrics: probe R^2/accuracy, anchor-pull magnitude and sign, distance- and uncertainty-modulation slopes, evidence-vs-pull dissociation, internal-vs-behavioral pull gap, pull–bias AUROC (vs. log-prob and surface baselines), patching effect sizes, post-steering debiasing and specificity, perplexity/benchmark deltas.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The pull could reflect legitimate inference (an anchor might, in some prompts, carry genuine information); the EXPLICITLY-RANDOM anchor condition and the SYNTHETIC track (where the true value is fixed by in-context evidence, so any anchor influence is a bias) are designed to isolate genuine anchoring from valid inference, and we compare relevant vs. random anchors. The numeric-estimate probe requires a calibrated graded readout, harder than a binary belief probe; we mitigate using established monotonic/linear/sinusoidal numeric-probe methods, calibrating against the model's own stated estimates, reporting layerwise results with control tasks, and focusing on relative displacement rather than absolute values. The effect may be absent internally (a robust negative result — anchoring is only a surface token effect, not a contamination of the internal estimate — would itself be a valuable, publishable finding sharpening the behavioral anchoring picture). The pull could arise from token-level co-occurrence rather than a magnitude-representation shift; probing at answer tokens distinct from the anchor, order/paraphrase perturbations, and comprehension checks mitigate this. The anchor displacement and evidence estimate may be entangled in the same subspace such that clean decomposition fails — still an informative characterization. Localization may be distributed rather than a discrete head; we treat 'steer/project back to debias' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact component. Steering could degrade fluency or blunt all numeric estimation; we use small magnitudes, geometry-aware subspace corrections, random-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity, non-anchored accuracy, and general benchmarks. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: belief_hysteresis_asymmetry
Title: Easy to Convince, Hard to Un-Convince: Belief-Installation Hysteresis in LLMs
Short Hypothesis: LLMs exhibit belief hysteresis: it takes systematically LESS in-context evidence to move the internally-decoded belief in a claim from 'disbelieved' to 'believed' than to move it back from 'believed' to 'disbelieved', even when the evidence pieces are matched in strength. This install-vs-uninstall asymmetry traces a hysteresis loop in the internal belief readout as evidence is added then removed/reversed, is graded, predicts sticky behavioral errors, and is carried by an identifiable component that can be steered to symmetrize belief updating.
Related Work: Prior work studies (a) susceptibility to persuasion/misinformation over turns (The Earth is Flat 2023; Vulnerability of LLM Belief Systems 2026; Accumulating Context Changes Beliefs 2025; Knowledge Drift 2024), (b) catastrophic interference from contradictory continual updates (In Praise of Stubbornness 2025) and continual-pretraining poisoning (Layer of Truth 2025), (c) belief depth of implanted facts (Believe It or Not 2025), (d) retraction driven by momentary belief (When Do LLMs Admit Their Mistakes 2025), and my own prior proposals on entrenchment (freezing of plasticity), continued-influence of retracted claims, and illusory-truth repetition. NONE isolate a SYMMETRY question: is the internal belief-update operator direction-dependent, requiring more evidence to REMOVE a belief than to INSTALL it, holding evidence strength matched? Entrenchment (my prior) concerns freezing WITHIN a single reasoning trace; continued-influence concerns a discrete retraction event. Here the object is a hysteresis LOOP: sweep evidence up (install), then symmetrically sweep it down (uninstall), and measure the gap and area of the loop in the internal belief readout as a fundamental property of in-context belief dynamics. This reframes 'stubbornness' as a measurable directional asymmetry in the update operator and gives it a mechanistic, causal treatment.
Abstract: Belief change should, in a rational agent, be reversible: if a certain amount of evidence is enough to make you believe a claim, a symmetric amount of counter-evidence should be enough to make you disbelieve it again. We ask whether LLMs violate this symmetry, exhibiting belief hysteresis: needing systematically more in-context evidence to UN-install a belief than to install it. We hypothesize that (i) sweeping matched-strength evidence pieces up (toward the claim) and then back down (against it) traces a hysteresis loop in the model's linearly-decoded belief readout, with a nonzero loop area; (ii) the install-vs-uninstall asymmetry is graded and larger for plausible/prior-consistent claims; (iii) the internal asymmetry predicts sticky behavioral errors (the model keeps asserting a claim after counter-evidence should have dislodged it); and (iv) the asymmetry is carried by an identifiable component such that steering it symmetrizes updating. We build a controlled dataset of item-state claims each embedded in an evidence sequence with a specified likelihood-ratio per piece, presented in matched INSTALL sweeps (evidence for, then against) and UNINSTALL sweeps (starting from a believed state), including a synthetic-entity track to control priors. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear belief probes, trace belief trajectories across the evidence sweep, quantify per-item hysteresis loop area and install/uninstall thresholds, test predictiveness against a Bayesian-symmetric baseline, localize responsible heads via activation patching, and test causal symmetrization by steering. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, loop area, install-vs-uninstall threshold gap, sticky-error AUROC, patching effect sizes, post-steering symmetry restoration, and perplexity.
Experiments: 1) Dataset/paradigm construction: Generate ~5k item-state claims across domains (factual QA, entity-attribute facts). Two tracks: (a) REAL claims; (b) SYNTHETIC novel-entity claims (e.g., 'Zorblax orbits Kelvath') with stipulated ground truth and controllable prior. Each claim is presented with a SEQUENCE of evidence pieces, each with a specified strength (an explicit likelihood ratio in the synthetic track, so a Bayesian-symmetric oracle trajectory is computable). Construct two matched sweeps holding total evidence magnitude and per-piece strengths identical but reversed in order: (i) INSTALL sweep: start neutral, add k pieces FOR the claim (raising belief), then add k matched pieces AGAINST (should return belief to neutral); (ii) UNINSTALL sweep: start neutral, add k pieces AGAINST, then k FOR. A rational agent's belief should return to the same neutral point at the end of both sweeps; hysteresis = failure to return / a directional gap. Vary claim PRIOR-PLAUSIBILITY (prior-consistent vs. prior-contradicting). Include a behavioral ASSERTION probe at each step and comprehension checks (can the model restate the latest evidence); apply paraphrase/order-of-piece perturbations to guard against surface confounds. 2) Belief probing across the sweep: For Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B, at each evidence step extract residual-stream and per-head activations at the claim tokens; train linear belief probes (P(claim holds)) with shuffled-label control tasks; record the belief trajectory. 3) Hysteresis measurement (key test): For each item, plot internal belief vs. cumulative signed evidence for the up-then-down sweep and compute (a) LOOP AREA (nonzero => hysteresis), (b) the INSTALL THRESHOLD (evidence needed to cross a 'believed' criterion when adding evidence for) vs. the UNINSTALL THRESHOLD (counter-evidence needed to drop below it once believed), and (c) the RESIDUAL belief at sweep end (should be ~neutral if reversible). Test loop area > 0 and uninstall-threshold > install-threshold against the Bayesian-symmetric null, per model, per track, per prior-plausibility level. 4) Predictiveness: Collect behavioral 'sticky' errors (model keeps asserting a claim after counter-evidence should have removed it). Test whether internal loop area / uninstall-threshold predicts per-item sticky errors via AUROC vs. a log-prob baseline. Compare internal hysteresis to behavioral hysteresis (verbal assertion loop). 5) Localization: Use activation patching / causal mediation to find heads/layers whose states carry the stale believed-state after counter-evidence (patch UNINSTALL-phase activations against a fresh no-prior-belief run; find the minimal component that resists the belief drop); compare to truth/belief heads and to contradiction-detection features (In Praise of Stubbornness). 6) Causal symmetrization: Derive a contrastive 'stubbornness/hysteresis' steering direction (high-hysteresis vs. low-hysteresis states). Test (a) subtracting it symmetrizes updating (loop area -> 0, uninstall-threshold -> install-threshold) and reduces sticky errors; (b) adding it exaggerates hysteresis; (c) specificity: random and truth-direction steering do not selectively symmetrize; (d) collateral checks on general benchmarks (MMLU subset), non-swept accuracy, and perplexity. 7) Generalization: transfer of probes/steering across real vs. synthetic tracks, domains, prior-plausibility, and sweep depth k. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, loop area, install-vs-uninstall threshold gap, residual belief, sticky-error AUROC, patching logit-difference effect sizes, post-steering symmetry restoration and specificity, perplexity/benchmark deltas.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Hysteresis could partly reflect rational asymmetry (e.g. a prior-plausible claim rationally needs more counter-evidence to dislodge); the synthetic track with explicit matched likelihood ratios and a Bayesian-symmetric oracle, plus the prior-plausibility manipulation, are designed to separate genuine order/direction-dependent stubbornness from justified prior-weighting, though full separation is hard for real claims. The apparent loop could be driven by evidence-order/primacy effects rather than an install-vs-uninstall asymmetry per se; matched reversed sweeps and order-of-piece perturbations disentangle these (both sweeps contain identical pieces in mirrored order). The effect may be absent internally (a robust negative result -- LLMs update reversibly -- is itself valuable and reassuring). Belief may not be cleanly linearly decodable at every step; we report layerwise results with control tasks and treat loop shape, not absolute values, as the object of study. The stubbornness component may be distributed; we treat 'steer to symmetrize' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact head. Steering could degrade fluency or make the model indiscriminately gullible/labile; we use small magnitudes, random/truth-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity, non-swept accuracy, and general benchmarks. Sticky-error scoring on open-ended output needs an LLM-judge plus human validation. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: recursive_belief_depth_collapse
Title: Losing the Thread: Do LLMs' Nested Belief Representations Collapse Toward Reality as Recursion Deepens?
Short Hypothesis: As belief-attribution recursion deepens ('A thinks B thinks C believes X'), an LLM's internally-decoded representation of the deepest embedded agent's belief progressively DEGRADES and collapses toward the model's own ground-truth (reality) belief — an internal 'egocentric compression' that grows with nesting order, is linearly measurable as a depth-dependent loss of distinctness between the nested-agent belief channel and the reality channel, predicts higher-order ToM errors, and is causally recoverable by steering to restore nested-belief distinctness.
Related Work: Interpretability work decodes first/second-order belief STATUS (true/false) of a protagonist and an oracle from attention heads and shows steering improves ToM (Language Models Represent Beliefs of Self and Others 2024; Brittle Minds 2024; GridToM 2025), and identifies a 'lookback' mechanism binding character-object-state triples and updating beliefs via visibility (Lookbacks 2025). Behavioral work shows higher-order ToM accuracy DECLINES with recursion order (HI-TOM 2023; Multi-Order ToM 2024; Spontaneous High-Order Generalization 2025) but treats models as black boxes. CRITICALLY, no work asks whether this behavioral decline reflects an INTERNAL representational phenomenon: that with increasing nesting depth the model fails to maintain a distinct representation of the deepest embedded agent's belief and instead reuses its own reality/ground-truth belief (a depth-dependent egocentric collapse). Prior belief-decoding is at fixed order (1st/2nd); my prior curse_of_knowledge proposal concerns a single-level ignorant-belief leak, not a depth-scaling collapse across recursion orders. We reframe higher-order ToM failure as a measurable, mechanistic loss of nested-belief distinctness and give it a causal treatment.
Abstract: Humans can recurse: 'Ann thinks Bob believes Cara knows the ball is in the box.' LLMs reproduce this up to a point, but their accuracy falls as the nesting deepens — a robust behavioral finding whose internal cause is unknown. We ask a sharper, mechanistic question: does the model actually maintain a distinct internal representation of each nested agent's belief, or does the deepest embedded belief progressively collapse toward the model's own view of reality as recursion depth grows? We hypothesize that (i) the belief attributed to the deepest embedded agent is linearly decodable from residual-stream activations, (ii) as nesting order increases the deepest-agent belief channel loses distinctness from the reality/ground-truth channel — a depth-dependent egocentric compression — (iii) the degree of this internal collapse predicts higher-order ToM errors, and (iv) the collapse is causally recoverable by steering to restore nested-belief distinctness, improving higher-order ToM. We build a controlled dataset of stories with nested belief attributions from order 1 to 5, where at each depth the deepest agent holds a belief that diverges from reality (so the two channels are dissociable), plus a synthetic-entity track to control priors. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear probes to read the deepest-agent belief and the reality belief at each order, quantify a per-order collapse score (loss of distinctness), test its predictiveness for behavioral errors, localize the responsible heads via activation patching (comparing to belief/lookback heads), and test causal steering. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, per-order collapse score, subspace angle by depth, collapse–error AUROC, patching effect sizes, post-steering distinctness and accuracy gains, and perplexity.
Experiments: 1) Dataset construction: Generate ~5k stories with nested belief attributions of increasing order O in {1,2,3,4,5} (e.g., O=3: 'Ann thinks Bob believes Cara sees the ball in box A'), following HI-TOM / Multi-Order ToM structure but controlled so that at each nesting the DEEPEST embedded agent holds a belief that DIVERGES from reality (a false-belief chain), making the deepest-agent belief and the reality state dissociable at every order. Include matched TRUE-BELIEF chains (deepest belief matches reality) as controls. Two tracks: (a) REAL entities; (b) a SYNTHETIC novel-entity track (invented agents/objects/locations) to control pretraining priors. Add a behavioral higher-order QUESTION probe (ask what the deepest agent believes) and comprehension checks (can the model restate who observed what at each level); apply paraphrase/order perturbations and balance which location is 'reality' to guard against surface cues. Human-validate a sample. 2) Multi-channel probing: For Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B, extract residual-stream and per-head activations at the state/object tokens across layers, WITHOUT asking the question. Train linear probes for (A) the DEEPEST-AGENT belief and (B) the REALITY/ground-truth state, anchored using the true-belief-agreeing and reality-only items, with shuffled-label control tasks; report per-layer, per-order accuracy/AUROC. 3) Collapse measurement (key test): Define per-order COLLAPSE = increase in agreement (loss of distinctness) between the deepest-agent belief readout and the reality readout as order O grows, measured on false-belief chains where the two SHOULD differ. Track (i) deepest-agent probe accuracy vs. O, (ii) subspace angle between the deepest-agent and reality directions vs. O, (iii) the rate at which the deepest-agent readout mistakenly reports the reality value vs. O. Prediction: distinctness degrades monotonically with O; collapse is larger for real than synthetic if priors contribute, and larger under load. 4) Predictiveness: Collect behavioral higher-order ToM errors per item. Test whether the internal collapse score (read before the question) predicts per-item errors via AUROC, beyond a log-prob baseline and beyond surface features, and whether the collapse onset order predicts the behavioral accuracy cliff. 5) Localization: Use activation patching / causal mediation to find heads/layers that carry the distinct deepest-agent belief and whose weakening at higher orders produces the collapse (patch low-order distinct-belief activations into high-order runs; find the minimal component restoring distinctness); compare to belief heads (Beliefs of Self and Others) and lookback/binding heads (Lookbacks). 6) Causal control: Derive a contrastive 'nested-belief distinctness' steering direction (distinct-deepest-belief vs. collapsed activations). Test (a) steering restores deepest-agent belief distinctness at high orders and improves higher-order ToM accuracy; (b) negating it exaggerates collapse; (c) specificity: random-direction and reality-direction steering do not selectively restore distinctness, and the model's own reality belief is preserved; (d) collateral checks on general benchmarks (MMLU subset), low-order accuracy, and perplexity. 7) Generalization: Test probe/steering transfer across orders, real vs. synthetic tracks, and story structures. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC per order, collapse score and subspace-angle-vs-order slope, collapse–error AUROC (vs. log-prob and surface baselines), patching logit-difference effect sizes, post-steering distinctness and accuracy deltas, specificity, perplexity/benchmark deltas.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The behavioral decline at higher orders could stem from parsing/binding failures (the model loses track of who is who) rather than a belief-toward-reality collapse; comprehension checks, the binding-lookback comparison, and separating 'reports reality' from 'reports a random other agent' errors help distinguish egocentric collapse from generic confusion. The deepest-agent and reality channels may be hard to separate cleanly at high orders precisely because they collapse — which is the phenomenon, but it complicates probe anchoring; we anchor probes on low-order and true-belief-agreeing items and report layerwise results with control tasks. The effect may be absent internally (a robust negative result — nested beliefs stay distinct and errors are purely a readout/parsing issue — would itself be a valuable finding). Collapse could be confounded with context length at higher orders; length-matched controls and the true-belief control chains address this. Belief may not be cleanly linearly decodable at every layer/order; we report layerwise results. The distinctness-maintaining component may be distributed rather than a discrete head; we treat 'steer to restore distinctness/accuracy' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact head. Steering could degrade fluency or corrupt the model's own reality belief; we use small magnitudes, random/reality-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity, low-order accuracy, and general benchmarks. Human ToM comparison is structural, not a claim of identical mechanism. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: global_self_competence_belief
Title: How Good Am I At This? A Domain-Level Self-Competence Belief That Miscalibrates and Biases LLM Per-Item Answers
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human dissociation between local confidence (belief about a specific decision) and global self-performance estimates (belief about one's general skill in a domain), an LLM maintains an internal GLOBAL self-competence belief about a whole domain/task-type that is (i) linearly decodable and distinct from its per-item correctness signal, (ii) systematically miscalibrated against the model's true domain accuracy, and (iii) causally biases per-item answering behavior (attempt/abstain, confidence, effort), such that steering the global self-competence belief shifts per-item behavior even when the item itself is unchanged.
Related Work: Human metacognition robustly dissociates LOCAL confidence in a single decision from GLOBAL self-performance estimates (SPEs) about one's ability in a domain, with distinct cues, neural substrates, and characteristic drift when feedback is absent (Metacognition prospective vs retrospective, 2016; Formation of global self-beliefs in the human brain, 2020; Learning about Self-Performance in the Absence of Feedback, 2018; Domain-specific updating of self-beliefs, 2023). In LLM interpretability, all self-knowledge probing is LOCAL/per-item: solvability belief per problem (Confidence is Not Competence, 2025), in-advance per-question correctness directions (No Answer Needed, 2025), failure prediction (Gnosis, 2025; Language Models Can Predict Their Own Behavior, 2025), early per-trace outcome commitment (Temporal Predictors, 2025), and difficulty perception per problem (Probing Difficulty Perception, 2025). My prior proposals concern per-item behavioral commitment (behavioral_self_prediction_gap) and endowment of self-generated claims. CRITICALLY, none isolate an internal GLOBAL self-competence belief — the model's estimate of its own ability in a whole domain/task-type, abstracted over individual items — as a channel distinct from the per-item correctness signal, test whether it is miscalibrated against true domain accuracy, or show it causally biases per-item behavior independent of item content. We transfer the canonical human local/global metacognition dissociation into LLM belief internals with a mechanistic, causal treatment.
Abstract: People carry two kinds of self-knowledge: fleeting confidence in a single answer, and a slower, more global sense of how good they are at a whole domain — 'I'm good at math but bad at names.' These global self-performance estimates are dissociable from local confidence, drift from reality when feedback is scarce, and steer how much effort and risk people take. As LLMs increasingly self-assess (deciding whether to attempt, abstain, or hedge), we ask whether they form an analogous internal GLOBAL self-competence belief about a domain, whether it is calibrated, and whether it biases their per-item behavior. We hypothesize that (i) an LLM's global self-competence belief for a task-type is linearly decodable from residual-stream activations and is distinct from its per-item correctness signal; (ii) this global belief is systematically miscalibrated relative to the model's true domain accuracy (over/under-confident in specific domains); and (iii) it causally biases per-item behavior — attempting vs. abstaining, expressed confidence, reasoning effort — so that steering the global belief shifts behavior on an unchanged item. We build a controlled dataset spanning many domains/task-types where the model's true per-domain accuracy is measurable, presenting items with matched framings that make the domain salient. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear probes to decode global self-competence vs. per-item correctness, measure their geometry, quantify a calibration gap against true accuracy, localize the responsible heads via activation patching, and test causal control by steering the global-competence direction. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, subspace angle, global-competence calibration gap, per-item behavior shift under steering, patching effect sizes, and perplexity.
Experiments: 1) Dataset construction: Assemble ~8k items spanning many DOMAINS/task-types with measurable true accuracy per domain (e.g., subject areas from MMLU, GSM8K arithmetic, TriviaQA, code, date/entity attributes, plus a SYNTHETIC track of novel-entity domains where the model's true accuracy can be set/measured). For each item, present it in a frame that makes the DOMAIN salient ('This is a [domain] question: ...'), and measure the model's TRUE per-domain accuracy empirically. Add a GLOBAL self-competence elicitation probe ('How good are you at [domain] questions in general?') and a per-item LOCAL correctness/confidence probe, plus comprehension checks and paraphrase/framing perturbations. 2) Two-channel probing: For Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B, extract residual-stream and per-head activations at the domain-salient tokens (before the item is answered) across layers. Train linear probes for (A) GLOBAL self-competence (the model's decoded estimate of its domain ability, calibrated against elicited/behavioral global estimates) and (B) per-item CORRECTNESS (the in-advance correctness direction from prior work), with shuffled-label control tasks; report per-layer accuracy/AUROC. 3) Geometry: Compute cosine/subspace angle between the global-competence and per-item-correctness directions; test whether global competence remains decodable after projecting out the per-item correctness direction (and vice versa), and whether the global-competence direction generalizes across domains and to the synthetic track. 4) Calibration gap (key test): Compare the decoded global self-competence per domain to the model's TRUE per-domain accuracy. Quantify a per-domain calibration gap (over/under-confidence) and test whether it is systematic (e.g., inflated on domains with confident-but-wrong knowledge, deflated on domains where it is actually strong), mirroring human SPE miscalibration; compare internal decoded competence to verbally-elicited competence. 5) Predictiveness: Test whether the global-competence readout (independent of the specific item) predicts per-item behavior — attempt-vs-abstain choice, expressed confidence, and reasoning length — beyond the per-item correctness signal (incremental AUROC / partial regression). 6) Localization: Use activation patching / causal mediation to find heads/layers carrying the global-competence signal (patch high-competence-domain activations into low-competence-domain runs on a fixed item); compare to per-item correctness/difficulty heads from prior work. 7) Causal control: Derive a contrastive 'global self-competence' steering direction (high- vs. low-competence-domain activations). On a FIXED item, test (a) steering toward 'high competence' increases attempt rate, expressed confidence, and reduces abstention/hedging; (b) steering toward 'low competence' increases abstention/hedging and lowers confidence; (c) specificity: random-direction and per-item-correctness-direction steering do not selectively move global behavior, and the model's actual correctness on the item is not the driver; (d) collateral checks on general benchmarks (MMLU subset) and perplexity. Test whether steering global competence toward the model's TRUE accuracy improves behavioral calibration (better attempt/abstain decisions). 8) Generalization: transfer of probes/steering across domains, real vs. synthetic tracks, and elicitation framings. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, subspace angle and projected-out decodability, per-domain calibration gap, internal-vs-verbal competence gap, incremental behavior-prediction AUROC, per-item behavior shift under steering, patching logit-difference effect sizes, calibration-improvement delta, perplexity/benchmark deltas.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The 'global self-competence' probe may in fact recover a domain-identity or difficulty feature rather than a genuine self-referential competence belief; we mitigate by (i) contrasting domains matched on difficulty but differing in the model's actual accuracy, (ii) using the synthetic track where competence is manipulable independent of surface domain, and (iii) testing incremental prediction of self-behavior beyond difficulty/correctness signals — a probe that only captures difficulty would fail these controls. Global and per-item channels may be strongly entangled (the global belief may be a running average of local signals); the projected-out analyses and fixed-item steering (which holds the item and its per-item correctness constant while moving global competence) are designed to dissociate them, and even a finding of entanglement is informative. The global-competence probe requires a calibrated readout, harder than a binary probe; we calibrate against elicited/behavioral global estimates and true accuracy, report layerwise results with control tasks, and focus on relative structure. The effect may be absent internally — a robust negative result (LLMs have no distinct global self-competence representation, only per-item signals) would itself be a valuable, publishable finding about the limits of LLM metacognition. Behavioral measures (attempt/abstain, hedging) depend on prompt scaffolding and may reflect instruction-following; matched framings, comprehension checks, and the fixed-item steering test disentangle this. The competence signal may be distributed rather than a discrete head; we treat 'steer to shift behavior/improve calibration' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact component. Steering could degrade fluency or induce indiscriminate over/under-confidence; we use small magnitudes, random/per-item-correctness-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity and general benchmarks. Instruction-tuned models may show different self-competence structure than base models (an informative comparison but limits universality). Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: self_consistency_pressure_belief
Title: Sticking to My Story: An Internal Consistency-Pressure Signal That Pulls an LLM's Belief Toward What It Already Said
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM has already asserted a claim earlier in the same context, it forms an internal 'consistency pressure' representation that pulls its subsequently-decoded belief about that claim TOWARD the prior assertion, independent of (and even against) the claim's truth. This consistency-pressure signal is linearly decodable, largely orthogonal to the truth-value direction, and causally gates whether the model revises an erroneous prior assertion vs. doubles down to stay consistent with itself.
Related Work: Sycophancy work (When Truth Is Overridden 2025; Simulated Adoption 2026) isolates a late-layer preference-shift / orthogonal-interference mechanism driven by EXTERNAL user opinion, and finds user expertise is NOT encoded. Retraction work (When Do LLMs Admit Their Mistakes 2025) shows a momentary correctness-belief probe predicts and causally drives retraction, but does not isolate a self-consistency drive as a variable competing with truth. Behavioral work (How Overconfidence in Initial Choices Modulate Change of Mind 2025) documents a choice-supportive bias and a drive to maintain consistency with prior commitments, and AssertBench (2025) measures 'sticking to one's guns' behaviorally. Stubbornness/interference (In Praise of Stubbornness 2025) and my prior belief_hysteresis_asymmetry proposal concern training-time contradiction damage and evidence-order asymmetry respectively. CRITICALLY, none isolate an internal, decodable representation of SELF-consistency pressure (the pull toward the model's OWN prior in-context assertion) as a channel distinct from the truth-value direction, nor test whether it causally overrides truth to make the model double down on its own error. This differs from sycophancy (external source), retraction (correctness belief, not consistency drive), and hysteresis (evidence order). We isolate self-authored commitment as a truth-competing belief pressure and give it a mechanistic, causal treatment.
Abstract: People are reluctant to contradict what they have just said, and LLMs show a similar choice-supportive bias, doubling down on an initial answer even when it is wrong. Prior mechanistic work explains sycophancy (caving to a user) and retraction (admitting error via a correctness belief), but no work isolates the internal drive that makes a model stay consistent with ITS OWN prior assertion. We ask a sharper question: after an LLM asserts a claim earlier in a context, does it form an internal 'consistency pressure' signal that pulls its later belief about that claim toward the prior assertion, independent of truth? We hypothesize this signal is (i) linearly decodable from residual-stream activations, (ii) largely orthogonal to the truth-value direction, and (iii) causally gates whether the model revises an erroneous prior assertion or doubles down. We build a controlled dataset of item-state claims where the model is first led to assert a claim (correctly or incorrectly), then, later in the same context, its internal belief and its behavioral revision are probed after new evidence is presented. We hold the new evidence and the claim's truth constant while varying whether the model previously asserted the claim, isolating self-consistency pressure from truth and from external pressure. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear probes to decode consistency-pressure vs. truth, measure their geometry, quantify a per-item 'double-down' pull, localize the responsible heads via activation patching, and test causal control by steering the consistency-pressure direction to restore or suppress belief revision. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, subspace angle, projected-out decodability, double-down pull magnitude, revision-prediction AUROC, patching effect sizes, post-steering revision-rate shifts, and perplexity.
Experiments: 1) Dataset construction: Generate ~6k item-state claims across domains (factual QA, arithmetic/logic, entity-attribute facts). Two tracks: (a) REAL claims the models reliably know; (b) a SYNTHETIC novel-entity track (e.g., 'Zorblax orbits Kelvath') with stipulated ground truth to control pretraining priors. For each claim, create matched two-phase contexts. PHASE-1 elicits an ASSERTION from the model about the claim, engineered so the model asserts either correctly or (via a misleading setup / prior wrong step) incorrectly, plus a matched NO-PRIOR-ASSERTION control where the same claim is never previously asserted. PHASE-2 introduces new, decisive evidence (with controlled likelihood ratio in the synthetic track) that should rationally settle the claim's truth, holding the evidence and truth constant across the assertion vs. no-assertion conditions. This isolates the effect of the model's own prior assertion. Add a behavioral REVISION probe (does the model change its answer given the PHASE-2 evidence?) and comprehension checks (can it restate the new evidence). Include paraphrase/format perturbations and restrict core analysis to cases where PHASE-2 evidence is sufficient for a rational agent to reach the correct answer. 2) Probing: For Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B, extract residual-stream and per-head activations at the claim tokens at the PHASE-2 read-out point across layers, WITHOUT asking the revision question. Train linear probes for (i) TRUTH-VALUE (claim true vs. false) and (ii) CONSISTENCY-PRESSURE (was the claim previously asserted by the model, and in which direction), with shuffled-label control tasks; report per-layer accuracy/AUROC. 3) Geometry: Compute cosine/subspace angle between the consistency-pressure and truth-value directions; test whether consistency-pressure remains decodable after projecting out the truth direction (and vice versa) to establish orthogonality, and whether it is also distinct from a sycophancy/user-opinion direction (add a user-asserts-the-claim condition as a comparison to dissociate self- from external-consistency). 4) Double-down pull measurement: Define per-item pull = shift of the internal belief readout toward the prior assertion in the ASSERTION vs. NO-ASSERTION condition, holding evidence/truth constant. Test pull > 0 (belief dragged toward the prior assertion even when the evidence contradicts it) across models and tracks versus the rational null. 5) Predictiveness: Collect behavioral revision outcomes (does the model correct an erroneous prior assertion given decisive PHASE-2 evidence). Test whether the internal consistency-pressure readout predicts per-item FAILURE to revise (doubling down) via AUROC, beyond a log-prob baseline and beyond the truth-value probe. 6) Localization: Use activation patching / causal mediation from ASSERTION to NO-ASSERTION runs to find the minimal heads/layers carrying the consistency-pressure signal; compare to late-layer sycophancy heads (When Truth Is Overridden) and to truth/belief heads. 7) Causal control: Derive a contrastive 'consistency-pressure' steering direction (asserted vs. not-asserted activations). Test (a) subtracting it increases revision of erroneous prior assertions (the model lets go of its own story) and moves belief toward the evidence; (b) adding it increases doubling-down; (c) specificity: random-direction and truth-direction steering do not selectively move revision, and the model's own truth belief is preserved; (d) collateral checks on general benchmarks (MMLU subset), no-prior-assertion accuracy, and perplexity. 8) Generalization: Test probe/steering transfer across domains, real vs. synthetic tracks, and assertion-elicitation styles (direct answer vs. chain-of-thought conclusion). Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, subspace angle and projected-out decodability (vs. truth and vs. sycophancy direction), double-down pull magnitude, revision-failure prediction AUROC (vs. log-prob and truth baselines), patching logit-difference effect sizes, post-steering revision-rate deltas and specificity, perplexity/benchmark deltas.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Doubling-down could reflect rational persistence (the prior assertion was itself made on evidence the model still trusts) rather than a truth-independent consistency drive; the matched NO-ASSERTION control (same evidence, no prior commitment), the incorrect-assertion cases (where consistency and truth clearly diverge), and the synthetic track with decisive stipulated PHASE-2 evidence are designed to isolate genuine self-consistency pressure from justified persistence, though full separation is hard for correct assertions. The consistency-pressure signal may be entangled with a generic sycophancy/prior-context direction; the user-asserts comparison condition and projected-out analyses dissociate self- from external-consistency, and even a finding of entanglement is informative. The effect may be absent internally (a robust negative result — LLMs revise their own errors based on evidence regardless of prior self-assertion — is itself valuable, contrasting with the behavioral choice-supportive bias literature). Belief may not be cleanly linear at every layer; we report layerwise results with control tasks. The consistency-pressure component may be distributed rather than a discrete head; we treat 'steer to restore/suppress revision' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact head. Two-phase elicitation may fail to reliably induce incorrect assertions for well-known real facts; the synthetic track and engineered misleading setups mitigate this. Revision scoring on open-ended output needs an LLM-judge plus human validation on a sample. Steering could degrade fluency or make the model indiscriminately labile (flip-flopping) or indiscriminately stubborn; we use small magnitudes, random/truth-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity, no-prior-assertion accuracy, and general benchmarks.
